lessons.notes_html:
Chemistry is the study of matter, including its composition, properties, structure and interactions with other matter and energy.

A scientist who understands chemistry is called a chemist. Chemists work in many subfields, such as physical, biochemistry, organic, inorganic and analytical chemistry.

Chemistry is crucial for understanding the natural world:

  • Earth (solids) — minerals in the Earth.
  • Air (gases) — atmospheric gases.
  • Sea (liquids) — properties of seawater.
  • Sky (plasma) — ions and molecules in plasma states.

Chemists study the composition, structure and changes of matter in these environments. These subjects connect with geology, meteorology and oceanography, but chemistry explains the interactions and transformations of matter within these systems. This interdisciplinary approach improves our understanding and our ability to address environmental challenges on our planet.

Plasma, sometimes called the fourth state of matter, makes up over 99% of the visible universe, including stars and lightning.

Remember: melting of ice is a physical change, but rusting of iron is a chemical change. Do not confuse the two.

Key Points

  • Chemistry is the study of matter, its composition, properties, structure and interactions with other matter and energy.
  • A person who understands chemistry is a chemist.
  • Chemistry explains Earth (solids), air (gases), sea (liquids) and sky (plasma).
  • Plasma makes up over 99% of the visible universe.
  • Chemistry plays a vital role in medicine, agriculture, materials science and environmental protection.
lessons.title: What is Chemistry?

Subfields

Subfields are specialised branches within a single discipline. Examples are organic chemistry, inorganic chemistry and analytical chemistry.

Interdisciplinary Fields

Interdisciplinary fields combine knowledge and methods from various disciplines to address complex problems. Examples in chemistry include biochemistry, physical chemistry and environmental chemistry.

lessons.notes_html:
Biochemistry: Studies the structure, composition and chemical reactions of substances found in living organisms. It focuses on biomolecules — carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids — and explains metabolic processes such as energy production, biosynthesis and disease-related changes.

Medicinal Chemistry: A specialised branch that focuses on the design, synthesis and development of pharmaceutical compounds. It combines organic chemistry, biochemistry and pharmacology to study how chemical substances interact with biological systems for therapeutic purposes.

Polymer Chemistry: Focuses on the synthesis, structure, properties and uses of polymers, large molecules made of repeating units called monomers. It includes natural polymers (proteins, cellulose, rubber) and synthetic polymers (plastics, fibres, resins). Synthetic polymers such as nylon are used in parachutes, ropes and medical sutures due to their exceptional strength and flexibility.

Geochemistry: The study of the chemical composition of Earth, focusing on how elements are distributed and transported within rocks, soils, water and the atmosphere. It explains geological processes through chemical principles and the cycles of elements.

Environmental Chemistry: Examines the chemical composition of the environment and the effects of human activities on it. It includes the study of pollutants, toxic substances and chemical processes in air, water and soil, to protect and improve environmental quality. It helps in pollution control and climate change.

Analytical Chemistry: Deals with the separation, identification and quantification of chemical components in a sample. Qualitative analysis tells what substances are present. Quantitative analysis tells how much of each is present.

Key Points

  • Biochemistry studies chemical substances and reactions in living organisms.
  • Medicinal chemistry designs and develops pharmaceutical compounds (medicines).
  • Polymers are large molecules made of repeating units called monomers.
  • Geochemistry studies the chemical composition of rocks, soils, water and the atmosphere.
  • Environmental chemistry studies pollutants in air, water and soil.
  • Analytical chemistry identifies a sample and measures how much of each substance it contains.

lessons.notes_html:
Physical Chemistry: Applies the laws and theories of physics to study the structure of matter and the changes it undergoes. It includes the behaviour of gases, liquids and solids, thermodynamics, kinetics, quantum chemistry and spectroscopy. It studies the behaviour of matter on the atomic and molecular level.

Organic Chemistry: Focuses on covalent compounds of carbon and hydrogen (hydrocarbons) and their derivatives. It includes natural and synthetic compounds, with applications in petroleum, petrochemicals and pharmaceuticals.

Inorganic Chemistry: Deals with all elements and their compounds, except most carbon-hydrogen compounds. It has wide applications in materials such as ceramics, glass, cement and metallurgy.

Nuclear Chemistry: Explores radioactivity, nuclear reactions and the chemical effects of radiation. It includes atomic energy, nuclear reactors, radiotherapy, food preservation and isotopic studies.

Astrochemistry: The study of the chemical composition and reactions of matter in outer space, including stars, planets, interstellar clouds and cosmic dust. It connects chemistry and astronomy to explain the origin of elements and molecules in the universe. This is the branch that studies planets and stars.

Industrial Chemistry (from the Essential Questions): How is soap produced? Write a simple word equation for the saponification process.

Essential Questions

  • Biochemistry: Why is water essential for living organisms?
  • Analytical Chemistry: How can we accurately determine the chemical composition of a sample?
  • Physical Chemistry: How does temperature affect the rate of a chemical reaction?
  • Organic Chemistry: What is a hydrocarbon? Provide an example.
  • Nuclear Chemistry: How does a nuclear reaction differ from a chemical reaction?
  • Astrochemistry: What is the composition of space? Can chemicals exist in space?

In your body: calcium ions (Ca2+) not only make up part of your bones and teeth, but also play an essential role in muscle contraction and nerve signalling.

Key Points

  • Physical chemistry applies the laws of physics to the behaviour of matter.
  • Organic chemistry studies carbon and hydrogen compounds (hydrocarbons) and their derivatives.
  • Inorganic chemistry deals with all elements and compounds except most carbon-hydrogen compounds.
  • Nuclear chemistry studies radioactivity and nuclear reactions.
  • Astrochemistry studies matter in stars, planets and interstellar clouds.
  • Every branch of chemistry is driven by its own essential questions.

lessons.notes_html:
Science, technology and engineering are interconnected, working together to help us understand and improve the world around us.

Science

Science is the systematic process of discovering new knowledge through observation, experimentation and analysis. It aims to understand and explain the principles and laws that govern the natural world, living organisms and natural phenomena. Scientists formulate theories by conducting experiments and collecting and analysing data to develop hypotheses and draw conclusions. Fields include chemistry, physics, astronomy and environmental science.

Applications: physics helps us understand electromagnetic waves, which enable internet, phone calls and videos. Newton Laws of Motion guide spacecraft and missiles. Atomic energy is used to produce clean and efficient power. Chemistry creates new materials such as strong composites and plastics, and is essential for developing medicines. Astronomy allows us to study stars and planets and employs satellites for communication and navigation.

Technology

Technology involves applying scientific knowledge and tools for practical purposes, aiming to solve problems and enhance our lives. It includes the creation of physical objects, new materials, systems and devices. It can be applied in engineering, social sciences, medicine, agriculture and architecture.

Applications: nanotechnology employs tiny materials to create innovative devices and medicines. Renewable energy technologies use solar panels, wind turbines and hydroelectric plants to generate clean energy. Medical imaging technologies such as X-rays and MRI scans enable doctors to visualise the inside of the body.

Engineering

Engineering involves the design, construction, testing and maintenance of structures, machines and systems to solve problems and fulfil specific requirements. Engineers apply principles of science, mathematics and creativity. Disciplines include civil, software, mechanical and electrical engineering.

Applications: mechanical engineering designs engines and machines that transform energy into work. Electrical engineering develops electrical systems for power and communication. Materials engineering creates new materials with unique properties for use from construction to aerospace.

Key Points

  • Science discovers new knowledge through observation and experiments, e.g. testing how substances react.
  • Technology applies science to create useful tools, such as microscopes or mobile phones.
  • Engineering applies science and technology to design and create functional structures, such as bridges, machines or water cleaning systems.
  • Science provides the foundational knowledge; engineering applies that knowledge to develop practical solutions.
lessons.title: Science, Technology and Engineering

lessons.notes_html:
Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass. It has both mass and volume.

Examples of matter: water, air, trees, stones, animals, plants, carbon, silver, gold, diesel, petrol and stars — all are different types of matter because they have both mass and volume.

Ancient philosophers suggested that all matter, whether living or non-living, was made up of five basic elements: earth, air, fire, water and sky. Modern scientists classify matter based on its physical and chemical characteristics.

Matter is classified in two ways:

  • By physical properties (state): solids, liquids, gases and plasma.
  • By chemical properties (composition): elements, compounds and mixtures.

In science, emotions and ideas such as love, hate, affection or thoughts are NOT classified as matter, because they do not have measurable mass or volume. These are considered abstract concepts. Sound is also not matter.

Key Points

  • Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space (has volume).
  • Water, air, trees, silver and stars are all matter.
  • Love, hate, thoughts and sound are not matter — they have no measurable mass or volume.
  • By state, matter is solid, liquid, gas and plasma.
  • By composition, matter is elements, compounds and mixtures.
lessons.title: What is Matter?

lessons.notes_html:
The study of macroscopic properties helps us distinguish among solids, liquids and gases.

Properties of Solids

A solid has a definite shape and volume. Examples: diamond, urea, ice, sucrose, paper, vegetables, fruits, wood and rocks. Crystalline solids have definite geometric shapes.

  • Density: Particles (atoms, ions or molecules) are very close, tightly packed and more ordered than liquids, so solids are slightly denser than liquids and much denser than gases.
  • Compressibility: Generally incompressible. Foam, wood and cork only seem compressible — pressure compresses the air spaces in them, the solid matter itself remains unchanged.
  • Fluidity: Particles are locked in place, so solids cannot flow (they are rigid) and retain their shape and volume.
  • Kinetic Energy: Lower than liquids and gases, and directly proportional to temperature.
  • Diffusion: Solid particles do not readily diffuse; diffusion in solids is very slow, even under high pressure.

Properties of Liquids

A liquid has a definite volume but lacks a definite shape. Examples: water, blood, mercury, diesel, vegetable oil and milk.

  • Density: Molecules are closely packed with negligible empty space, so liquids are generally denser than gases but usually less dense than solids.
  • Compressibility: Generally considered incompressible; slightly more compressible than solids, much less than gases.
  • Fluidity: Molecules are in constant motion and slip and slide over one another, so liquids take the shape of their container.
  • Kinetic Energy: Higher than solids, lower than gases; it increases with a rise in temperature.
  • Diffusion: Liquids diffuse into other miscible liquids, more slowly than gases. Liquids diffuse slowly.

Properties of Gases

A gas has neither a definite volume nor a definite shape. Examples: oxygen, carbon dioxide and methane. One litre of water can produce over 1,600 litres of steam at 1 atm when boiled, showing the large spacing of gas molecules.

  • Density: Much lower than solids and liquids.
  • Compressibility: Molecules are widely separated, so gases compress easily.
  • Fluidity: Molecules are in constant, random motion, colliding with each other and with the walls of the container. This gives diffusion, effusion, expansion and compression.
  • Kinetic Energy: Higher than liquids and solids, due to high mobility, negligible intermolecular forces and large spaces. The average kinetic energy of gas molecules is directly proportional to the temperature of the gas.
  • Diffusion: Gases diffuse faster than liquids and solids. Lighter gases diffuse more rapidly: helium gas (molar mass = 2g/mol) diffuses faster than oxygen gas (molar mass = 32g/mol).
PropertySolidsLiquidsGases
ShapeDefiniteIndefiniteIndefinite
VolumeDefiniteDefiniteIndefinite
Attractive ForcesStrongModerateNegligible
ParticlesTightly packedLoosely packedIndependent
DensityHighLowVery low
CompressibilityIncompressibleSlightHigh
FluidityCannot flowCan flowCan flow
RigidityHighLessNegligible
Kinetic EnergyLowIntermediateHigh
DiffusionNegligibleLessHigh

Key Points

  • Solids: definite shape and volume, tightly packed particles, incompressible, cannot flow.
  • Liquids: definite volume, no fixed shape, can flow and diffuse slowly.
  • Gases: no definite shape or volume, widely separated particles, highly compressible.
  • Average kinetic energy of gas molecules is directly proportional to temperature.
  • Diffusion is fastest in gases, slow in liquids and negligible in solids.
lessons.title: Properties of Solids, Liquids and Gases

lessons.notes_html:
The three most common states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. Several other exotic (unusual) and intermediate states also exist. Each state has unique characteristics determined by the arrangement and behaviour of its particles.

Plasma

Plasma is a unique form of matter, often regarded as the fourth state, distinct from solid, liquid and gas. It is formed by heating and ionising a gas to extremely high temperatures, yielding a mixture of positively charged ions and free electrons.

Unlike ordinary gases, plasma lacks a defined shape or volume. Its charged particles move freely and are influenced by electric and magnetic fields. Natural plasmas: stars (including the Sun), lightning, neon lights, auroras and flames. Artificial plasmas made in laboratories and industries: plasma TVs, fluorescent lights, plasma lamps and experimental fusion reactors.

Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC)

Bose-Einstein condensate is a unique fifth state of matter that typically forms at extremely low temperatures, close to absolute zero (zero kelvin).

In this state, a group of atoms from certain elements ceases to behave as separate particles and begins to function as a single entity. Particle movement nearly stops, and atoms start to clump together. Satyendra Nath Bose and Albert Einstein first predicted this phenomenon in the 1920s, and experimental evidence confirmed it in 1995. BECs are frequently created using extremely cold gases of alkali metals (Li, Na, K and Rb), with applications in modern technologies such as the production of super-fast computer chips.

Liquid Crystals

Liquid crystals (LCs) represent a unique state of matter with properties between those of a typical liquid and a solid crystal: Solid → Liquid Crystals → Liquid.

Some solids first change into a turbid liquid before transforming into a clear liquid. These turbid liquids possess properties of both solids, such as optical activity, and of liquids, such as fluidity and viscosity, and are called liquid crystals. They are frequently used in display technologies such as LCDs (liquid crystal displays) — in digital wristwatches, clocks, flat-panel televisions, computers, laptop screens, cellphones and pH meters. Liquid crystals also detect blockages in veins and arteries and infected areas such as tumours, and are used in thermometers to measure the body temperature of infants.

Key Points

  • Plasma is the fourth state: an ionised gas of positive ions and free electrons at extremely high temperature.
  • Plasma is found in stars, the Sun and lightning; plasma TVs and fluorescent lights are artificial plasma.
  • BEC is the fifth state, formed close to absolute zero, where atoms act as a single entity.
  • BEC was predicted by Bose and Einstein in the 1920s and confirmed in 1995.
  • Liquid crystals lie between a solid crystal and a liquid, and are used in LCD devices.
lessons.title: Exotic and Intermediate States of Matter

mcqs.q: Allotropes are defined in the notes as what?
options: The various forms of the same element, with different atomic arrangements
mcqs.why: Allotropes are the various forms of the same element, composed of atoms of the same element but with different atomic arrangements in each structure.

mcqs.q: Allotropes have identical chemical properties but differ in what?
options: Their physical properties such as hardness, density and colour
mcqs.why: Despite having identical chemical properties, allotropes' physical properties differ, including hardness, density and colour.

mcqs.q: The three main types of carbon allotropes in the notes are what?
mcqs.why: The three main carbon allotropes are diamond, graphite and fullerenes; tin, sulphur and phosphorus are other elements that show allotropy.

mcqs.q: Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
options: All four valence electrons are utilised for bonding, so it lacks free electrons
It has layers held by weak forces
mcqs.why: Each carbon in diamond is bonded to four others and all four valence electrons are used for bonding, so diamonds lack free electrons and do not conduct electricity.

mcqs.q: Each carbon atom in diamond is bonded to how many other carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: Diamonds consist of a three-dimensional tetrahedral network where each carbon atom is bonded to four others through strong covalent bonds.

mcqs.q: Each carbon atom in a graphite layer is bonded to how many other carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: Each carbon atom in a graphite layer is bonded to three other carbon atoms through covalent bonds, forming flat hexagonal rings.

mcqs.q: Why is graphite used in lead pencils and locks, according to the notes?
options: Because it is the hardest substance
Because it is a hollow sphere
Because of the weak forces between its layers
mcqs.why: Graphite is commonly used in lead pencils and locks due to the weak forces between its layers, which are stacked above one another.

mcqs.q: The Buckyball (C60) contains how many faces, pentagons and hexagons?
mcqs.why: The Buckyball (C60) resembles a soccer ball, containing 32 faces, 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons. Checking the total: 12 + 20 = 32 faces.

mcqs.q: Amorphous solids are described in the notes as solids that do what?
options: Soften gradually rather than melting sharply, with irregularly arranged particles
mcqs.why: In amorphous (shapeless) solids particles are arranged irregularly, so they soften gradually rather than melting sharply; examples are glass, wax, butter, plastics and rubber.

mcqs.q: Fullerenes are typically used in which applications in the notes?
options: Energy storage devices such as batteries, lubricants and coatings
mcqs.why: Fullerenes are used in energy storage devices (such as batteries), lubricants and coatings, and help remove contaminants from water.

lessons.notes_html:
The various forms of the same element are known as allotropes (or allotropic forms). They are composed of atoms of the same element, but their atomic arrangement varies in each structure. Despite having identical chemical properties, their physical properties differ, including hardness, density and colour.

There are three main types of carbon allotropes: diamond, graphite and fullerenes. Other elements that exist in allotropic forms include tin, sulphur and phosphorus.

Note: In amorphous (shapeless) solids, the particles are arranged irregularly, so they have no fixed structure. They look hard like true solids but soften gradually rather than melting sharply. Examples: glass, wax, butter, plastics, rubber and some types of candy.

Diamond

Diamond is the purest form of carbon and occurs naturally in the earth crust. It is the hardest substance, possessing high density and melting points. Diamonds are transparent and colourless, valued in jewellery for their brilliance and sparkle, and used in cutting and grinding tools due to their hardness.

Diamonds consist of a three-dimensional network of carbon atoms arranged tetrahedrally. Each carbon atom is bonded to four others through strong covalent bonds. Because all four valence electrons are utilised for bonding, diamonds lack free electrons and consequently do not conduct electricity.

Graphite

Graphite is another form of pure carbon, with properties quite different from diamond. It has a giant covalent structure composed of layers or sheets of carbon atoms stacked above one another. Each carbon atom in a layer is bonded to three other carbon atoms through covalent bonds, forming flat hexagonal rings. The various layers are held together by weak forces.

Graphite is an excellent conductor of electricity because of its layered structure. It is commonly used in lead pencils and locks due to the weak forces between its layers. Its high melting point results from the strong covalent bonds within each layer. Graphite appears opaque and black.

Fullerene

Fullerenes (also known as Buckyballs) are allotropes of carbon that consist of molecules made entirely of carbon atoms. The most common form is C60, arranged as hollow spheres, ellipsoids or tubes. The Buckyball (C60) resembles a soccer ball, containing 32 faces, 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons. Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three other carbon atoms, and fullerene molecules are held together by weak forces.

Fullerenes are rare. Small amounts occur as C60, C70, C76, C82 and C84 molecules, discovered in soot and the residue of carbon arc lamps, and also generated by lightning discharges in the atmosphere. They typically do not conduct electricity; their conductivity is generally more similar to semiconductors or insulators. They are used in energy storage devices (such as batteries), lubricants and coatings, and help remove contaminants from water.

AllotropeStructureConducts electricity?
Diamond3D tetrahedral network, each C bonded to 4 othersNo — no free electrons
GraphiteLayers of hexagonal rings, each C bonded to 3 othersYes — excellent conductor
Fullerene (C60)Hollow sphere like a soccer ball, 12 pentagons and 20 hexagonsGenerally no — like a semiconductor or insulator

Key Points

  • Allotropes are different forms of the same element with different atomic arrangements.
  • Carbon allotropes are diamond, graphite and fullerenes; tin, sulphur and phosphorus also show allotropy.
  • Diamond is the hardest substance and does not conduct electricity.
  • Graphite has layers held by weak forces and is an excellent conductor of electricity.
  • C60 fullerene is a hollow sphere resembling a soccer ball.

mcqs.q: A pure substance is composed of what, according to the notes?
options: Only one kind of particle, either atoms or molecules
mcqs.why: Pure substances are composed of only one kind of particle, either atoms or molecules, and show uniform properties throughout their mass.

mcqs.q: An element is defined in the table as what?
options: An impure substance with no chemical bonds
A pure substance consisting of only one kind of atom
A compound in a fixed ratio
mcqs.why: The table defines an element as a pure substance consisting of only one kind of atom, such as carbon, nitrogen, zinc or gold.

mcqs.q: A compound is defined in the notes as what?
options: Two or more different elements in fixed ratios, chemically combined
mcqs.why: A compound is a pure substance of two or more different elements in fixed ratios, chemically combined, such as water, ammonia or sodium chloride.

mcqs.q: Mixtures are categorised in the table as what kind of substance?
mcqs.why: The table categorises a mixture as an impure substance of two or more substances with no chemical bonds, while elements and compounds are pure substances.

mcqs.q: How can the components of a mixture be separated?
options: They cannot be separated at all
mcqs.why: The notes state components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods, while compounds need chemical reactions or electricity to separate their elements.

mcqs.q: The properties of a mixture are described in the table as what?
options: The same as the individual components
mcqs.why: The table says a mixture's properties are the same as the individual components, while a compound's properties are different from the elements it contains.

mcqs.q: A homogeneous mixture is described in the notes as what?
options: Not uniform, like sand in water
Uniform throughout, like salt solution, with components that cannot be seen separately
mcqs.why: A homogeneous mixture is uniform throughout, like salt solution, and its components cannot be seen separately, unlike a heterogeneous mixture such as sand in water.

mcqs.q: Sand in water is given in the notes as an example of what?
mcqs.why: Sand in water is a heterogeneous mixture: it is not uniform and its different parts can often be seen and separated physically.

mcqs.q: Which of these is listed in the table as an example of a compound?
mcqs.why: The table lists water, ammonia and sodium chloride as compounds; carbon and gold are elements and concrete is a mixture.

mcqs.q: An element cannot be broken down how, according to the key points?
options: By chemical means into simpler substances
mcqs.why: The key points state an element consists of only one type of atom and cannot be broken down by chemical means into simpler substances.

lessons.notes_html:
Matter is generally classified into pure substances (elements and compounds) and mixtures (homogeneous and heterogeneous).

Pure substances are types of matter composed of only one kind of particle, either atoms or molecules, and show uniform properties throughout their mass. Examples: carbon, oxygen, silver, gold, water and carbon dioxide.

PropertyElementCompoundMixture

CategoryPure substancePure substanceImpure substance
TypesMetals, non-metals and metalloidsCovalent, ionicHomogeneous, heterogeneous
CompositionOne kind of atomsDifferent types of atoms (elements)Different substances
PropertiesUnique, determined by the type of atomDifferent from the elements they containSame as the individual components
SeparationCannot be broken down into simpler substancesElements can be separated by chemical reactions or electricityComponents can be separated by physical methods
BondingCan form chemical bonds with other elementsCan form chemical bonds with other elementsCannot form chemical bonds between components

A homogeneous mixture is uniform throughout, like salt solution, and its components cannot be seen separately. A heterogeneous mixture is not uniform, like sand in water, and its different parts can often be seen and separated physically.

Key Points

  • An element consists of only one type of atom and cannot be broken down by chemical means.
  • A compound is two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, e.g. water, H2O.
  • A mixture is physically combined in any ratio; its components keep their own properties.
  • Mixture components can be separated by physical methods.
  • Pure substances are elements and compounds; mixtures are impure substances.
lessons.title: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures

mcqs.q: A solution is which type of mixture, according to the notes?
options: A homogeneous mixture with particles uniformly distributed
mcqs.why: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more components, with particles uniformly distributed throughout; it is transparent and does not scatter light.

mcqs.q: In salt water, salt and water are respectively what?
options: The solute (dissolved) and the solvent (dissolves it)
mcqs.why: The solute is the substance dissolved (salt in salt water) and the solvent is the substance that dissolves it (water).

mcqs.q: Colloid particles have which size range in the table?
mcqs.why: The table gives colloid particles as 1 nm to 1000 nm, between solutions (0.01 nm to 1 nm) and suspensions (greater than 1000 nm).

mcqs.q: Which mixture shows the Tyndall effect, according to the table?
options: A solution, which cannot scatter light
mcqs.why: Colloids scatter light (Tyndall effect visible), while solutions cannot scatter light and show no Tyndall effect.

mcqs.q: Which mixture settles down on standing, according to the table?
mcqs.why: Suspensions settle down on standing, while solutions and colloids do not settle down, as shown in the comparison table.

mcqs.q: Which mixture can be filtered through ordinary filter paper?
mcqs.why: Suspensions are filterable through ordinary filter paper, while solutions and colloids are non-filterable through ordinary filter paper.

mcqs.q: Milk is classified in the self-check in the notes as what?
mcqs.why: Milk is a colloid: its tiny fat and protein particles are dispersed through water, do not settle out, and scatter light, making milk look white and opaque. The self-check also lists milk as a colloid.

mcqs.q: Vinegar in water is classified in the self-check as what?
mcqs.why: The self-check from the book lists vinegar in water as a solution, milk and fog as colloids, and muddy water as a suspension.

mcqs.q: Fog is classified in the notes as what?
mcqs.why: Fog is a colloid, listed in the examples and the self-check alongside milk, smoke, clouds and toothpaste as colloids.

mcqs.q: For colloids, the terms used for solute and solvent are what?
options: Dispersed phase for solute and dispersing medium for solvent
mcqs.why: For colloids, the notes use the terms dispersed phase for solute and dispersing medium for solvent, unlike the solute/solvent terms for a solution.

lessons.notes_html:
Mixtures are classified into solutions, colloids and suspensions.

Solution

A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more components, with particles uniformly distributed throughout. It is transparent and does not scatter light. The solute particles in solutions are so small that they cannot be observed by the naked eye or a microscope. The solute is the substance dissolved (e.g. salt in salt water) and the solvent is the substance that dissolves it (e.g. water). A true solution is clear, does not scatter light and its solute does not settle out.

Colloid

A colloid (or colloidal dispersion) is a heterogeneous mixture of two or more components. For colloids, we use the terms dispersed phase for solute and dispersing medium for solvent. Milk is a colloid: its tiny fat and protein particles are dispersed through water, do not settle out, and scatter light, which is why milk looks white and opaque rather than clear. Fog is also a colloid.

Suspension

A suspension is also a heterogeneous mixture; the particles are large enough to be seen with a microscope and can often be observed with the naked eye. Suspensions scatter light.

Effect of lightCannot scatter light (no Tyndall effect)Scatter light (Tyndall effect visible)Scatter light strongly
TransparencyTransparentCloudyOpaque
Settling on standingDo not settle downDo not settle downSettle down
FilterabilityNon-filterable through ordinary filter paperNon-filterable through ordinary filter paperFilterable through ordinary filter paper
Visibility of particlesInvisible to naked eye and microscopeInvisible to naked eye and under an ordinary microscopeVisible to the naked eye
ExamplesSalt solution, sugar solution, vinegar in water, petrol, air, soft drinksMilk, starch solution, fog, smoke, clouds, toothpasteMuddy water, sand in water, flour in water, soot, milk of magnesia

Self-check from the book: Milk — colloid; Vinegar in water — solution; Muddy water — suspension; Fog — colloid.

Key Points

  • A solution is homogeneous, transparent and does not scatter light.
  • Colloid particles are 1nm to 1000nm, scatter light (Tyndall effect) and do not settle.
  • Suspension particles are greater than 1000nm, are visible, settle on standing and can be filtered.
  • In a solution, the solute dissolves in the solvent, e.g. salt (solute) in water (solvent).
  • Milk and fog are colloids; muddy water is a suspension.
lessons.title: Solutions, Colloids and Suspensions

mcqs.q: Solubility is typically expressed in what units, according to the notes?
options: Grams of solute per 100 grams or per litre of solvent
mcqs.why: Solubility is typically expressed in grams of solute per 100 grams or per litre of solvent, under specific temperature and pressure conditions.

mcqs.q: How much sugar dissolves in 100 g of water at 0°C and at 100°C, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: Sugar (sucrose) in 100 g of water is 179 g at 0°C but 487 g at 100°C - a large increase. The increase is 487 - 179 = 308 g.

mcqs.q: By how much does the solubility of NaCl change from 0°C to 100°C in 100 g of water?
options: It does not change at all
It increases slightly, from 35.7 g to 39.2 g
mcqs.why: NaCl is only slightly affected: 35.7 g in 100 g of water at 0°C and 39.2 g at 100°C. The increase is 39.2 - 35.7 = 3.5 g, which is a slight increase.

mcqs.q: Lithium carbonate shows which solubility trend in the notes?
options: It decreases, from 1.54 g at 0°C to about 0.72 g at 100°C
mcqs.why: Some solids decrease with temperature: lithium carbonate is 1.54 g at 0°C and approximately 0.72 g at 100°C. The decrease is 1.54 - 0.72 = 0.82 g.

mcqs.q: The solubility of gases in water does what as temperature increases?
options: It decreases, because higher temperature raises gas molecules' kinetic energy and reduces attractive forces with water
mcqs.why: The solubility of gases in water decreases with increasing temperature, because higher temperatures elevate the kinetic energy of gas molecules, reducing attractive forces with water molecules.

mcqs.q: Why does a soft drink lose its fizz quickly when warmed?
options: Because dissolved CO2 becomes less soluble and escapes more rapidly
Because CO2 turns into a solid
mcqs.why: A soft drink loses its fizz quickly when warmed because dissolved CO2 becomes less soluble as temperature rises and escapes more rapidly, like gases generally.

mcqs.q: An unsaturated solution is one that can do what?
options: Hold more than a saturated solution
Dissolve more solute, because it has not reached the maximum concentration
mcqs.why: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute; the solvent has not reached the maximum solute concentration at a given temperature and pressure.

mcqs.q: A saturated solution is described in the notes as what?
options: Completely filled with solute and cannot dissolve more at a given temperature
mcqs.why: A saturated solution is completely filled with solute and cannot dissolve more at a given temperature; additional solute remains undissolved and settles at the bottom.

mcqs.q: How is a supersaturated solution prepared, according to the notes?
options: First prepare a saturated solution at a high temperature, then cool it down
mcqs.why: The method is to first prepare a saturated solution at a high temperature, then cool it down; during cooling some excess solute tends to crystallise, leaving a supersaturated solution.

mcqs.q: A saturated solution of sodium thiosulphate at 20°C contains how much salt per 100 cm3 of water, and what happens to one made saturated at 30°C and cooled to 20°C?
options: 20.9 g; it would contain more than 20.9 g, so it would be supersaturated
mcqs.why: A saturated solution of sodium thiosulphate in water at 20°C contains 20.9 g of salt per 100 cm3 of water; one prepared saturated at 30°C and cooled to 20°C would contain more than 20.9 g, so it would be supersaturated.

lessons.notes_html:
Solubility refers to the ability of a substance (the solute) to dissolve in a specified amount of another substance (the solvent) under specific temperature and pressure conditions. It is typically expressed in grams of solute per 100 grams or per litre of solvent.

Temperature affects not only the rate of dissolving but also the solubility. Generally, the rate at which a solute dissolves increases with a temperature rise. However, the quantity of dissolved solute may either increase or decrease as the temperature rises. Tea leaves, coffee beans and sugar dissolve more as temperature rises.

Solubility of Solids in Liquids

Solids show strong attractive forces among their particles, requiring energy to overcome these forces when dissolved in a liquid. Generally, the solubility of solids in liquids increases with an increase in temperature.

  • Sugar (sucrose) in 100g of water: 179g at 0°C, but 487g at 100°C.
  • NaCl is only slightly affected: 35.7g in 100g of water at 0°C, and 39.2g at 100°C.
  • Some solids decrease: lithium carbonate is 1.54g at 0°C and approximately 0.72g at 100°C. Cerium sulphate also decreases with rising temperature.
Substance (in 100g water)0°C100°CTrend
NaCl35.7g39.2gSlight increase
Sugar C12H22O11179g487gLarge increase
Li2CO31.54g0.72gDecrease
CO2 at SP0.335g—Decrease
O2 at SP0.00694g0.00gDecrease

Solubility of Gases in Liquids

The solubility of gases in water decreases with increasing temperature, because higher temperatures elevate the kinetic energy of gas molecules, which reduces the attractive forces with water molecules. When water is heated, bubbles appear before boiling as gases escape. A soft drink loses its fizz quickly when warmed, because dissolved CO2 becomes less soluble and escapes more rapidly.

Unsaturated, Saturated and Supersaturated Solutions

  • Unsaturated solution: Can dissolve more solute. The solvent has not reached the maximum solute concentration at a given temperature and pressure.
  • Saturated solution: Completely filled with solute and cannot dissolve more at a given temperature. Additional solute remains undissolved and settles at the bottom.
  • Supersaturated solution: Contains more solute than is needed to form a saturated solution at a specific temperature. These solutions are unstable. Method: first prepare a saturated solution at a high temperature, then cool it down; during cooling, some excess solute tends to crystallise, leaving behind a supersaturated solution. Example: a saturated solution of sodium thiosulphate in water at 20°C contains 20.9g of salt per 100cm3 of water; a solution prepared saturated at 30°C and cooled to 20°C would contain more than 20.9g, so it would be supersaturated.

Temperature and saturation: As the temperature rises, many solutes dissolve more readily, leading to a saturated solution with higher concentrations of dissolved substances.

Key Points

  • Solubility is expressed in grams of solute per 100g or per litre of solvent.
  • Solubility of most solids in liquids increases with temperature; solubility of gases decreases.
  • Sugar: 179g at 0°C and 487g at 100°C in 100g water; NaCl changes only slightly.
  • An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute; a saturated solution cannot.
  • A supersaturated solution holds more solute than a saturated solution and is unstable.
lessons.title: Solubility and Saturated Solutions

mcqs.q: What is an atom, as defined in the notes?
options: The smallest unit of a mixture that can be filtered out
The smallest unit of an element that retains all its chemical properties
A group of molecules joined together in a shell
The central part of a cell that contains protons
mcqs.why: The notes define an atom as the smallest unit of an element that retains all its chemical properties, which is why elements keep their identity at the atomic level.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, 50 million hydrogen atoms placed in a row would stretch across only what distance?
mcqs.why: The notes state that 50 million hydrogen atoms in a row would stretch across only 1 millimetre, showing how extremely small atoms are.

mcqs.q: What are protons and neutrons together called?
mcqs.why: Protons and neutrons sit together in the nucleus and are together called nucleons, while electrons move around the nucleus in shells.

mcqs.q: Where are electrons found in an atom?
options: Inside the nucleus with the protons
Orbiting around the nucleus in shells
mcqs.why: The notes place protons and neutrons in the central nucleus, while electrons orbit around the nucleus in shells.

mcqs.q: What are the relative charge and relative mass of an electron (e-)?
mcqs.why: The subatomic particle table gives the electron a relative charge of -1 and a much smaller relative mass of 0.00054, far below the proton and neutron masses.

mcqs.q: What is the relative mass of a proton (p+)?
mcqs.why: The table in the notes gives the proton a relative mass of 1.007276 and a relative charge of +1, almost the same mass as a neutron.

mcqs.q: What is the relative charge of a neutron (n0)?
mcqs.why: A neutron carries no charge, so its relative charge is 0, while its relative mass of 1.008665 is almost identical to that of a proton.

mcqs.q: Why is an atom electrically neutral?
options: Because it has no electrons at all
Because neutrons cancel the charge of electrons
Because the number of electrons equals the number of protons
mcqs.why: A proton has a charge equal in magnitude but opposite in sign to an electron, so when the number of electrons equals the number of protons the atom is electrically neutral.

mcqs.q: For the carbon atom described in the notes, what is in the nucleus and in the shells?
mcqs.why: The notes show carbon with a nucleus of 6 protons and 6 neutrons, and electrons arranged as 2 in the first shell plus 4 in the second shell.

mcqs.q: Why is the mass of electrons neglected when calculating the mass of an atom?
options: Because electrons have exactly zero mass
Because the electron mass is much smaller, so the atom mass is determined mainly by protons and neutrons
Because electrons are outside the atom
Because protons and electrons have identical masses
mcqs.why: The electron mass of 0.00054 is much smaller than the proton and neutron masses near 1, so the mass of an atom is determined mainly by its protons and neutrons.

lessons.notes_html:
Everything in the universe is made of tiny particles called atoms — the atomic theory of matter. Atoms are too small to see: 50 million hydrogen atoms in a row would stretch across only 1 millimetre.

An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains all its chemical properties. In this unit you will learn the structure of the atom: a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in shells.

Atoms are made of smaller subatomic particles: protons, neutrons and electrons. Protons and neutrons together are called nucleons. They sit in the nucleus, while electrons orbit around the nucleus in shells.

Subatomic ParticleSymbolRelative ChargeRelative Mass
Electrone--10.00054
Protonp++11.007276
Neutronn001.008665

Protons and neutrons have almost identical masses. The electron has a much smaller mass, so the mass of electrons is neglected in calculations. A proton has a charge equal in magnitude but opposite in sign to an electron.

Atoms are electrically neutral because the number of electrons equals the number of protons. The mass of an atom is determined mainly by its protons and neutrons.

Key Points

  • An atom is the smallest unit of an element with all its chemical properties.
  • Protons (+) and neutrons (no charge) are in the nucleus; electrons (-) move in shells.
  • Protons and neutrons are called nucleons.
  • Atoms are neutral: number of protons = number of electrons.
  • Almost all the mass of an atom is in its protons and neutrons.
lessons.title: Subatomic Particles of an Atom

mcqs.q: What else are orbits around the nucleus called?
mcqs.why: The notes say electrons are arranged in orbits, also called shells or energy levels, around the nucleus, and the energy of an electron depends on its position.

mcqs.q: Electrons closer to the nucleus have what energy, and why?
options: Lower energy, because they feel a stronger attraction to the nucleus
Higher energy, because they feel a stronger attraction to the nucleus
Lower energy, because they feel a weaker attraction to the nucleus
Higher energy, because they feel a weaker attraction to the nucleus
mcqs.why: Electrons closer to the nucleus feel a stronger attraction, so they have lower energy, while electrons farther away feel a weaker attraction and have higher energy.

mcqs.q: How do electrons farther from the nucleus compare with inner electrons?
options: They have lower energy and a smaller average distance
They have higher energy and a greater average distance from the nucleus
They have the same energy and the same distance
They have lower energy and a greater average distance
mcqs.why: The notes state that electrons farther away feel a weaker attraction, so they have higher energy and a greater average distance from the nucleus.

mcqs.q: Lithium has atomic number 3. How are its electrons arranged, and which electron has the higher energy?
options: 3 in the first shell; all have equal energy
1 in the first shell and 2 in the second; the first-shell electrons have higher energy
2 in the second shell and 1 in the third; the inner electron has higher energy
2 in the first shell and 1 in the second; the second-shell electron has higher energy
mcqs.why: Working: 2 + 1 = 3 electrons, matching atomic number 3. The notes give lithium as 2 electrons in the first shell and 1 in the second, and the second-shell electron has higher energy.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between an orbit and a shell given in the notes?
options: An orbit is spherical and 3D, while a shell is circular and 2D
An orbit was circular and two-dimensional, while a shell is spherical and three-dimensional
An orbit holds protons, while a shell holds only neutrons
mcqs.why: The notes remind us that an orbit was circular and two-dimensional, while a shell is spherical and three-dimensional (3D).

mcqs.q: What does the nuclear force do inside the nucleus?
options: It pushes protons apart from each other
It holds electrons in their shells
It binds protons and neutrons together, overcoming the repulsion between protons
mcqs.why: The nuclear force binds protons and neutrons together inside the nucleus and overcomes the electrostatic repulsion between positively charged protons.

mcqs.q: Over what distance range does the strong nuclear force work?
mcqs.why: The strong nuclear force works only over very short distances, 0.8 to 2.5 femtometres, and within this range it holds the nucleons closely together.

mcqs.q: One femtometre (1 fm) is equal to what?
mcqs.why: The notes define the femtometre used for the nuclear force range by stating that 1 fm = 10^-15 m, an extremely short distance inside the nucleus.

mcqs.q: How does the strong nuclear force compare with the electromagnetic force?
options: It is weaker than the electromagnetic force
It is significantly stronger than the electromagnetic force
It is exactly equal to the electromagnetic force
It is the same force as the electromagnetic force
mcqs.why: The notes say the strong nuclear force is significantly stronger than the electromagnetic force, which is the force that makes protons repel each other.

mcqs.q: How much of an atom's mass is in its nucleus, and how much volume does the nucleus occupy?
options: About 50% of the mass, in about half the volume
About 90% of the mass, in most of the volume
More than 99.9% of the mass, in only a tiny fraction of the total volume
Less than 10% of the mass, in a tiny fraction of the volume
mcqs.why: More than 99.9% of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus, yet the nucleus occupies only a tiny fraction of the total volume of the atom.

lessons.notes_html:
Energy of Electrons in Orbits

Electrons are arranged in orbits, also called shells or energy levels, around the nucleus. The energy of an electron depends on its position.

  • Electrons closer to the nucleus feel a stronger attraction, so they have lower energy.
  • Electrons farther away feel a weaker attraction, so they have higher energy and a greater average distance from the nucleus.

Example: lithium has atomic number 3, with two electrons in the first shell and one electron in the second shell. The second-shell electron has higher energy than the first-shell electrons.

Remember: an orbit was circular and two-dimensional, while a shell is spherical and three-dimensional (3D).

Nuclear Force

The nuclear force binds protons and neutrons together inside the nucleus. It overcomes the electrostatic repulsion between positively charged protons.

  • The strong nuclear force works only over very short distances, 0.8 to 2.5 femtometres (1 fm = 10-15 m).
  • It is significantly stronger than the electromagnetic force, which makes protons repel each other.
  • When nucleons are within this range, the strong force holds them closely together.

More than 99.9% of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus, yet the nucleus occupies only a tiny fraction of the total volume of the atom.

Key Points

  • Shells are energy levels; a larger shell means higher energy and greater distance from the nucleus.
  • Lithium (2,1): the outer electron has more energy than the inner electrons.
  • The strong nuclear force holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus.
  • It acts over 0.8 to 2.5 fm and is stronger than the electromagnetic force.
  • More than 99.9% of an atom's mass is in its tiny nucleus.
lessons.title: Energy of Electrons in Orbits and Nuclear Force

mcqs.q: The word atom comes from the Greek word atomos. What does atomos mean?
mcqs.why: The notes explain that the word atom comes from the Greek atomos, meaning indivisible, reflecting the early idea that atoms could not be divided.

mcqs.q: In Thomson's Plum Pudding Model (1904), how is the atom described?
options: A tiny nucleus with electrons in fixed orbits around it
Electrons in subshells and orbitals around a nucleus
A hollow sphere with all charge on its surface
A sphere of positive charge with negatively charged electrons embedded in it
mcqs.why: Thomson's 1904 model describes the atom as a sphere of positive charge with negatively charged electrons embedded in it, like plums in a pudding.

mcqs.q: What did Thomson's model confirm and explain?
options: It confirmed the nucleus exists and explained atomic spectra
It confirmed electrons exist inside the atom and explained the electrical neutrality of the atom
It confirmed neutrons exist and explained ionisation of gases
It confirmed fixed orbits and explained the stability of atoms
mcqs.why: Thomson's model confirmed that electrons exist inside the atom and explained the electrical neutrality of the atom, because the embedded negative electrons balance the positive sphere.

mcqs.q: Which experiment led to Rutherford's Atomic Model (1911)?
mcqs.why: Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed a tiny, positively charged nucleus at the centre of the atom, with electrons moving around it.

mcqs.q: What could Rutherford's model NOT explain?
options: The stability and spectrum of an atom
The existence of electrons inside the atom
The electrical neutrality of the atom
The existence of a central nucleus
mcqs.why: Although Rutherford's model showed the tiny central nucleus where the entire mass is concentrated, it could not explain the stability and spectrum of an atom.

mcqs.q: In Bohr's Atomic Model (1913), when do electrons lose or gain energy?
options: Continuously as they revolve around the nucleus
Only when they jump from one orbit to another
Only when the atom is heated to a plasma
Never, because their energy is always zero
mcqs.why: In Bohr's model electrons revolve in fixed-energy circular orbits and lose or gain energy only when they jump from one orbit to another.

mcqs.q: Which set of things did Bohr's model explain?
options: Subshells, orbitals and plum pudding structure
Gold foil scattering and neutron masses
The stability of atoms, atomic spectra and the ionisation of gases
Nuclear force, half-life and relative atomic mass
mcqs.why: The notes credit Bohr's 1913 model with explaining the stability of atoms, atomic spectra and the ionisation of gases, which Rutherford's model could not explain.

mcqs.q: In the Quantum Mechanical Model (1927), how are electrons described?
options: Embedded in a sphere of positive charge
Moving in fixed circular orbits only
Arranged in subshells and orbitals, challenging the idea of fixed orbits
Fixed in place inside the nucleus
mcqs.why: The 1927 quantum mechanical model uses quantum mechanics and arranges electrons in subshells and orbitals, challenging the older idea of fixed orbits.

mcqs.q: In a uniform electric field, toward which plate do protons and electrons move?
options: Protons to the positive plate, electrons to the negative plate
Protons to the negative plate, electrons to the positive plate
Both protons and electrons to the negative plate
Both protons and electrons to the positive plate
mcqs.why: Protons are positive so they move toward the negative plate, while electrons are negative so they move toward the positive plate, with equal but opposite charges giving equal-magnitude forces.

mcqs.q: Which technologies does the notes say atomic models led to?
options: Lasers, nuclear power, MRI machines and microchips
Steam engines, telegraphs, radios and televisions
Plasma TVs, fluorescent lights and fusion reactors only
Particle accelerators, batteries and electroplating only
mcqs.why: The notes list lasers, nuclear power, MRI machines and microchips as technologies that atomic models led to, showing the practical value of the models.

lessons.notes_html:
Atoms cannot be seen with the naked eye, so scientists use models to understand their behaviour. An atomic model is an aid to understand the structure of an atom. The word atom comes from the Greek atomos, meaning indivisible.

Thomson's Plum Pudding Model (1904)

The atom is a sphere of positive charge with negatively charged electrons embedded in it. It confirmed electrons exist inside the atom and explained the electrical neutrality of the atom.

Rutherford's Atomic Model (1911)

His gold foil experiment showed a tiny, positively charged nucleus at the centre, with electrons moving around it. The nucleus is much smaller than the atom and the entire mass is concentrated in it. It could not explain the stability and spectrum of an atom.

Bohr's Atomic Model (1913)

Electrons revolve around the positively charged nucleus in fixed-energy circular orbits (shells). They lose or gain energy only when they jump from one orbit to another. This model explained the stability of atoms, atomic spectra and the ionisation of gases.

Quantum Mechanical Model (1927)

It uses quantum mechanics to describe electrons. Electrons are arranged in subshells and orbitals, challenging the idea of fixed orbits. Atomic models led to technologies such as lasers, nuclear power, MRI machines and microchips.

Behaviour in a Uniform Electric Field

An electric field is uniform when it has consistent strength and direction. Protons and electrons carry equal but opposite charges, so the forces on them are equal in magnitude.

  • Protons (positive) move toward the negative plate.
  • Electrons (negative) move toward the positive plate.

Electric fields are used in applications such as particle accelerators.

Key Points

  • Thomson (1904): positive sphere with electrons embedded in it.
  • Rutherford (1911): tiny central nucleus; could not explain stability or spectra.
  • Bohr (1913): electrons in fixed-energy orbits; explained stability and spectra.
  • Quantum model (1927): electrons in subshells and orbitals, not fixed orbits.
  • In an electric field, protons go to the negative plate and electrons to the positive plate.
lessons.title: Atomic Models and Charged Particles in an Electric Field

mcqs.q: What is the atomic number (Z) of an element?
options: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
The number of electrons in the outermost shell only
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom
The number of neutrons in the nucleus of an atom
mcqs.why: The atomic number, symbol Z, is the number of protons in the nucleus. It is unique for each element and identifies the element in the Periodic Table.

mcqs.q: What is the mass number (A), also called the nucleon number?
options: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
The number of electrons plus protons
mcqs.why: Mass number A is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus, which is why it is also called the nucleon number in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the number of neutrons in an atom?
mcqs.why: Since A = protons + neutrons and Z = protons, rearranging gives number of neutrons = A - Z, as stated in the key points of the notes.

mcqs.q: Oxygen-16 has 8 protons. How many neutrons does it have?
mcqs.why: Working: neutrons = A - Z = 16 - 8 = 8. The notes confirm oxygen-16 has mass number 16 with 8 protons and 8 neutrons.

mcqs.q: Potassium (K) has Z = 19 and A = 39. How many neutrons does a potassium atom have?
mcqs.why: Working: neutrons = A - Z = 39 - 19 = 20. This matches the table in the notes, which lists potassium with 19 protons, 19 electrons and 20 neutrons.

mcqs.q: Zinc (Zn) has Z = 30 and A = 65. How many neutrons does it have?
mcqs.why: Working: neutrons = A - Z = 65 - 30 = 35. The notes table lists zinc with 30 protons, 30 electrons and 35 neutrons.

mcqs.q: A neutral neon atom has Z = 10 and A = 20. How many electrons and neutrons does it have?
mcqs.why: Working: in a neutral atom electrons = protons = 10, and neutrons = A - Z = 20 - 10 = 10. The notes table gives neon exactly 10 protons, 10 electrons and 10 neutrons.

mcqs.q: Nitrogen-14 is written with the symbol N. What are its A and Z values in that notation?
mcqs.why: An atom is written as A on top and Z below before the symbol X. For nitrogen-14 the notes give A = 14 and Z = 7 for N.

mcqs.q: Nitrogen has 7 protons. What happens if one more proton is added, according to the notes?
options: It stays nitrogen with a larger mass only
It is no longer nitrogen; it becomes oxygen with 8 protons
It becomes a neutron with no charge
mcqs.why: Working: 7 + 1 = 8 protons. The notes say adding one more proton means it is no longer nitrogen; it becomes oxygen, with 8 protons, because the proton number identifies the element.

mcqs.q: How are elements arranged in the Periodic Table, according to the notes?
options: In order of increasing mass number only
In order of increasing atomic number
In alphabetical order of their symbols
In order of increasing number of neutrons
mcqs.why: The atomic number identifies each element and is used to arrange elements in the Periodic Table in order of increasing atomic number.

lessons.notes_html:
Atomic Number (Proton Number)

The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. Its symbol is Z. Each element has a unique atomic number; no two elements have the same atomic number.

The atomic number identifies the element and is used to arrange elements in the Periodic Table in order of increasing atomic number. Example: nitrogen has 7 protons. Add one more proton and it is no longer nitrogen; it becomes oxygen, with 8 protons.

Atoms with the same number of protons belong to the same element; atoms with different numbers of protons are different elements.

Mass Number (Nucleon Number)

The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. Its symbol is A. It is also called the nucleon number.

Mass Number = number of protons + number of neutrons

Example: oxygen-16 has mass number 16, with 8 protons and 8 neutrons. An atom is written as A on top, Z below, before the symbol X. Nitrogen-14 is written with A = 14 and Z = 7 for N.

In a neutral atom, number of electrons = number of protons, but the number of neutrons is not always equal to the number of protons. Number of neutrons = A - Z.

ElementSymbolZAProtonsElectronsNeutrons
HydrogenH11110
CarbonC612666
NeonNe1020101010
PotassiumK1939191920
ZincZn3065303035

Key Points

  • Atomic number Z = number of protons; it is unique for each element.
  • Elements in the Periodic Table are arranged by increasing atomic number.
  • Mass number A = protons + neutrons (nucleon number).
  • Neutrons = A - Z; in a neutral atom, electrons = protons.
lessons.title: Atomic Number and Mass Number

mcqs.q: What are isotopes?
options: Atoms of different elements with the same mass number
Atoms of the same element with the same protons but different numbers of neutrons
Atoms with equal protons and electrons but no neutrons
Ions of the same element with different charges
mcqs.why: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

mcqs.q: How do the chemical and physical properties of isotopes compare?
options: Different chemical properties, identical physical properties
Identical chemical and identical physical properties
Similar chemical properties, but different physical properties
Different chemical properties and different physical properties
mcqs.why: Isotopes have similar chemical properties because their electronic structures are identical, but different physical properties because their masses differ.

mcqs.q: Tritium is H-3, an isotope of hydrogen with 1 proton. How many neutrons does tritium have?
mcqs.why: Working: neutrons = A - Z = 3 - 1 = 2. The hydrogen isotope table lists protium H-1 with 0 neutrons, deuterium H-2 with 1 neutron and tritium H-3 with 2 neutrons.

mcqs.q: Carbon-14 has 6 protons. How many neutrons does it have?
mcqs.why: Working: neutrons = A - Z = 14 - 6 = 8. The notes use exactly this calculation for carbon-14: 6 protons and 14 - 6 = 8 neutrons.

mcqs.q: Fluorine-19 has 9 protons. How many neutrons does it have?
mcqs.why: Working: neutrons = A - Z = 19 - 9 = 10. The notes give fluorine-19 as 9 protons and 19 - 9 = 10 neutrons.

mcqs.q: Argon-40 has 18 protons. How many neutrons does it have?
mcqs.why: Working: neutrons = A - Z = 40 - 18 = 22. The notes give argon-40 as 18 protons and 40 - 18 = 22 neutrons.

mcqs.q: What is the half-life of carbon-14, and up to what age can it date materials?
options: Half-life 5730 years; dates materials up to 50,000 years old
Half-life 5730 years; dates materials up to 5,000 years old
Half-life 131 years; dates materials up to 99 years old
Half-life 18 years; dates materials up to 201 years old
mcqs.why: The notes state carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years and dates materials up to 50,000 years old by comparing remaining carbon-14 with the expected amount after an organism dies.

mcqs.q: Which isotope-use pairing is given in the notes for medical imaging?
options: Carbon-14 is used in PET scans
Iodine-131 is used for thyroid disorders
Fluorine-18 is used for thyroid disorders
Thallium-201 is used in SPECT for organ function
mcqs.why: The notes list fluorine-18 for PET scans, Technetium-99m in SPECT for organ function, Iodine-131 for thyroid disorders and Thallium-201 in cardiac imaging.

mcqs.q: Carbon is 98.89% carbon-12 and 1.11% carbon-13. What is its relative atomic mass (Ar)?
mcqs.why: Working: (12 x 98.89) = 1186.68 and (13 x 1.11) = 14.43; then 1186.68 + 14.43 = 1201.11, and 1201.11 / 100 = 12.0111, which rounds to 12.01 amu, the value calculated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Chlorine has Ar = 35.5 and one isotope of mass 35 at 75% abundance. What is the mass of the other isotope?
mcqs.why: Working: Ar x 100 = 35.5 x 100 = 3550, and 35 x 75 = 2625; then 3550 - 2625 = 925, and 925 / 25 = 37 amu, which is the chlorine-37 isotope named in the notes.

lessons.notes_html:
Isotopes

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. They are named by the element name followed by the mass number.

Isotopes have similar chemical properties because their electronic structures are identical, but different physical properties because their masses differ. The difference in isotopic mass does not significantly affect chemical behaviour, but isotopes can affect molecular mass.

Isotope of HydrogenSymbolProtonsNeutrons
ProtiumH-110
DeuteriumH-211
TritiumH-312

Chlorine has two isotopes: chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. Finding particles: carbon-14 has 6 protons and 14 - 6 = 8 neutrons; fluorine-19 has 9 protons and 19 - 9 = 10 neutrons; argon-40 has 18 protons and 40 - 18 = 22 neutrons.

Importance of Isotopes

Carbon dating: carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years and dates materials up to 50,000 years old. After an organism dies, comparing the remaining carbon-14 with the expected amount reveals the time of death.

Medical imaging: radioactive isotopes emit positrons or gamma rays. Fluorine-18 is used in PET scans, Technetium-99m in SPECT for organ function, Iodine-131 for thyroid disorders, and Thallium-201 in cardiac imaging.

Relative Atomic Mass

The relative atomic mass (Ar) of an element is the average mass of its isotopes compared to 1/12th of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. Masses are expressed in atomic mass units (amu); 1 amu = 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom, about 1.66 x 10-27 kg.

Relative Atomic Mass = [(M1 x A1) + (M2 x A2) + ...] / 100, where M = mass of each isotope and A = its percentage abundance.

Example: carbon is 98.89% carbon-12 and 1.11% carbon-13, so Ar = [(12 x 98.89) + (13 x 1.11)] / 100 = 1201.11 / 100 = 12.01 amu.

The mass of one isotope can also be found: M1 = [Ar x 100 - (M2 x A2 + ...)] / A1. For chlorine (Ar = 35.5) with an isotope of mass 35 at 75%, the other isotope = [3550 - 2625] / 25 = 37 amu.

Key Points

  • Isotopes: same protons, different neutrons; same chemical properties, different physical properties.
  • Hydrogen isotopes: protium, deuterium, tritium.
  • Carbon-14 (half-life 5730 years) is used in carbon dating; isotopes like Technetium-99m are used in medical imaging.
  • Relative atomic mass is the average mass of isotopes compared with 1/12th of carbon-12.
  • Ar = sum of (isotope mass x percentage abundance) divided by 100.
lessons.title: Isotopes and Relative Atomic Mass

mcqs.q: How is a two-letter element symbol written?
options: Both letters capital, e.g. CA for calcium
The first letter capital and the second letter lowercase, e.g. Ca for calcium
Both letters lowercase, e.g. ca for calcium
The first letter lowercase and the second capital, e.g. cA for calcium
mcqs.why: Each element symbol has one or two letters; the first letter is always capital and the second letter, if present, is lowercase, as in Be for beryllium and Ca for calcium.

mcqs.q: The symbol Na for sodium comes from which Latin name?
mcqs.why: Some symbols come from Latin names. The notes table gives sodium from Natrium with symbol Na, potassium from Kalium, iron from Ferrum and lead from Plumbum.

mcqs.q: The symbol K for potassium comes from which Latin name?
mcqs.why: The notes table gives potassium from the Latin name Kalium with symbol K and common ion K+, while Argentum gives Ag for silver and Aurum gives Au for gold.

mcqs.q: The symbol Fe for iron comes from which Latin name, and what common ions does iron form?
options: From Aurum, forming Au+ and Au3+
From Plumbum, forming Pb2+ and Pb4+
From Ferrum, forming Fe2+ and Fe3+
mcqs.why: The notes table gives iron from the Latin name Ferrum with symbol Fe and common ions Fe2+ and Fe3+, distinct from silver, gold and lead in the same table.

mcqs.q: What is an ion, and how is its charge written in its symbol?
options: A neutral atom; its charge is written before the symbol
An atom or group of atoms carrying a charge from loss or gain of electrons; the charge is written as a superscript after the symbol
A molecule with no electrons; the charge is written below the symbol
An isotope with extra neutrons; the charge is written as a subscript
mcqs.why: An ion is an atom or group of atoms that carries a charge due to loss or gain of electrons, and its symbol is the element symbol followed by the charge as a superscript, e.g. Na+, Ca2+ and Cl-.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a polyatomic ion as written in the notes?
mcqs.why: Polyatomic ions are written the same way as simple ions, with the charge as a superscript. The notes give SO4 2-, NO3- and NH4+ as polyatomic examples, while Cl-, Na+ and O2- contain one atom each.

mcqs.q: An atom has more electrons than protons. What does it form?
mcqs.why: Ions form when protons and electrons are unequal: more electrons than protons gives a negative anion, while more protons than electrons gives a positive cation.

mcqs.q: A sodium atom (2,8,1) forms Na+. How does this happen?
options: It gains one electron from another atom
It loses one proton from its nucleus
It gains one proton in its nucleus
It loses its outer electron: Na -> Na+ + e-
mcqs.why: Cations form when an atom loses electrons. Sodium (2,8,1) loses its outer electron, written as Na -> Na+ + e-, leaving the stable (2,8) arrangement noted in the key points.

mcqs.q: How many protons and electrons does the Na+ ion have?
mcqs.why: Working: a sodium atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons; after losing 1 electron, electrons = 11 - 1 = 10. So Na+ has 11 protons and 10 electrons, a net charge of 1+.

mcqs.q: A chlorine atom (2,8,7) gains one electron to form Cl-. How many protons and electrons does Cl- have?
mcqs.why: Working: chlorine has 17 protons and 17 electrons; after gaining 1 electron, electrons = 17 + 1 = 18. So Cl- has 17 protons and 18 electrons, a net charge of 1-, with arrangement (2,8,8).

lessons.notes_html:
Symbols of Elements

Each element has a unique symbol of one or two letters. The first letter is always capital; the second letter, if present, is lowercase. Examples: beryllium Be, calcium Ca. Some symbols come from Latin names.

ElementLatin NameSymbolCommon Ion
SodiumNatriumNaNa+
PotassiumKaliumKK+
IronFerrumFeFe2+, Fe3+
SilverArgentumAgAg+
GoldAurumAuAu+, Au3+
LeadPlumbumPbPb2+, Pb4+

Symbols of Ions

An ion is an atom or group of atoms that carries a charge due to loss or gain of electrons. Its symbol is the element symbol followed by the charge as a superscript: cations Na+, Ca2+, Fe3+; anions Cl-, O2-, N3-. Polyatomic ions are written the same way, e.g. SO4 2-, NO3-, NH4+.

Formation of Ions

Ions form when an atom or molecule has an unequal number of protons and electrons. More electrons than protons gives a negative anion; more protons than electrons gives a positive cation.

Cations form when an atom loses one or more electrons. Metals such as sodium, calcium and aluminium commonly form cations. A sodium atom (2,8,1) has 11 protons and 11 electrons. It loses its outer electron: Na → Na+ + e-. The Na+ ion has 11 protons and 10 electrons, a net charge of 1+.

Anions form when an atom gains one or more electrons. Non-metals such as nitrogen, oxygen and chlorine commonly form anions. A chlorine atom (2,8,7) needs one electron to complete its octet. It gains one electron: Cl + e- → Cl-. The Cl- ion has 17 protons and 18 electrons, a net charge of 1-.

Common cations: Al3+, Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, H+. Common anions: Br-, Cl-, F-, I-, N3-, O2-, S2-.

Key Points

  • Element symbols: first letter capital, second letter lowercase.
  • Some symbols come from Latin names: Na (Natrium), K (Kalium), Fe (Ferrum), Au (Aurum), Pb (Plumbum).
  • An ion's charge is written as a superscript after the symbol.
  • Losing electrons forms a positive cation; gaining electrons forms a negative anion.
  • Na (2,8,1) → Na+ (2,8); Cl (2,8,7) → Cl- (2,8,8).
lessons.title: Symbols of Elements and Formation of Ions

mcqs.q: What are chemical bonds, as defined in the notes?
options: The forces that bind atoms together in a molecule
The electrons in the innermost shell of an atom
The spaces between molecules in a gas
The charges carried by free ions in solution
mcqs.why: The notes define the forces that bind atoms together in a molecule as chemical bonds or chemical forces, and atoms form these bonds to achieve a stable electronic configuration.

mcqs.q: Why do atoms form bonds?
options: To increase the number of protons in the nucleus
To achieve a stable electronic configuration
To become gases at room temperature
To lose their outermost shells completely
mcqs.why: Atoms form bonds to achieve a stable electronic configuration, like the completely filled outermost shells that make noble gases chemically stable and largely unreactive.

mcqs.q: Why are noble gases such as helium, neon and argon chemically stable and largely unreactive?
options: Because they have incomplete outermost shells
Because they have no electrons at all
Because they have completely filled outermost shells
Because they easily lose electrons to other atoms
mcqs.why: Noble gases have completely filled outermost shells, which makes them chemically stable and largely unreactive, unlike representative elements with incomplete outer shells.

mcqs.q: How many valence electrons do helium and the other noble gases have?
mcqs.why: The notes state helium has two electrons (1s2), while the other noble gases have eight valence electrons (ns2np6), as also shown in the noble gas table.

mcqs.q: What are the shell configurations of neon and argon in the notes table?
mcqs.why: The noble gas table gives neon (atomic number 10) the configuration 2, 8 and argon (atomic number 18) the configuration 2, 8, 8, each with 8 valence electrons.

mcqs.q: What is the shell configuration of krypton (Kr, atomic number 36) in the notes table?
mcqs.why: The table gives krypton the configuration 2, 8, 18, 8 with 8 valence electrons; xenon is 2, 8, 18, 18, 8 and radon is 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 8.

mcqs.q: Who introduced the Octet Rule, in which year, and what does it say?
options: Bohr in 1913; electrons move in fixed-energy orbits
Lewis in 1916; atoms gain, lose or share electrons to complete their valence shell with eight electrons
Thomson in 1904; electrons are embedded in a positive sphere
Lewis in 1927; electrons are arranged in subshells and orbitals
mcqs.why: In 1916, G. N. Lewis introduced the Octet Rule: atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to complete their valence shell with eight electrons, achieving the stable configuration of the nearest noble gas.

mcqs.q: Which elements follow the Duplet Rule, and what do they aim for?
options: Sodium, magnesium and nitrogen; they aim for eight electrons
Helium, neon and argon; they aim for eight electrons
Hydrogen, lithium and beryllium; they aim for two electrons in their valence shell, like helium
Groups VA-VIIA elements; they aim for three electrons
mcqs.why: Very light elements such as hydrogen, lithium and beryllium follow the Duplet Rule: they aim for two electrons in their valence shell, similar to helium, instead of the octet of eight.

mcqs.q: How do sodium and magnesium attain the configuration of neon, according to the notes?
options: Sodium gains one electron and magnesium gains two electrons
Sodium loses two electrons and magnesium loses one electron
Both share electrons with neon atoms
Sodium loses one electron and magnesium loses two electrons
mcqs.why: Groups IA and IIA elements tend to lose one or two electrons to achieve the previous noble gas configuration: sodium loses one electron and magnesium loses two to attain the configuration of neon.

mcqs.q: How does nitrogen achieve the configuration of neon, and how are noble gases classified?
options: Nitrogen gains three electrons; noble gases are group VIIIA, fully filled and inert, not representative elements
Nitrogen loses three electrons; noble gases are group IA representative elements
Nitrogen gains one electron; noble gases are group VIIA representative elements
Nitrogen shares three protons; noble gases have incomplete shells and are highly reactive
mcqs.why: Groups VA-VIIA elements gain electrons to complete their octet, and nitrogen gains three electrons to achieve neon. Noble gases (group VIIIA) have fully filled shells, are inert and are not classified as representative elements.

lessons.notes_html:
Everything around us is made of matter. Matter is made of atoms that combine to form molecules. The forces that bind atoms together in a molecule are called chemical bonds or chemical forces. Atoms form bonds to achieve a stable electronic configuration.

Noble Gases

Noble gases such as helium, neon and argon have completely filled outermost shells. This makes them chemically stable and largely unreactive. Helium has two electrons (1s2), while the other noble gases have eight valence electrons (ns2np6). Neon lights glow because electricity excites the electrons, but the stable configuration prevents chemical reactions.

Noble GasAtomic NumberShell ConfigurationValence Electrons
Helium (He)222
Neon (Ne)102, 88
Argon (Ar)182, 8, 88
Krypton (Kr)362, 8, 18, 88
Xenon (Xe)542, 8, 18, 18, 88
Radon (Rn)862, 8, 18, 32, 18, 88

Octet and Duplet Rules

In 1916, G. N. Lewis introduced the Octet Rule: atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to complete their valence shell with eight electrons, achieving the stable configuration of the nearest noble gas. Very light elements such as hydrogen, lithium and beryllium follow the Duplet Rule: they aim for two electrons in their valence shell, similar to helium.

  • Groups IA and IIA elements tend to lose one or two electrons to achieve the configuration of the previous noble gas. Example: sodium (Na) loses one electron and magnesium (Mg) loses two electrons to attain the configuration of neon.
  • Groups VA-VIIA elements tend to gain three, two or one electron(s) to complete their octet. Example: nitrogen (N) gains three electrons to achieve the configuration of neon.

Representative elements are in groups IA to VIIA. They have incomplete outer shells, so they are chemically reactive. Noble gases (group VIIIA) have fully filled outer shells, are chemically inert, and are not classified as representative elements. By comparing configurations, chemists can predict reactivity: noble gas-like configurations are stable with very low reactivity, while incomplete configurations are highly reactive. Valence electrons decide whether an element forms ionic bonds (by transfer) or covalent bonds (by sharing).

Key Points

  • Atoms bond to achieve a stable noble gas electronic configuration.
  • Octet Rule: atoms gain, lose or share electrons to get 8 valence electrons.
  • Duplet Rule: light elements like H, Li and Be aim for 2 valence electrons.
  • Noble gases have full outer shells, so they are stable and unreactive.
  • Groups IA-IIA lose electrons; groups VA-VIIA gain electrons.
lessons.title: Noble Gas Configuration and the Octet-Duplet Rules

mcqs.q: How is a cation formed, and what charge does it carry?
options: By gaining electrons; it carries a negative charge
By losing electrons; it carries a positive charge
