By gaining protons; it carries a negative charge
By sharing electrons; it carries no charge
mcqs.why: Cations are positively charged ions formed when atoms, usually metals, lose one or more electrons to achieve a stable noble gas configuration, so protons outnumber electrons.

mcqs.q: How is an anion formed, and what charge does it carry?
options: By losing electrons; it carries a positive charge
By losing protons; it carries a positive charge
By gaining electrons; it carries a negative charge
By sharing electrons equally; it carries no charge
mcqs.why: Anions are negatively charged ions formed when atoms, usually non-metals, gain one or more electrons, so electrons outnumber protons in the ion.

mcqs.q: How do cation and anion sizes compare with their parent atoms?
options: Cations are larger and anions are smaller than the parent atom
Both cations and anions are larger than the parent atom
Both cations and anions are smaller than the parent atom
Cations are smaller and anions are larger than the parent atom
mcqs.why: The comparison table in the notes states cations are smaller than the parent atom, while anions are larger than the parent atom.

mcqs.q: Which set gives examples of cations and anions from the notes table?
options: Cations H+, Mg2+, Al3+; anions F-, O2-, N3-
Cations F-, O2-, N3-; anions H+, Mg2+, Al3+
Cations Na and Ca atoms; anions Mg and Al atoms
Cations Cl- and Br-; anions K+ and H+
mcqs.why: The notes table lists H+, Mg2+ and Al3+ as cation examples (formed by electron loss, positive) and F-, O2- and N3- as anion examples (formed by electron gain, negative).

mcqs.q: What do sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+) ions do in the body, according to the notes?
options: They carry oxygen in the blood
They regulate heartbeat and nerve transmission, and their balance lets muscles contract properly
They dissolve salts to give water its polarity
They form the rigid lattice of table salt
mcqs.why: The notes state that sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+) ions regulate heartbeat and nerve transmission, and without their proper balance our muscles would not contract properly.

mcqs.q: Why are metals described as electropositive?
options: Because they gain electrons easily due to high ionisation energies
Because they are on the right side with many valence electrons
Because they tend to lose electrons easily to form positive ions, having low ionisation energies
Because they never form ions at all
mcqs.why: Metals are electropositive because they tend to lose electrons easily to form positive ions; they have low ionisation energies, sit on the left side of the periodic table and have fewer valence electrons.

mcqs.q: Calcium (2,8,8,2) forms Ca2+. Which equation and configuration are correct?
options: Ca -> Ca2+ + 2e-, giving Ca2+ (2,8,8), similar to argon
Ca -> Ca+ + 1e-, giving Ca+ (2,8,8,1), similar to argon
Ca + 1e- -> Ca-, giving Ca- (2,8,8,3), similar to neon
mcqs.why: Working: calcium starts with 2 + 8 + 8 + 2 = 20 electrons and loses 2, leaving 2 + 8 + 8 = 18 electrons. The notes give Ca -> Ca2+ + 2e-, with Ca2+ (2,8,8) similar to argon.

mcqs.q: Oxygen (2,6) forms O2-. Which equation and configuration are correct?
options: O -> O2- + 2e-, giving O2- (2,4), similar to helium
O + 1e- -> O-, giving O- (2,7), similar to neon
O + 2e- -> O2-, giving O2- (2,8), similar to neon
O loses two protons from its nucleus, forming a different element
mcqs.why: Working: oxygen starts with 2 + 6 = 8 electrons and gains 2, giving 2 + 8 = 10 electrons. The notes give O + 2e- -> O2-, with O2- (2,8) similar to neon.

mcqs.q: Why do non-metals form anions rather than cations?
options: Because they have low ionisation energies and lose electrons easily
Because they have high ionisation energies, so losing electrons is difficult, and they gain electrons easily
Because they are on the left side with fewer valence electrons
Because they have completely filled outer shells already
mcqs.why: Non-metals are electronegative and gain electrons easily to form negative ions; they have high ionisation energies so it is difficult for them to lose electrons, and they sit in the top right with more valence electrons.

mcqs.q: What does the electronegativity of oxygen enable in the body, according to the notes?
options: It gives water its polarity, enabling water to dissolve salts and nutrients so blood can carry them through the body
It regulates heartbeat and nerve transmission directly
It makes oxygen lose electrons to form positive ions in blood
It prevents water from dissolving any salts or nutrients
mcqs.why: The notes say the electronegativity of oxygen gives water its polarity, which enables water to dissolve salts and nutrients, allowing blood to carry essential substances throughout the body.

lessons.notes_html:
An ion is formed when an atom loses or gains electrons to achieve a stable noble gas configuration, so protons and electrons are no longer equal in number.

Cations and Anions

Cations are positively charged ions formed when atoms (usually metals) lose electrons. Anions are negatively charged ions formed when atoms (usually non-metals) gain electrons.

FeatureCationsAnions
FormationLoss of one or more electronsGain of one or more electrons
ChargePositiveNegative
SizeSmaller than parent atomLarger than parent atom
ElectronegativityLowHigh
ExamplesH+, Mg2+, Al3+F-, O2-, N3-

Sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+) ions regulate heartbeat and nerve transmission. Without the proper balance of these ions, our muscles would not contract properly.

Electropositive Nature of Metals

Metals are electropositive: they tend to lose electrons easily to form positive ions. This is because metals have low ionisation energies. Metals are on the left side of the periodic table, with fewer valence electrons and a greater tendency to lose them. Example: calcium (Ca) in Group 2 has two outer electrons (2,8,8,2). It readily loses them to form Ca2+ (2,8,8), similar to argon: Ca → Ca2+ + 2e-.

Electronegative Nature of Non-metals

Non-metals are electronegative: they tend to gain electrons easily to form negative ions. They have high ionisation energies, so it is difficult for them to lose electrons. They are in the top right side of the periodic table, with more valence electrons. Example: oxygen (O) in Group VIA has six outer electrons (2,6). By gaining two electrons it forms O2- (2,8), similar to neon: O + 2e- → O2-.

The electronegativity of oxygen gives water its polarity. This enables water to dissolve salts and nutrients, allowing blood to carry essential substances throughout the body. Chemical bonds between atoms are typically classified as ionic or covalent.

Key Points

  • Cations form by loss of electrons and carry a positive charge.
  • Anions form by gain of electrons and carry a negative charge.
  • Metals are electropositive with low ionisation energy; they form cations.
  • Non-metals are electronegative with high ionisation energy; they form anions.
  • Example: Ca → Ca2+ + 2e- and O + 2e- → O2-.
lessons.title: Formation of Cations and Anions

mcqs.q: What is an ionic bond?
options: A strong attraction formed by mutual sharing of electrons
A sea of delocalised electrons around metal ions
A strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions
A weak force between separate covalent molecules
mcqs.why: An ionic bond is a strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed after electron transfer creates cations and anions.

mcqs.q: Between which kinds of atoms does an ionic bond form?
options: Between two metals with low electronegativity
Between a high-electronegativity non-metal and a low-electronegativity metal
Between two atoms with a small difference in electronegativity
Between two noble gases with filled shells
mcqs.why: An ionic bond forms when an atom with high electronegativity (a non-metal) bonds with an atom with low electronegativity (a metal), and the non-metal attracts electrons away from the metal.

mcqs.q: How does the ionic bond in sodium chloride (NaCl) form?
options: Sodium and chlorine share one pair of electrons equally
Chlorine transfers its outer electron to sodium
Sodium transfers two outer electrons to chlorine
Sodium transfers its one outer electron to chlorine, forming Na+ and Cl- which attract each other
mcqs.why: In NaCl, sodium transfers its one outer electron to chlorine. Na becomes Na+ and Cl becomes Cl-, and the oppositely charged ions attract each other ionically.

mcqs.q: How does the ionic bonding in magnesium oxide (MgO) form?
options: Magnesium transfers its two outer electrons to oxygen, forming Mg2+ and O2-
Oxygen transfers two electrons to magnesium, forming O2+ and Mg2-
Magnesium and oxygen share two pairs of electrons
Magnesium transfers one electron to oxygen, forming Mg+ and O-
mcqs.why: In MgO, magnesium transfers its two outer electrons to oxygen. Mg becomes Mg2+ and O becomes O2-, held together by ionic bonds between the opposite charges.

mcqs.q: Why do ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points?
options: Because of weak forces between separate molecules
Because of the strong electrostatic forces between ions in their crystal lattice, needing much heat energy to break
Because their ions are free to move at room temperature
Because they share electrons in double bonds
mcqs.why: Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points due to the strong electrostatic forces between ions in their crystal lattice; much heat energy is needed to break the ionic bonds, unlike weaker covalent compounds.

mcqs.q: What is a covalent bond, and when does it form?
options: Transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal with a large electronegativity difference
Attraction between delocalised electrons and metal cations
A strong attraction formed by mutual sharing of electrons, when there is a small difference in electronegativity
Attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice
mcqs.why: A covalent bond is a strong attraction formed by the mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms, forming when there is a small difference in electronegativity; it can be nonpolar (equal sharing) or polar (unequal sharing).

mcqs.q: How many shared pairs are in a single covalent bond, and which is an example?
mcqs.why: The bond table gives a single bond as one shared pair shown by a single dash, with examples H2 (H-H), Cl2 and HCl (H-Cl).

mcqs.q: How many shared pairs are in a double covalent bond, and which is an example?
mcqs.why: A double bond shares two pairs of electrons and is shown by a double dash; the notes give O2 (O=O), CO2 (O=C=O) and ethene C2H4 as double-bond examples.

mcqs.q: How many shared pairs are in a triple covalent bond, and which is an example?
mcqs.why: A triple bond shares three pairs of electrons; the notes give N2, hydrogen cyanide HCN and ethyne C2H2 as triple-bond examples.

mcqs.q: Why is the bond in O2 called a double bond?
options: Because there are two separate O2 molecules joined together
Because each oxygen donates two electrons to a metal
Because oxygen forms two ionic bonds in a lattice
Because the two oxygen atoms share two pairs of electrons, giving each atom the two electrons it needs to complete its octet
mcqs.why: Each oxygen needs two more electrons to complete its octet, and sharing two pairs gives each atom the two electrons it needs, so the bond in O2 is a double bond.

lessons.notes_html:
Chemical bonds are the forces that hold atoms together to form molecules and compounds. Bonds form through sharing or transferring electrons to reach a stable electron configuration.

Ionic Bond

An ionic bond is a strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions. It forms when an atom with high electronegativity (a non-metal) bonds with an atom with low electronegativity (a metal). The non-metal attracts electrons away from the metal, forming cations and anions.

  • Sodium chloride (NaCl): sodium transfers its one outer electron to chlorine. Na becomes Na+ and Cl becomes Cl-, and the oppositely charged ions attract each other.
  • Magnesium oxide (MgO): magnesium transfers its two outer electrons to oxygen. Mg becomes Mg2+ and O becomes O2-, held together by ionic bonds.

Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points due to the strong electrostatic forces between ions in their crystal lattice. Much heat energy is needed to break the ionic bonds. Covalent compounds have weaker forces and lower melting and boiling points.

Covalent Bond

A covalent bond is a strong attraction formed by the mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms. It forms when there is a small difference in electronegativity. Covalent bonds can be nonpolar (equal sharing) or polar (unequal sharing).

TypeShared PairsSymbolExamples
Single bondOne pairSingle dash (-)H2 (H-H), Cl2, HCl (H-Cl)
Double bondTwo pairsDouble dash (=)O2 (O=O), CO2 (O=C=O), Ethene C2H4 (CH2=CH2)
Triple bondThree pairsTriple dashN2, Hydrogen cyanide HCN (H-C triple bond N), Ethyne C2H2 (H-C triple bond C-H)

The bond in O2 is called a double bond because the two oxygen atoms share two pairs of electrons. Each oxygen needs two more electrons to complete its octet, and sharing two pairs gives each atom the two electrons it needs.

Key Points

  • Ionic bond: transfer of electrons, strong attraction between opposite ions.
  • Covalent bond: mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms.
  • Single bond shares 1 pair, double bond shares 2 pairs, triple bond shares 3 pairs.
  • Examples: NaCl and MgO are ionic; H2, O2 and N2 are covalent.
lessons.title: Ionic and Covalent Bonds

mcqs.q: What is a coordinate covalent (dative) bond?
options: A bond where each atom donates one electron to the shared pair
A bond formed when a shared pair of electrons is donated by one of the bonded atoms
A bond between delocalised electrons and metal cations
A bond between oppositely charged ions only
mcqs.why: A coordinate covalent bond is formed when a shared pair of electrons is donated by one of the bonded atoms; both shared electrons come from that one atom, the donor.

mcqs.q: In a coordinate bond, what are the donor and acceptor, and how is the bond shown?
options: The donor accepts the pair, the acceptor donates it, shown by a double dash
The donor donates the shared pair, the acceptor accepts it, shown by an arrow
Both atoms are donors, shown by a single dash
The donor is always a metal cation, shown by brackets
mcqs.why: The atom that donates the shared pair is called the donor and the atom that accepts it is called the acceptor, and this bond is shown by an arrow, as in NH4+ and H3O+.

mcqs.q: In the ammonia-boron trifluoride example, who donates and who accepts the electron pair?
options: Boron in BF3 donates its pair to nitrogen in NH3
Nitrogen in NH3 donates its lone pair to boron in BF3, forming NH3 -> BF3
Both NH3 and BF3 donate one electron each equally
Fluorine donates its pair to hydrogen
mcqs.why: The notes state that nitrogen in NH3 donates its lone pair to boron in BF3, forming NH3 -> BF3, making nitrogen the donor and boron the acceptor.

mcqs.q: How does the ammonium ion in ammonium chloride form?
options: Nitrogen in NH3 donates a pair to H+ from HCl, forming NH4+ with Cl-
Chlorine donates a pair to nitrogen, forming Cl+
H+ donates a pair to chlorine, forming HCl2
NH3 gains a proton by losing its lone pair to Cl-
mcqs.why: In ammonium chloride, nitrogen in NH3 donates a pair to H+ from HCl, forming the ammonium ion NH4+ with Cl-, a coordinate bond example from the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the hydronium ion (H3O+), according to the notes?
options: An ion that forms only in molten salts
An ion that forms whenever an acid dissolves in water, and is the actual carrier of acidity in solutions
A metal ion found in sodium and magnesium metal
An anion that makes solutions alkaline
mcqs.why: The hydronium ion (H3O+) forms whenever an acid dissolves in water, and the notes identify this ion as the actual carrier of acidity in solutions.

mcqs.q: What is a metallic bond?
options: Attraction between shared electrons and two nuclei only
Attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice
A strong electrostatic attraction between a sea of delocalised electrons and positively charged metal ions
A shared pair donated by one atom to another
mcqs.why: A metallic bond is a strong electrostatic attraction between a cloud (or sea) of delocalised electrons and positively charged metal ions, as shown in the notes for sodium and magnesium metal.

mcqs.q: Which physical state and examples match metallic bonds in the comparison table?
options: Solid, liquid and gas; examples H2, N2, H2O, CH4
Solid only with no exceptions; examples NaCl, CaO, KBr
Liquid except mercury; examples Fe, Au, Ag
Solid except mercury; examples Fe, Au, Ag
mcqs.why: The comparison table gives metallic bonds the physical state solid except mercury, with examples Fe, Au and Ag, while NaCl, CaO and KBr are ionic examples.

mcqs.q: How does electrical conductivity compare across the three bond types in the table?
options: Ionic very high, covalent low, metallic very low
Ionic low, covalent very low, metallic very high
All three have very high conductivity
Metallic low, ionic very high, covalent very high
mcqs.why: The table gives electrical conductivity as low for ionic bonds, very low for covalent bonds and very high for metallic bonds, because free delocalised electrons carry charge in metals.

mcqs.q: Which bonds are directional and which are non-directional?
options: Ionic bonds are directional; covalent and metallic are non-directional
Metallic bonds are directional; ionic and covalent are non-directional
Covalent bonds are directional; ionic and metallic bonds are non-directional
All three bond types are directional
mcqs.why: The notes state that ionic and metallic bonds are non-directional, while covalent bonds are directional, a key comparison point between the three bond types.

mcqs.q: What is the effect of electronegativity on metallic bonds, and why are metals ductile conductors?
options: Electronegativity strongly controls metallic bonds; metals conduct because their ions are fixed
Electronegativity has little or no influence on metallic bonds; free delocalised electrons make metals very good conductors and ductile
Electronegativity makes metallic bonds directional; metals are ductile because they share pairs
Electronegativity has no influence on ionic bonds; metals conduct because they form anions
mcqs.why: Electronegativity influences ionic and covalent bond strength but has little or no influence on metallic bonds; free delocalised electrons make metals very good conductors and ductile, and metallic bonds are listed as ductile in the table.

lessons.notes_html:
Coordinate Covalent Bond (Dative Bond)

A coordinate covalent bond is formed when a shared pair of electrons is donated by one of the bonded atoms. The atom that donates the shared pair is called the donor, while the atom that accepts it is called the acceptor. This bond is shown by an arrow (→).

  • Ammonia-Boron Trifluoride: nitrogen in NH3 donates its lone pair to boron in BF3, forming NH3 → BF3.
  • Ammonium chloride: nitrogen in NH3 donates a pair to H+ from HCl, forming the ammonium ion NH4+ with Cl-.
  • The hydronium ion (H3O+) forms whenever an acid dissolves in water. This ion is the actual carrier of acidity in solutions.

Metallic Bond

A metallic bond is a strong electrostatic attraction between a cloud (or sea) of delocalised electrons and positively charged metal ions. Metal atoms lose their valence electrons, forming a sea of electrons. The delocalised electrons can move freely within the metal lattice and are attracted to all the cations. Fig. 4.1 in the book shows this for sodium metal and magnesium metal.

FeatureIonic BondsCovalent BondsMetallic Bonds
DefinitionAttraction between oppositely charged ionsAttraction between shared electrons and two nucleiAttraction between delocalised electrons and positive cations
Bond strengthStronger than covalent and metallicWeaker than ionic, stronger than metallicWeaker than ionic and covalent
Physical stateSolidSolid, liquid and gasSolid except mercury
Electrical conductivityLowVery lowVery high
DuctilityNot ductileNot ductileDuctile
Melting / boiling pointsHigherLowerHigh
ExamplesNaCl, CaO, KBrH2, N2, H2O, CH4Fe, Au, Ag

Electronegativity influences the strength of ionic and covalent bonds, but has little or no influence on metallic bonds. Ionic and metallic bonds are non-directional; covalent bonds are directional.

Key Points

  • In a coordinate bond, both shared electrons come from one atom, the donor.
  • Coordinate bond is shown by an arrow, e.g. in NH4+ and H3O+.
  • Metallic bond: sea of delocalised electrons around positive metal ions.
  • Free delocalised electrons make metals very good conductors and ductile.
lessons.title: Coordinate Covalent and Metallic Bonds

mcqs.q: Why do ionic compounds need a substantial amount of energy to melt or boil?
options: Because of weak forces between their separate molecules
Because of their strong ionic bonds in the lattice, which need much energy to break and to overcome in the liquid
Because their ions move freely even in the solid
mcqs.why: Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points because of strong ionic bonds in the lattice; substantial energy is needed to break these bonds to form liquid and to overcome forces in the liquid to form gas.

mcqs.q: Why do covalent compounds generally have lower melting and boiling points than ionic compounds?
options: Because of stronger electrostatic forces in their lattice
Because of the weaker forces between covalent molecules, so less energy is needed
Because their ions are mobile in the solid state
Because they are electrolytes in water
mcqs.why: Covalent compounds generally have lower melting and boiling points because of the weaker forces between covalent molecules, so less energy is needed compared with breaking ionic lattice bonds.

mcqs.q: When do ionic compounds conduct electricity, and why not in the solid state?
options: Only in the solid state, because ions are fixed in place
In every state, because ions are always mobile
When melted or dissolved in water, because ions become mobile; in the solid, ions are fixed in a rigid lattice
Never, because they have no charged particles at all
mcqs.why: Ionic compounds do not conduct in the solid state because ions are fixed in a rigid lattice; when melted or dissolved in water, ions become mobile and can conduct electricity.

mcqs.q: Why are covalent compounds generally poor conductors, and what is the exception?
options: They have many free ions; the exception is diamond
They lack free charged particles in any state; the exception is graphite, which conducts due to delocalised electrons
Their electrons are delocalised like metals; there is no exception
They ionise fully in water; the exception is NaCl
mcqs.why: Covalent compounds are poor conductors due to lack of free charged particles in any state; graphite is the exception because it conducts due to delocalised electrons.

mcqs.q: Why are metals excellent conductors of heat and electricity?
options: Because their ions are fixed in a rigid lattice
Because they have no free electrons
Because delocalised electrons move freely in the lattice
Because they dissolve in water to form electrolytes
mcqs.why: Metallic bonds give excellent conduction of heat and electricity due to delocalised electrons moving freely in the lattice, unlike ionic solids where ions are fixed.

mcqs.q: What are electrolytes, and what happens when HCl dissolves in water?
options: Substances that never conduct; HCl stays as whole molecules only
Substances that ionise in water and conduct electricity; HCl ionises into H+ (aq) and Cl- (aq)
Only metals that conduct in the solid state; HCl forms H2 and Cl2
Covalent compounds with no ions; HCl forms OH- (aq) only
mcqs.why: Substances that ionise in water and conduct electricity are called electrolytes. The notes give HCl in water ionising into H+ (aq) and Cl- (aq), with strong acids, strong bases and salts as other electrolytes.

mcqs.q: Which solubility rule is given in the notes?
options: Polar and ionic compounds frequently dissolve in polar solvents such as water
Ionic compounds dissolve only in non-polar solvents
Covalent compounds always dissolve in water
Metals dissolve in water to form electrolytes
mcqs.why: Solubility depends on bonding and polarity: polar and ionic compounds frequently dissolve in polar solvents such as water, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which graphite uses depend on it conducting electricity?
options: Cutting, grinding and drilling tools in mining
Electrodes for batteries and electrical wires, and use in rechargeable lithium-ion batteries
Lenses, prisms and semiconductor heat sinks only
Cooking salt and construction calcium carbonate
mcqs.why: Graphite conducts electricity, so it is used as electrodes for batteries and electrical wires, and in rechargeable lithium-ion batteries for smartphones and laptops, alongside its lubricant and heat-sink uses.

mcqs.q: Why is diamond used for cutting, grinding and drilling tools, and where does it form naturally?
options: Because it conducts electricity; it forms at the Earth surface
Because it is soft and malleable; it forms in seawater
Because it is the most rigid material; it forms naturally 150-200 km beneath the Earth surface under extreme pressure and temperature
Because it is ductile like gold; it forms in lithium-ion batteries
mcqs.why: Diamond is the most rigid material, ideal for cutting, grinding and drilling tools in mining, construction and machining, and diamonds form naturally 150-200 km beneath the Earth surface under extreme pressure and temperature.

mcqs.q: Which metallic uses and gold fact are given in the notes?
options: NaCl in cooking and CaCO3 in construction; gold forms sheets thicker than steel plates
Copper in electrical wiring and steel in construction; gold can be hammered into sheets thinner than human hair due to free movement of delocalised electrons
Graphite in pencils and diamond in lenses; gold cannot be shaped at all
Copper in cooking and steel in batteries; gold dissolves in water as an electrolyte
mcqs.why: Metallic uses in the notes include copper in electrical wiring and steel in construction for strength and durability, and gold can be hammered into sheets thinner than human hair because of free movement of delocalised electrons. NaCl and CaCO3 are the ionic uses.

lessons.notes_html:
Melting and Boiling Points

Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points because of their strong ionic bonds in the lattice. A substantial amount of energy is needed to break these bonds and change solid to liquid, and to overcome the forces in the liquid to form gas. Covalent compounds generally have lower melting and boiling points because of the weaker forces between covalent molecules, so less energy is needed. Metallic bonds have considerable strength, which gives metals significant tensile strength and hardness.

Conductivity

  • Ionic compounds: do not conduct in the solid state because ions are fixed in a rigid lattice. When melted or dissolved in water, ions become mobile and can conduct electricity.
  • Covalent compounds: poor conductors due to lack of free charged particles in any state. Exception: graphite conducts due to delocalised electrons.
  • Metallic bonds: excellent conductors of heat and electricity due to delocalised electrons moving freely in the lattice.

Substances that ionise in water and conduct electricity are called electrolytes. Example: HCl in water ionises into H+ (aq) and Cl- (aq). Other electrolytes are strong acids, strong bases and salts. Solubility depends on bonding and polarity: polar and ionic compounds frequently dissolve in polar solvents such as water. Ionic compounds are hard with high strength; metallic compounds show malleability and ductility. Ionic compounds are typically more reactive than metallic compounds.

Uses from Bonding

  • Ionic: NaCl is used in cooking; calcium carbonate CaCO3 is used in construction materials.
  • Metallic: copper is used in electrical wiring; steel is used in construction for strength and durability.

Industrial Uses: Graphite, Diamond and Metals

Graphite: conducts electricity, so used as electrodes for batteries and electrical wires; good thermal conductivity for heat sinks, crucibles and refractories; high thermal stability for aerospace industry; lubricating properties decrease friction in locks, pencils and bearings. It is used in rechargeable lithium-ion batteries for smartphones and laptops.

Diamond: most rigid material, ideal for cutting, grinding and drilling tools in mining, construction and machining; high thermal conductivity for heat sinks and the semiconductor industry; high refractive index for lenses, prisms and cutting tools; resistant to most chemicals. Diamonds form naturally 150-200 km beneath the Earth surface under extreme pressure and temperature.

Metals: strong and rigid for construction and manufacturing; high electrical conductivity for wires and cables; malleable and ductile, shaped for automotive, aerospace and consumer electronics; high thermal conductivity for heat exchangers and electronic components. Gold can be hammered into sheets thinner than human hair because of free movement of delocalised electrons.

Key Points

  • Ionic compounds: high melting/boiling points; conduct only when molten or dissolved.
  • Covalent compounds: low melting/boiling points; generally poor conductors.
  • Metals: excellent conductors; strong, malleable and ductile.
  • Graphite for electrodes and lubricants; diamond for cutting tools; metals for wires and construction.
lessons.title: Properties, Conductivity and Industrial Uses

mcqs.q: What do dot-and-cross diagrams use to represent outer shell electrons?
options: Lines for electrons and arrows for bonds only
Dots and crosses for the arrangement of outer shell electrons
Letters and numbers from the periodic table
mcqs.why: Dot-and-cross diagrams use dots (.) and crosses (x) to represent the arrangement of outer shell electrons in an ionic or covalent compound, showing lone pairs and electron distribution.

mcqs.q: What do dot-and-cross diagrams show about a compound?
options: Only the melting point and boiling point
The total number of lone pairs on each atom and the electron distribution in compounds
Only the charges of free ions in solution
mcqs.why: The notes state dot-and-cross diagrams show the total number of lone pairs on each atom and the electron distribution in compounds, using dots and crosses for all electrons shown.

mcqs.q: In the steps for dot-and-cross diagrams, which atom is the central atom?
options: The atom with the fewest bonds
The atom with the highest number of bonds, with other atoms arranged around it
mcqs.why: One step is to identify the central atom (the one with the highest number of bonds) and arrange other atoms around it, before writing configurations with dots and crosses.

mcqs.q: How is the charge of each ion indicated in a dot-and-cross diagram?
options: By underlining the symbol in red
Using brackets, with the charge at the upper right corner
By writing the charge below the symbol as a subscript
By drawing an arrow from cation to anion
mcqs.why: The steps say to indicate the charge of each ion using brackets, with the charge at the upper right corner, after illustrating transfer or sharing of electrons using arrows.

mcqs.q: In dot-and-cross diagrams, how many electrons should each atom have around it?
options: Eight electrons in lone or shared pairs for each atom, apart from hydrogen
Two electrons for every atom including oxygen
One electron for each atom regardless of bonding
mcqs.why: The steps require arranging eight electron positions around each atom and ensuring each atom, apart from hydrogen, has eight electrons in lone or shared pairs.

mcqs.q: In Lewis dot structures, what do dots and lines represent?
options: Dots for protons and lines for neutrons
Dots for electrons and lines for bonds
Dots for ions and lines for charges
Dots for lone pairs only and lines for lone pairs only
mcqs.why: Lewis dot structures represent the distribution of outer shell electrons, predict electron pairs and bonds, using dots for electrons and lines for bonds.

mcqs.q: What is the first step in drawing a Lewis dot diagram?
options: Assign lone pairs to every atom first
Draw double and triple bonds first to satisfy octets
Draw a skeletal diagram linking all atoms with single bonds
Enclose every atom in brackets with its charge
mcqs.why: The Lewis steps begin by drawing a skeletal diagram linking all atoms with single bonds, then assigning lone pairs, and only if needed drawing double or triple bonds to satisfy octet configurations.

lessons.notes_html:
Dot-and-cross diagrams use dots and crosses to represent the arrangement of outer shell electrons in an ionic or covalent compound. All electrons are shown by dots (.) and crosses (x). They show the total number of lone pairs on each atom and the electron distribution in compounds.

Steps for Dot-and-Cross Diagrams

  • Write the symbols for each atom or ion.
  • Identify the central atom (the one with the highest number of bonds) and arrange other atoms around it.
  • Write the electronic configuration for each atom or ion, using dots and crosses.
  • Arrange eight electron positions around each atom.
  • Illustrate the transfer or sharing of electrons using arrows.
  • Indicate the charge of each ion using brackets, with the charge at the upper right corner.
  • Ensure each atom, apart from hydrogen, has eight electrons in lone or shared pairs.

Lewis Dot Structure

Lewis dot structures represent the distribution of outer shell electrons around an atom or molecule. They predict electron pairs and bonds, using dots for electrons and lines for bonds. Examples in the book include Oxygen, Nitrogen, Hydrogen Cyanide, Water, Methane, Ammonium ion and Nitrate ion.

Steps for Lewis Dot Diagrams

  • Draw a skeletal diagram linking all atoms with single bonds.
  • Assign lone pairs of electrons to each atom.
  • If needed, draw double or triple bonds to satisfy octet configurations.
  • Surround each atom with eight electrons (except hydrogen).
  • Represent ionic bonds as full valence shells, where the more electronegative element gains electrons.
  • Use brackets to enclose charged atoms and superscript the charge, if necessary.

Dot-and-Cross Models

Ionic compounds: NaBr - sodium transfers its one outer electron to bromine, forming Na+ and Br- held by ionic bonds. NaF - sodium transfers one electron to fluorine, forming Na+ and F-. CaCl2 - calcium transfers its two outer electrons, one to each chlorine, forming Ca2+ and two Cl- ions. Table salt and calcium chloride used to melt ice on roads are ionic compounds.

Covalent compounds: dot-and-cross diagrams and Lewis structures are drawn for H2, Cl2, O2, N2, H2O, CH4, NH3, HCl, CH3OH, C2H4, CO2 and HCN. Compare the rigid three-dimensional lattice of NaCl with the simple molecular structure of CH4.

Key Points

  • Dot-and-cross diagrams show outer electrons with dots and crosses.
  • Lewis structures use dots for electrons and lines for bonds.
  • Ionic diagrams show electron transfer and charges in brackets.
  • Covalent diagrams show shared pairs; every atom except H gets an octet.
lessons.title: Dot-and-Cross Diagrams and Lewis Dot Structures

lessons.notes_html:
Stoichiometry is a branch of chemistry that focuses on the relationships between the quantities of substances involved in a chemical reaction. The word comes from two Greek words: stoicheion, meaning element, and metron, meaning measure. It uses balanced chemical equations to determine the quantities of reactants and products, including their masses, moles and volumes. It is used in medicine to determine appropriate drug dosages.

Chemical Formula

The chemical formula is the symbolic representation of a molecule or compound. It uses atomic symbols and numerical subscripts to indicate the number and types of atoms present in a substance. For example, sodium chloride is NaCl — one atom of sodium and one atom of chlorine. Nitric acid is HNO3 — one atom of hydrogen, one atom of nitrogen and three atoms of oxygen. There are two main types of chemical formulae: molecular and empirical.

Molecular Formula

The molecular formula indicates the exact number of atoms in a molecule. It specifies the number of atoms of each element present in a given molecule, using subscripts for the quantities. In water, H2O, the subscript 2 shows two hydrogen atoms, and no subscript for oxygen means a single oxygen atom. In carbon dioxide, CO2, no subscript for carbon means one carbon atom, and the subscript 2 shows two oxygen atoms.

Empirical Formula

The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of different atoms in a compound. It represents the relative number of atoms of each element. The molecular formula of glucose is C6H12O6 — six carbon, twelve hydrogen and six oxygen atoms. The simplest whole-number ratio of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen is 1:2:1, so the empirical formula of glucose is CH2O. The word empirical comes from Greek empeirikos, meaning experimental.

CompoundMolecular FormulaEmpirical Formula
WaterH2OH2O
Acetic acidCH3COOHCH2O
GlucoseC6H12O6CH2O
AcetyleneC2H2CH
BenzeneC6H6CH
Sodium chloride (ionic)NaClNaCl
Calcium hydroxide (ionic)Ca(OH)2Ca(OH)2

Key Points

  • Stoichiometry deals with quantitative relationships between reactants and products in a chemical reaction.
  • A chemical formula uses symbols and subscripts to show the number and type of atoms in a substance.
  • The molecular formula shows the exact number of atoms in one molecule.
  • The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms, e.g. glucose C6H12O6 → CH2O.
  • No subscript after a symbol means only one atom of that element.
lessons.title: Chemical Formula, Molecular Formula and Empirical Formula

lessons.notes_html:
Compounds made of atoms from two different elements are known as binary compounds. For example, sodium chloride is a binary compound of sodium and chlorine, and ammonia contains nitrogen and hydrogen. To determine the formula and name of binary ionic compounds from their ions, it is essential to know the charges of cations and anions.

Steps to Deduce the Formula and Name

  • Step i: Identify the cations (typically metals) and anions (generally nonmetals) present in the compound.
  • Step ii: Determine the charges of the cations and anions. For main group elements the charge typically corresponds to the group number: elements in group IA have a +1 charge, those in group IIA have a +2 charge, elements in group VIA have a -2 charge, and elements in group VIIA have a -1 charge.
  • The charges of the cation and anion become the subscripts of one another in the formula of the compound, and these subscripts should be simplified to the lowest possible ratio.
  • Step iii: The name of the cation comes before the name of the anion. The cation name remains the same as the name of the element, whereas the anion name is made by replacing the ending of the element name with -ide. Sometimes it is -ite or -ate.

Examples from the Book

  • Sodium ions (Na+) and fluoride ions (F-) give NaF, named sodium fluoride.
  • Iron(III) ions (Fe3+) and oxide ions (O2-) give Fe2O3, known as iron(III) oxide or ferric oxide. The III shows that iron has a +3 oxidation state.
CationAnionFormulaName
Sodium (Na+), +1Chloride (Cl-), -1NaClSodium chloride
Magnesium (Mg2+), +2Oxide (O2-), -2MgOMagnesium oxide
Calcium (Ca2+), +2Fluoride (F-), -1CaF2Calcium fluoride
Aluminium (Al3+), +3Bromide (Br-), -1AlBr3Aluminium bromide
Magnesium (Mg2+), +2Nitride (N3-), -3Mg3N2Magnesium nitride
Iron(II) (Fe2+), +2Sulphide (S2-), -2FeSIron(II) sulphide

Key Points

  • A binary compound contains atoms of two different elements.
  • Cations are typically metals and anions are generally nonmetals.
  • Ion charges become each other's subscripts, simplified to the lowest ratio.
  • Group IA = +1, group IIA = +2, group VIA = -2, group VIIA = -1.
  • Name the cation first; change the anion ending to -ide, e.g. Mg2+ and Cl- give MgCl2.
lessons.title: Formula and Name of Binary Ionic Compounds from Ions

lessons.notes_html:
To deduce the formula of a molecular substance from the structure of its molecules, a systematic approach is used. The structure shows which elements are present and how many atoms of each element are joined in one molecule.

Steps

  • i) Identify the atoms present: Examine the molecular structure and identify the symbols that represent different elements. Note each type of atom present within the molecule.
  • ii) Count the number of each type of atom: Analyse the molecular structure to determine the quantity of each type of atom. Pay attention to the subscripts and coefficients associated with each atom in the structure, as they indicate the number of atoms present.
  • iii) Identify elements: In the book example, the structural formula has carbon (C), hydrogen (H) and oxygen (O).
  • iv) Count the atoms: That structural formula contains 2 atoms of C, 4 atoms of H and 2 atoms of O.

So, from the structural formula (acetic acid, shown as H3C-C(=O)-OH), the deduced molecular formula is C2H4O2.

The book activity uses modelling kits, or beads and toothpicks, to build and draw molecules from structural formulae such as MgO, CH4, C2H6, C3H6 and C6H6. Building a model helps in counting every atom correctly and in simplifying atom ratios where needed.

Key Points

  • First identify every element shown in the molecular structure.
  • Then count the atoms of each element carefully, watching subscripts and coefficients.
  • Write the counts as subscripts to get the molecular formula.
  • Book example: 2 C, 4 H and 2 O atoms give the molecular formula C2H4O2.
lessons.title: Deducing Molecular Formulae from Molecular Structures

lessons.notes_html:
Atoms are extremely small particles, making it impossible to weigh or count them directly. Samples are increased to a size where we can weigh or count them. They cannot be counted in pairs, dozens or reams. The chemist's unit of measurement is called a mole.

Mole

The word mole means 'huge mass'. Its symbol is 'mol' and it is represented by 'n'. One mole is the amount of substance that contains as many particles (atoms, molecules, ions or formula units) as the number of atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12. The concept of the mole was first proposed by Wilhelm Ostwald in 1895.

Avogadro's Number

One mole contains 6.0221421 x 10^23 particles, which we usually round to 6.022 x 10^23. Scientists call this value Avogadro's number in honour of the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro (1776-1856). It is represented by NA and its unit is read as 'particles per mole'. The particles can be atoms, molecules, ions or electrons.

Relationship Between Mole and Avogadro's Number

One mole of any substance contains 6.022 x 10^23 tiny particles. Avogadro's number helps us connect the very small world of atoms and molecules to the amounts we can measure in the lab. For example, one mole of water has 6.022 x 10^23 water molecules, and one mole of sodium has the same number of sodium atoms.

SubstanceFormulaMass of One MoleParticles in One Mole
Oxygen atomO16 g/mol6.022 x 10^23 atoms
Oxygen moleculeO232 g/mol6.022 x 10^23 molecules
WaterH2O18 g/mol6.022 x 10^23 molecules
Potassium nitrateKNO3101 g/mol6.022 x 10^23 formula units
Carbonate ionCO3 2-60 g/mol6.022 x 10^23 ions

Key Points

  • A mole (mol, symbol n) is the chemist's counting unit for very small particles.
  • One mole contains as many particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12.
  • Avogadro's number NA = 6.022 x 10^23 particles per mole.
  • One mole of any substance — atoms, molecules, ions or formula units — always has this same number of particles.
lessons.title: The Mole and Avogadro's Number

lessons.notes_html:
The molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance (atoms, molecules or formula units), expressed in grams. Its unit is grams per mole (g/mol). To determine it, we convert the units from atomic mass units to grams. A hydrogen atom has an atomic mass of 1.008 amu, so its molar mass is 1.008 g/mol and it contains 6.022 x 10^23 atoms. Ammonia (NH3) has a molecular mass of 17 amu, so its molar mass is 17 g/mol and it contains 6.022 x 10^23 molecules. Examples: carbon 12.0 g/mol, sulphur 32.0 g/mol, carbon dioxide 44.0 g/mol, sodium chloride 58.5 g/mol, copper(II) sulphate CuSO4 159.6 g/mol.

Example 5.1 — Molar Mass of Hydrogen Peroxide (H2O2)

  • 2 moles of hydrogen x 1 g/mol = 2 g
  • 2 moles of oxygen x 16 g/mol = 32 g
  • Molar mass of H2O2 = 34 g, so molar mass is 34 g/mol

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Amount of substance (mol) = mass / molar massTo find number of moles
Mass of substance = moles x molar massTo find mass in grams
Molar mass = given mass / moles of substanceTo find molar mass
Number of particles = n x NATo find atoms, molecules or formula units

Worked Examples from the Book

  • Example 5.2 — Moles in 27 g of H2O: Molar mass of H2O = 18 g/mol. Moles = 27 g / 18 g/mol = 1.5 mol.
  • Example 5.3 — Mass of 10 moles of H2O: Molar mass = 2(1) + 1(16) = 18 g/mol. Mass = 18 g/mol x 10 mol = 180 g.
  • Example 5.4 — Molar mass of CO2: 22 g of CO2 equals 0.5 moles. Molar mass = 22 g / 0.5 mol = 44 g/mol.
  • Example 5.5 — Molecules in 2 moles of CO2: Number of particles = n x NA = 2 mol x 6.02 x 10^23 molecules/mol = 12.04 x 10^23 molecules.

Stoichiometry also works in the body: complete combustion of glucose (C6H12O6) in cells requires exactly 6 moles of O2 for each mole of glucose.

Key Points

  • Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in g/mol; it has the same number as the atomic, molecular or formula mass in amu.
  • Amount of substance = mass / molar mass.
  • Mass = moles x molar mass, and molar mass = mass / moles.
  • Number of particles = number of moles x Avogadro's number (n x NA).
  • Water has molar mass 18 g/mol and carbon dioxide 44 g/mol.
lessons.title: Molar Mass and Calculations Using Amount, Mass and Molar Mass

lessons.notes_html:
A chemical equation is the symbolic representation of a chemical reaction. In a chemical equation, the starting substances, or reactants, are on the left; the final substances, or products, are on the right, with an arrow placed between them to indicate a transformation.

The numbers and types of atoms are the same on both sides of the reaction arrow, as required by the law of conservation of mass. A chemical equation in which the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides is called a balanced chemical equation. The symbols written after a substance represent its physical state.

SymbolMeaning
+Plus or added to (placed between substances)
→Yields; produces (points to products)
(s)Solid state (written after a substance)
(l)Liquid state (written after a substance)
(g)Gaseous state (written after a substance)
(aq)Aqueous solution (substance dissolved in water)
Heat symbol over arrowHeat is added (when written above or below arrow)

Examples of Balanced Chemical Equations

  • Combustion of methane: One mole of methane (CH4) reacts with two moles of oxygen (O2) to produce one mole of carbon dioxide (CO2) and two moles of water vapour (H2O). CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g)
  • Decomposition of calcium carbonate: Calcium carbonate (CaCO3) decomposes upon heating to form calcium oxide (CaO) and carbon dioxide (CO2). CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g)
  • Neutralisation: Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide to produce sodium chloride and water. HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)

Ionic Equations

The full ionic equation for the neutralisation is: H+(aq) + Cl-(aq) + Na+(aq) + OH-(aq) → Na+(aq) + Cl-(aq) + H2O(l). The sodium (Na+) and chloride (Cl-) ions are spectator ions — ions that do not participate in the reaction and appear unchanged on both sides. Cancelling them gives the net ionic equation: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) → H2O(l).

Key Points

  • Reactants are written on the left and products on the right, joined by an arrow.
  • In a balanced equation, atoms of each element are equal on both sides — conservation of mass.
  • State symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous solution.
  • A balanced equation shows formulas, mole ratios and physical states.
  • Spectator ions appear unchanged on both sides; removing them gives the net ionic equation, e.g. H+(aq) + OH-(aq) → H2O(l).
lessons.title: Construction of Chemical Equations
Redox Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
Electrochemistry is a branch of chemistry that studies the conversion of chemical energy into electrical energy, and the chemical changes caused by an electric current. It mainly involves oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions. It explains corrosion and its prevention, and applications like batteries, electroplating and metal refining.

In a redox reaction, both oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously. Oxidation is the loss of electrons by one substance and reduction is the gain of electrons by another. They cannot occur independently; they always happen together in equivalent amounts, so for every atom or molecule oxidised, another must be reduced.

Three Definitions of Oxidation and Reduction

BasisOxidationReduction
OxygenAddition of oxygenRemoval of oxygen
HydrogenRemoval of hydrogenAddition of hydrogen
ElectronsLoss of electronsGain of electrons
  • Oxygen: PbO(s) + C(s) → Pb(s) + CO(g). Lead oxide is reduced to lead by losing oxygen, while carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide by gaining oxygen.
  • Hydrogen: H2S(g) + Cl2(g) → S(l) + 2HCl(g). Hydrogen sulphide is oxidised to sulphur by losing hydrogen, while chlorine is reduced to HCl by gaining hydrogen.
  • Electrons: 2Na(s) + Cl2(g) → 2NaCl(s). Sodium is oxidised to a sodium ion by losing electrons, while chlorine is reduced to a chloride ion by gaining electrons.

The element that loses electrons is oxidised and its oxidation number increases. The element that gains electrons is reduced and its oxidation number decreases. Remember OILRIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

Do You Know? Alessandro Volta developed the first battery in 1800 using zinc and copper plates separated by a saline cloth. In 1836, John Frederic Daniell designed the more reliable Daniell cell, which powered early telegraph systems.

Key Points

  • Electrochemistry studies conversion between chemical energy and electrical energy through redox reactions.
  • In a redox reaction, oxidation and reduction always occur together in equivalent amounts.
  • Oxidation = gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen, or loss of electrons.
  • Reduction = loss of oxygen, gain of hydrogen, or gain of electrons.
  • OILRIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

lessons.title: Oxidation States and Roman Numerals
lessons.notes_html:
The oxidation state, or oxidation number, of an atom represents the hypothetical charge it would have in a compound. This charge is positive when electrons are lost (oxidation) and negative when electrons are gained (reduction). It helps us track electron movement during chemical reactions, especially redox reactions. It does not always show the actual charge on the atom. For example, in H2O (water), hydrogen has an oxidation state of +1 and oxygen has an oxidation state of -2.

Roman Numerals for Variable Oxidation States

Roman numerals indicate the oxidation state of an element in a compound when it can exist in more than one oxidation state. For example, in FeCl2, iron has an oxidation state of +2, denoted II as Fe(II). In FeCl3, iron has an oxidation state of +3, represented as Fe(III).

Roman NumeralOxidation Number
I+1
II+2
III+3
IV+4
V+5
VI+6
VII+7
VIII+8

Elements with Variable Oxidation States

  • Lead: Lead(II) ion: Pb2+; Lead(IV) ion: Pb4+.
  • Manganese can exist in four common oxidation states: +2, +4, +6 and +7. Manganese(II) ion: Mn2+; Manganese(IV) ion: Mn4+; Manganese(VI) ion: Mn6+; Manganese(VII) ion: Mn7+.

Chemistry in Your Body: Cellular respiration is a redox process: glucose is oxidised to release energy, while oxygen is reduced to form water.

Key Points

  • Oxidation number is the hypothetical charge an atom would have in a compound.
  • It is positive on loss of electrons and negative on gain of electrons.
  • Roman numerals are used when an element has more than one oxidation state, e.g. Fe(II) is +2 and Fe(III) is +3.
  • In water, hydrogen is +1 and oxygen is -2.

lessons.title: Oxidising and Reducing Agents
lessons.notes_html:
A substance that loses electrons during a chemical reaction is called a reducing agent or reductant. A substance that gains electrons during a chemical reaction is called an oxidising agent or oxidant.

  • The oxidising agent oxidises other substances, increasing their oxidation state, and is itself reduced.
  • The reducing agent reduces other substances, decreasing their oxidation state, and is itself oxidised.
  • The total number of electrons gained by the oxidising agent is always equal to the total number of electrons lost by the reducing agent.

Examples from the Book

  • H2SO3 + 2NO → H2SO4 + N2O. Sulphurous acid is the reducing agent because sulphur loses electrons, while nitric oxide is the oxidising agent as nitrogen gains electrons. Electrons are transferred from sulphur to nitrogen.
  • 2HNO3 + Mg → Mg(NO3)2 + H2. Nitric acid acts as an oxidising agent, while magnesium acts as a reducing agent.
  • H2S + Cl2 → 2HCl + S. Hydrogen sulphide acts as a reducing agent and chlorine as an oxidising agent.

Strong Agents

  • Among the elements, metals are reducing agents, while non-metals are oxidising agents. Alkali metals are strong reducing agents because they readily form positive ions, and halogens are strong oxidising agents because they readily form negative ions.
  • Among the compounds, potassium dichromate (K2Cr2O7) and potassium permanganate (KMnO4) are the most important strong oxidising agents, whereas hydrogen sulphide (H2S), sulphur dioxide (SO2) and ferrous sulphate (FeSO4) are some important reducing agents.

Key Points

  • Reducing agent loses electrons and is itself oxidised.
  • Oxidising agent gains electrons and is itself reduced.
  • Electrons gained by the oxidising agent equal electrons lost by the reducing agent.
  • Metals are reducing agents; non-metals are oxidising agents.
  • Strong oxidising agents include K2Cr2O7 and KMnO4.

lessons.title: Oxidation Numbers: Free State and Principles
lessons.notes_html:
Oxidation Number of Elements in Their Free State

When elements are in their pure form or free state, their oxidation number is always zero. This applies to all elements, whether they exist as single atoms (such as Na or Mg), diatomic molecules (such as O2 or N2), or larger structures. The oxidation number can change when elements form compounds or undergo chemical reactions involving gain or loss of electrons.

Oxidation Number of Monatomic Ions

The oxidation state of a monatomic ion is equivalent to its charge. For example, Na+ has an oxidation number of 1+, Mg2+ has 2+, Al3+ has 3+, Cl- has 1-, O2- has 2-, and N3- has 3-.

IonOxidation Number
Na++1
Mg2++2
Al3++3
Cl--1
O2--2
N3--3

Sum of Oxidation Numbers in a Neutral Compound

The sum of the oxidation numbers of all the elements in a neutral compound is equal to zero. For example, in potassium permanganate (KMnO4), potassium is 1+, manganese is 7+, and oxygen is 2-. Hence the sum is 1(1+) + 1(7+) + 4(2-) = 0.

Sum of Oxidation Numbers in an Ion

The sum of the oxidation numbers of all the elements in an ion is equal to the charge on the ion. For example, in the sulphate ion (SO4 2-), sulphur is 6+ and oxygen is 2-. Hence the sum is 1(6+) + 4(2-) = 2-, which is the charge on the ion.

Key Points

  • Every element in its free state has oxidation number zero, e.g. Na, Mg, O2, N2.
  • For a monatomic ion, oxidation number = charge on the ion.
  • In a neutral compound, oxidation numbers add up to zero.
  • In an ion, oxidation numbers add up to the charge on the ion.
  • Example: in KMnO4, K is +1, Mn is +7 and O is -2, summing to zero.

lessons.title: Formula of Ionic Compounds from Ionic Charges
lessons.notes_html:
The formula of an ionic compound can be derived from the ionic charges of cations and anions, as well as their oxidation numbers. The formula is written so that the charges of the cation and anion sum to zero.

General Steps

  • Step 1: Identify the charges of the cations and anions present in the compound. The charges can frequently be determined from the oxidation states of the elements.
  • Step 2: Determine the smallest whole-number ratio of cations to anions that produces a neutral compound.
  • Step 3: Balance the charges of the ions to establish the formula. The subscripts are adjusted to ensure the net charge remains zero.

Worked Examples

  • Sodium chloride (NaCl): Sodium forms Na+ with a +1 charge and chlorine forms Cl- with a -1 charge. The charges are already balanced (both 1+ and 1-), so the smallest ratio is 1:1 and the formula is NaCl.
  • Sodium phosphate (Na3PO4): Na has charge +1 and PO4 has charge -3. Three Na atoms give total ion charge +3 and one PO4 gives -3, so the total charge on the molecule is 0.

Calcium (Ca2+)Chloride (Cl-)CaCl2Calcium chloride

Iron (Fe3+)Oxide (O2-)Fe2O3Iron(III) oxide

Zinc (Zn2+)Oxide (O2-)ZnOZinc oxide
Lead (Pb2+)Oxide (O2-)PbOLead(II) oxide

Key Points

  • An ionic formula is written so total positive and negative charges sum to zero.
  • Use the smallest whole-number ratio of cations to anions.
  • Ion charges often come from the oxidation states of the elements.
  • Examples: Na+ and Cl- give NaCl; Na+ and PO4 3- give Na3PO4.

lessons.title: Identification of Redox Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
Identification of Redox Reactions

Redox reactions can be identified by observing the colour changes that occur when acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) or aqueous potassium iodide is used. Potassium manganate(VII) is a powerful oxidising agent and has a purple colour, while potassium iodide is a reducing agent and is colourless in solution.

When acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) is added to the solution of aqueous potassium iodide, the purple colour of the potassium manganate(VII) disappears. This is because the potassium manganate(VII) is reduced to manganese(II), which is colourless. On the other hand, the colourless potassium iodide solution is oxidised to iodine, which is brown in colour.

2KMnO4 + 8H2SO4 + 10KI → 2MnSO4 + 6K2SO4 + 5I2 + 8H2O

SubstanceAt StartChangeAt End

Potassium iodide, KIColourlessOxidised to iodine, I2Brown

Key Points

  • Redox reactions are identified by colour changes with acidified KMnO4 and KI.
  • Acidified potassium manganate(VII) is purple and is a powerful oxidising agent.
  • When reduced to manganese(II), the purple colour disappears (colourless).
  • Colourless potassium iodide is oxidised to brown iodine.

lessons.title: Corrosion and Rusting of Iron
lessons.notes_html:
Corrosion

Corrosion is the term applied to metal rust caused by an electrochemical process. Most of you are familiar with the corrosion of iron, which develops as a reddish-brown rust. There are other examples of corrosion as well, such as the black tarnish on silver and the red or green corrosion that may develop on copper and brass.

Corrosion leads to the deterioration of essential properties in a material. Corrosion is primarily due to redox reactions that occur in the presence of oxygen, moisture, and acidic oxides, such as CO2. It damages metals and converts them into oxides, which are ultimately converted into hydroxides; for example, iron is converted into Fe2O3.nH2O (rust). Corrosion causes significant damage to metals and other materials worldwide, costing billions of dollars each year.

Rusting of Iron

The rusting of iron chemically means the electrochemical reaction of iron with oxygen and water to form Fe(OH)3, Fe(OH)2, or even Fe2O3.H2O. Chemically, the corrosion of iron is written as:

4Fe + 3O2 + H2O → 2Fe2O3.nH2O (Hydrated Ferric oxide)

Misconception vs Reality: Rusting does not occur instantly when iron comes into contact with water. Rusting is a slow electrochemical process that requires water, oxygen, and often salts to speed up the reaction.

Amazing Fact: If all the rust produced worldwide each year could be collected, it would weigh millions of tonnes, enough to build thousands of ships.

Key Points

  • Corrosion is metal rust caused by an electrochemical process.
  • Examples: reddish-brown rust on iron, black tarnish on silver, red or green corrosion on copper and brass.
  • Corrosion is due to redox reactions in the presence of oxygen, moisture and acidic oxides such as CO2.
  • Rust is hydrated ferric oxide, Fe2O3.nH2O: 4Fe + 3O2 + H2O → 2Fe2O3.nH2O.
  • Rusting is slow and needs water and oxygen; salts speed it up.

lessons.title: Prevention of Corrosion
lessons.notes_html:
Several methods have been developed to protect metal from corrosion.

Alloying

Corrosion can be prevented or minimised by reducing reactivity through alloying. Stainless steel, an alloy of iron, chromium, silicon, and nickel, is highly resistant to corrosion. It is used for knives, spoons, forks, utensils, scissors, and surgical instruments.

Oil or Grease Coating

Covering the surface with grease or oil protects nuts, bolts, tools, machinery parts, and engine components from rusting.

Paint Coating

Covering the surface with paint protects iron bridges, windows, doors, gates, and the bodies of rickshaws, cars, buses, and trucks from corrosion (rusting).

Galvanising

Galvanising is coating metal (iron) sheets with a thin layer of zinc to prevent corrosion. It is also known as zinc coating or anode coating, and is done by dipping a clean iron sheet into a molten zinc bath. If the zinc coating is damaged by a scratch or dent, the zinc reacts with the air to form a new protective layer. Zinc plating remains effective even under high humidity and moisture, and gives durable and cost-effective rust protection for steel.

Electroplating

Electroplating deposits a thin layer of metal onto the surface of another metal using an electric current. Metals are commonly coated with nickel, chromium, silver, or gold to enhance corrosion resistance and improve appearance. The object to be coated is placed in an electrolyte solution and acts as the cathode, while the coating metal serves as the anode. When current is applied, metal ions from the solution are deposited onto the object. It is used in jewellery making to coat inexpensive metals with gold or silver, giving a shiny, durable finish.

Sacrificial Coating

In sacrificial protection, a sacrificial anode, made of a more reactive metal, is intentionally attached to the surface of the less reactive metal (cathode) that requires protection. The more reactive metal corrodes preferentially when exposed to oxygen and water, sacrificing itself to prevent corrosion of the less reactive and more valuable metal. For example, magnesium blocks are used on ships to protect the steel hull from rusting.

Key Points

  • Alloying reduces reactivity, e.g. stainless steel resists corrosion.
  • Oil or grease coating and paint coating cover and protect the surface.
  • Galvanising coats iron with zinc and protects even when scratched.
  • Electroplating deposits Ni, Cr, Ag or Au with electric current; object is cathode, coating metal is anode.
  • Sacrificial coating: a more reactive metal, e.g. magnesium on ships, corrodes instead of the protected metal.

lessons.title: Chemical System and Surroundings
lessons.notes_html:
Thermodynamics is the study of energy, work, heat, temperature, and their interrelations. It also addresses the transformation of energy between objects or substances. Chemical energetics applies thermodynamic principles to understand and predict energy changes in chemical reactions. This includes the absorption or release of heat, the formation and breaking of chemical bonds, and the overall energy balance of a reaction. It also considers the energy stored in the chemical bonds of molecules.

System and Surroundings

A system refers to anything (substance or mixture) under observation or experimentation in the laboratory. Everything in the universe that is not part of the system is termed the surroundings. In thermodynamics, the combination of the system and its surroundings is collectively known as the universe.

Universe = System + Surrounding

Types of Chemical Systems

Type of SystemExchanges with SurroundingsExamples
Open systemBoth energy and matterOpen reaction flask, a rocket, an uncovered cup of tea
Closed systemEnergy only, not matter (mass)Sealed reaction flask, a gas in a closed container
Isolated systemNeither energy nor matterThermos flask containing hot green tea

Chemical energetics commonly studies closed systems, focusing on energy changes.

Key Points

  • Chemical energetics studies energy changes during chemical reactions.
  • System = the substance or mixture under observation; surroundings = everything else.
  • Universe = system + surroundings.
  • Open system exchanges energy and matter; closed system exchanges energy only; isolated system exchanges neither.

mcqs.why: The notes state the combination of the system and its surroundings is collectively known as the universe in thermodynamics.

lessons.title: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions and Enthalpy Change
lessons.notes_html:
Chemical reactions can be either exothermic or endothermic.

Exothermic Reactions (Delta H Less Than 0)

Reactions or processes in which heat is released from the system to the surroundings are called exothermic reactions (Greek: exo = outside; hence, heat flows out). The combustion of petrol, coal and wood is an example. Other exothermic processes include freezing, condensation and deposition. The amount of heat released is indicated by Delta H with a negative sign because heat flows from the system to the surroundings. The majority of reactions that occur at room temperature are exothermic in nature.

Endothermic Reactions (Delta H Greater Than 0)

Reactions or processes in which heat is absorbed from the surroundings to the system are called endothermic reactions (Greek: endon = within; thus, heat flows in). Photosynthesis in plants is an example. Other endothermic processes include melting, evaporation and sublimation. Melting of ice is an endothermic process, and sweating cools the body because evaporation of water is endothermic and draws heat from the skin. The amount of heat absorbed is indicated by Delta H with a positive sign, as heat flows from the surroundings to the system.

ReactionTypeDelta H
CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → 2H2O(l) + CO2(g)Exothermic-890.3 kJ/mol
C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g)Exothermic-393.51 kJ/mol
C(s) + H2O(g) → CO(g) + H2(g)Endothermic+131.4 kJ/mol
N2(g) + O2(g) → 2NO(g)Endothermic+180.51 kJ/mol

Enthalpy Change: Thermal Energy in Chemical Reactions

Enthalpy (H) is the total heat content of a system. In thermochemical processes, the change in enthalpy (Delta H) indicates the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure. The enthalpy change measures the heat transferred during a chemical reaction and is usually expressed in kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol). It indicates the difference between the energy released when new bonds form in the products and the energy absorbed in breaking the old bonds of the reactants. The symbol Delta means change in.

Do You Know? The heat produced by burning just 1 gram of fat is almost twice the energy from burning 1 gram of carbohydrate.

Key Points

  • Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings; Delta H is negative.
  • Endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings; Delta H is positive.
  • Enthalpy (H) is the total heat content of a system.
  • Delta H is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure, in kJ/mol.
  • Combustion is exothermic; photosynthesis, melting and evaporation are endothermic.

mcqs.why: Exothermic reactions release heat from the system to the surroundings; exo means outside, so heat flows out of the system.

mcqs.why: The notes give the combustion of petrol, coal and wood as an example of an exothermic reaction that releases heat.

In no direction, because endothermic reactions involve no heat
mcqs.why: Endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings to the system; endon means within, thus heat flows in.

mcqs.q: What is the sign of ΔH for an endothermic reaction?
options: Positive, as heat flows from the surroundings to the system
Negative, as heat flows from the system to the surroundings
mcqs.why: The amount of heat absorbed in an endothermic reaction is indicated by ΔH with a positive sign, as heat flows from the surroundings into the system.

mcqs.q: Which example is given in the notes for an endothermic process?
mcqs.why: Photosynthesis in plants is given as an endothermic example, and melting, evaporation and sublimation are also listed as endothermic processes.

mcqs.why: Sweating cools the body because evaporation of water is endothermic and draws heat from the skin, as explained in the notes.

options: The total heat content of a system

mcqs.why: The notes define enthalpy, H, as the total heat content of a system, and ΔH indicates heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

mcqs.why: The enthalpy change measures heat transferred during a chemical reaction and is usually expressed in kilojoules per mole, written kJ/mol.

lessons.title: Activation Energy
lessons.notes_html:
The minimum amount of energy required to initiate a chemical reaction is known as activation energy, represented by Ea. Its units are joules or kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol).

The reactants are not directly converted into products. They first gain energy to form an activated complex, which then decomposes into products. Activation energy represents an energy barrier (or energy hill) between the reactants and products. The reactant molecules must cross this energy barrier before they can form the products.

Crossing this barrier is similar to carrying a ball to the top of a mountain and then rolling it down the other side. If the ball fails to reach the peak, it will roll back down. Similarly, if activation energy is not provided, the reaction will not start and the reactants will not be converted into products. For example, striking a match provides, through friction, the activation energy needed to ignite the chemicals on the match head.

Exothermic and Endothermic Energy Diagrams

  • In exothermic reactions, the potential energy of the reactants is higher than that of the products. This difference is indicated by Delta H, which is negative.
  • In endothermic reactions, the potential energy of the reactants is lower than that of the products. This difference is indicated by Delta H, which is positive. We must provide the activation energy, Ea, to initiate the reaction to form an activated complex.
  • Activation energy is the energy difference between the reactants and the activated complex.

Forward and Reverse Reactions

  • For exothermic reactions, the activation energy for the forward reaction is lower than that of the reverse reaction, because the reactants are at a higher energy level than the products.
  • For endothermic reactions, the activation energy for the forward reaction is higher than that of the reverse reaction, because the reactants are at a lower energy level than the products.
  • Reactions that are exothermic in the forward direction will be endothermic in the reverse direction.
  • Fast reactions typically have low activation energies, whereas slow reactions have high activation energies. The greater the activation energy, the more energy is needed to start a reaction.

Key Points

  • Activation energy (Ea) is the minimum energy needed to start a reaction, in J or kJ/mol.
  • Reactants must cross the energy barrier and form an activated complex before products form.
  • Exothermic: reactants have higher potential energy than products; Delta H is negative.
  • Endothermic: reactants have lower potential energy than products; Delta H is positive.
  • Low activation energy means a fast reaction; high activation energy means a slow reaction.

mcqs.q: What is activation energy, Ea?
options: The minimum amount of energy required to initiate a chemical reaction
The total heat content of a system
The energy released when new bonds form
The energy difference between products and surroundings
mcqs.why: Activation energy is defined in the notes as the minimum amount of energy required to initiate a chemical reaction, represented by Ea.

mcqs.q: Before forming products, reactants first gain energy to form what?
mcqs.why: Reactants are not directly converted into products; they first gain energy to form an activated complex, which then decomposes into products.

mcqs.why: The notes state that activation energy is the energy difference between the reactants and the activated complex at the top of the barrier.

mcqs.why: If activation energy is not provided, the reaction will not start and the reactants will not be converted into products, like a ball that fails to reach the peak.

options: Friction provides the activation energy needed to ignite the chemicals on the match head
The match head acts as an enzyme that is consumed

The match removes the energy barrier completely
mcqs.why: Striking a match provides, through friction, the activation energy needed to ignite the chemicals on the match head.

mcqs.q: In an exothermic energy diagram, how does the potential energy of reactants compare with that of products?
options: Reactants have lower potential energy than products
Reactants have higher potential energy than products

Products have higher potential energy and ΔH is negative
mcqs.why: In exothermic reactions the potential energy of the reactants is higher than that of the products, and this difference is indicated by a negative ΔH.

mcqs.q: In an endothermic reaction, how does the potential energy of reactants compare with that of products?
options: Reactants have higher potential energy than products
Reactants and products have equal potential energy
Reactants have lower potential energy than products
Products have lower potential energy and ΔH is positive
mcqs.why: In endothermic reactions the potential energy of the reactants is lower than that of the products, and this difference is indicated by a positive ΔH.

mcqs.q: For an exothermic reaction, how does the activation energy of the forward reaction compare with that of the reverse reaction?
options: Forward activation energy is higher than reverse
Forward and reverse activation energies are always equal
Forward activation energy cannot be compared with reverse
Forward activation energy is lower than reverse
mcqs.why: For exothermic reactions the forward activation energy is lower than that of the reverse reaction, because reactants are at a higher energy level than products.

mcqs.q: A reaction that is exothermic in the forward direction will be what in the reverse direction?
options: Faster in the reverse direction in every case
mcqs.why: The notes state that reactions that are exothermic in the forward direction will be endothermic in the reverse direction.

mcqs.q: What does a low activation energy typically indicate about a reaction?
options: It cannot form an activated complex
mcqs.why: Fast reactions typically have low activation energies, whereas slow reactions have high activation energies, because less energy is needed to start them.

lessons.title: Catalysts and Enzymes on the Reaction Pathway
lessons.notes_html:
Catalysts are substances that alter the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed in the process. Enzymes are biological catalysts, typically proteins that accelerate biochemical reactions in living organisms.

Catalysts and enzymes change the reaction pathway by providing an alternative, more favourable route. This new reaction pathway has a lower activation energy compared to the uncatalysed reaction. Consequently, they facilitate the conversion of reactants into products more efficiently. A catalyst does not change the reactants or products; it only lowers the energy barrier, so more particles have enough energy to react.

Catalase Example

Catalase is abundant in tissues such as the liver and red blood cells, where it plays a vital role in protecting cells from oxidative damage. The rapid breakdown of hydrogen peroxide by catalase helps maintain cellular health and prevents the accumulation of potentially toxic substances within the body.

2H2O2(l) → 2H2O(l) + O2(g)

Key Points

  • A catalyst alters the rate of a reaction without being consumed.
  • Enzymes are biological catalysts, typically proteins, in living organisms.
  • Catalysts and enzymes provide an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.
  • A lower activation energy makes conversion of reactants into products more efficient.
  • Catalase rapidly breaks down hydrogen peroxide in the liver and red blood cells.

options: A substance that is consumed while slowing a reaction
A substance that alters the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed in the process
A reactant that becomes part of the products

mcqs.why: Catalysts are substances that alter the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed in the process, as defined in the notes.

mcqs.q: What are enzymes?
options: Inorganic catalysts used in power plants

Substances that raise the activation energy in living organisms
mcqs.why: Enzymes are biological catalysts, typically proteins, that accelerate biochemical reactions in living organisms.

mcqs.q: How do catalysts and enzymes change the reaction pathway?
options: By providing an alternative, more favourable route with lower activation energy
By changing the reactants into different substances before reaction
By increasing the energy barrier between reactants and products
By changing the products formed at the end of the reaction
mcqs.why: Catalysts and enzymes provide an alternative, more favourable route; this new pathway has a lower activation energy than the uncatalysed reaction.

options: It changes both the reactants and the products

It changes the products but not the reactants

mcqs.why: A catalyst does not change the reactants or products; it only lowers the energy barrier, so more particles have enough energy to react.

mcqs.q: Why does a lower activation energy help a reaction proceed?
options: Because fewer particles then need energy to react
Because more particles have enough energy to react

Because the products gain a different chemical identity
mcqs.why: With a lower energy barrier, more particles have enough energy to react, so conversion of reactants into products becomes more efficient.

mcqs.q: Which substance does catalase rapidly break down?
mcqs.why: Catalase rapidly breaks down hydrogen peroxide, helping prevent accumulation of this potentially toxic substance within the body.

mcqs.why: The equation in the notes shows hydrogen peroxide breaking down to form water and oxygen gas in the catalase-catalysed reaction.

mcqs.why: Catalase is abundant in tissues such as the liver and red blood cells, where it protects cells from oxidative damage.

mcqs.q: How does catalase help maintain cellular health?
options: By producing hydrogen peroxide inside cells

mcqs.why: The rapid breakdown of hydrogen peroxide by catalase helps maintain cellular health and prevents accumulation of potentially toxic substances.

mcqs.q: What is the overall effect of a catalyst on conversion of reactants into products?
options: It makes the conversion more efficient
It makes the conversion impossible without extra reactants
