It stops the conversion at the activated complex
It changes the conversion into a different reaction
mcqs.why: By providing a lower activation energy pathway, catalysts facilitate the conversion of reactants into products more efficiently.

lessons.title: Bond Breaking, Bond Formation and Calculation of Enthalpy Change
lessons.notes_html:
Energy Changes: Bond Breaking and Formation

During chemical reactions, old bonds are broken and new bonds are formed. Bond breakage is an endothermic process, whereas bond formation is an exothermic process.

  • If the energy needed to break old bonds in the reactants is less than the energy released by new bond formation in the products, the reaction is exothermic (Delta H less than 0). Some potential energy is converted into thermal energy. The products have less potential energy than the reactants, so the products are more stable and their bonds are stronger.
  • If the energy required to break old bonds is greater than the energy released by new bond formation, the reaction is endothermic (Delta H greater than 0). Some thermal energy is converted into potential energy. The products have greater potential energy, are less stable, and their bonds are weaker.

Exothermic reactions in power plants drive turbines to produce electricity, while endothermic processes such as photosynthesis support life on Earth. Energy calculations are essential in designing fuels for rockets, cars and power stations.

Calculation of Enthalpy Change of a Reaction

Bond energy is always a positive value because it indicates the amount of energy needed to break one mole of a specific bond in gaseous molecules. Since breaking bonds requires energy, the process is endothermic. Conversely, when new bonds form, energy is released, making the process exothermic. Bond energy is measured in kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol) and helps us estimate the heat of chemical reactions.

Delta H = Sum of B.E. (bonds broken in reactants) - Sum of B.E. (bonds formed in products), where Sigma denotes the sum of all bond energies and B.E. represents bond energy.

Worked Example: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl

Two moles of HCl gas are produced when one mole of hydrogen gas reacts with one mole of chlorine gas. One H-H bond and one Cl-Cl bond are broken, while two H-Cl bonds are formed.

BondBond Energy (kJ/mol)
H-H436
Cl-Cl242
H-Cl431
  • Step 1 — Energy absorbed to break bonds (reactants): 436 + 242 = 678 kJ
  • Step 2 — Energy released when new bonds form (products): 2 x 431 = 862 kJ
  • Step 3 — Enthalpy change: Delta H = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ/mol

The negative sign shows the reaction is exothermic.

Key Points

  • Bond breaking is endothermic (absorbs energy); bond formation is exothermic (releases energy).
  • Delta H is the sum of energies absorbed in bond breaking and released in bond forming.
  • Delta H = sum of bond energies of bonds broken - sum of bond energies of bonds formed.
  • Bond energy is always positive and is measured in kJ/mol.
  • For H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl: Delta H = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ/mol, so it is exothermic.

mcqs.q: Bond breaking during a chemical reaction is which type of process?
options: Neither, because bonds break without energy change
Exothermic only when the overall reaction is exothermic
mcqs.why: Bond breakage is an endothermic process, whereas bond formation is exothermic; breaking bonds requires energy to be absorbed.

mcqs.q: Bond formation during a chemical reaction is which type of process?
options: A process that always requires a catalyst
Neither endothermic nor exothermic in any reaction
mcqs.why: Bond formation is an exothermic process because energy is released when new bonds form in the products.

mcqs.q: When is a reaction exothermic in terms of bond energies?
options: When the energy needed to break old bonds is less than the energy released by new bond formation
When the energy needed to break old bonds is greater than the energy released by new bond formation
When no old bonds are broken in the reactants
When bond energy values are all negative
mcqs.why: If energy needed to break old bonds is less than energy released by forming new bonds, the reaction is exothermic and the products have less potential energy.

mcqs.q: When is a reaction endothermic in terms of bond energies?
options: When energy released by new bond formation is greater than energy needed to break old bonds
When products have less potential energy than reactants
When products have stronger bonds than reactants
When the energy required to break old bonds is greater than the energy released by new bond formation
mcqs.why: If energy required to break old bonds is greater than energy released by new bond formation, the reaction is endothermic and thermal energy becomes potential energy.

mcqs.q: Which formula is given in the notes for calculating enthalpy change from bond energies?
options: ΔH is bonds formed minus bonds broken
ΔH is the sum of bond energies of bonds broken minus the sum of bond energies of bonds formed
ΔH is activation energy minus bond energy
ΔH is bonds broken multiplied by bonds formed
mcqs.why: The notes give ΔH as the sum of bond energies of bonds broken in reactants minus the sum of bond energies of bonds formed in products.

mcqs.q: Why is bond energy always a positive value?
options: Because it indicates the amount of energy needed to break one mole of a specific bond in gaseous molecules
Because bond formation always absorbs energy
Because all reactions using bond energies are endothermic
Because it is measured only for products, never for reactants
mcqs.why: Bond energy is always positive because it indicates the amount of energy needed to break one mole of a specific bond in gaseous molecules.

mcqs.q: For H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl, what is the total energy absorbed to break the bonds in the reactants? (H–H: 436 kJ/mol, Cl–Cl: 242 kJ/mol)
mcqs.why: Working: one H–H bond plus one Cl–Cl bond must be broken, so 436 + 242 = 678, giving 678 kJ absorbed to break the reactant bonds.

mcqs.q: For H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl, what is the total energy released when the new bonds form in the products? (H–Cl: 431 kJ/mol)
mcqs.why: Working: two moles of H–Cl bonds are formed, so 2 × 431 = 862, giving 862 kJ released when the product bonds form.

mcqs.q: Using the bond energies in the worked example, what is ΔH for H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl?
mcqs.why: Working: energy absorbed breaking bonds is 436 + 242 = 678; energy released forming bonds is 2 × 431 = 862; then 678 - 862 = -184, so ΔH is -184 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: What does the negative ΔH in the H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl worked example show?
options: No energy is transferred in the reaction
Bond breaking released more energy than bond formation
mcqs.why: Working: 678 - 862 = -184; the negative sign for ΔH shows the reaction is exothermic, as stated at the end of the worked example.

mcqs.q: Chemical equilibrium is the state in a reversible reaction where what happens?
options: The forward reaction stops and the reverse reaction continues
The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal
All reactants are completely converted into products
The concentrations of products become zero
mcqs.why: Chemical equilibrium is the state in a reversible reaction where the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal and concentrations stay constant.

mcqs.q: An irreversible reaction is represented by which symbol?
options: Double arrows pointing in opposite directions (⇌)
A double-headed arrow for equilibrium only
No arrow, because it goes to completion
mcqs.why: Irreversible reactions go to completion and are represented by a single-headed arrow, while reversible reactions use double arrows.

mcqs.q: A reversible reaction is represented by which symbol?
options: An equals sign between reactants and products
Double arrows pointing in opposite directions (⇌)
A single arrow pointing only to the left
mcqs.why: Reversible reactions are represented by double arrows pointing in opposite directions, showing that they can occur in both directions.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes a reversible reaction?
options: It proceeds in only one direction to completion
Reactants form products, but products can never reform reactants
It is shown by a single-headed arrow
Reactants form products, and products can also reform the reactants
mcqs.why: A reversible reaction can occur in both forward and reverse directions: reactants form products, and products can also reform the reactants.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of an irreversible reaction given in the notes?
options: Formation of carbon dioxide in soda
mcqs.why: Burning of wood is listed as an irreversible reaction, along with cooking an egg, digestion of food, rusting of iron and explosion of fireworks.

mcqs.q: Which set contains only irreversible reactions from the notes?
options: Formation of ammonia, soda carbon dioxide, respiration
Rusting of iron, cooking an egg and explosion of fireworks
Soda carbon dioxide, rusting of iron, ammonia formation
Respiration, digestion of food, formation of ammonia
mcqs.why: Rusting of iron, cooking an egg and explosion of fireworks are all listed as irreversible reactions that proceed in only one direction.

mcqs.q: In a sealed bottle of soda, equilibrium is established between what?
options: Dissolved carbon dioxide in the drink and carbon dioxide gas in the bottle
Water in the drink and ice in the bottle
Sugar in the drink and gas above the liquid
Carbon dioxide gas and the glass of the bottle
mcqs.why: In a sealed soda bottle, equilibrium is established between dissolved CO2 in the drink and CO2 gas in the space above the liquid.

mcqs.q: What happens when a soda bottle is opened, according to the notes?
options: Pressure rises and more carbon dioxide dissolves
Pressure drops, equilibrium is disturbed, and CO2 escapes from the liquid forming bubbles
Equilibrium remains unchanged at the higher pressure
Carbon dioxide stops escaping because a new equilibrium forms instantly with no fizz loss
mcqs.why: When the bottle is opened, pressure drops and equilibrium is disturbed; CO2 escapes to establish a new equilibrium at lower pressure, so bubbles form.

mcqs.q: Which everyday example is given in the notes for a reversible reaction?
mcqs.why: Everyday reversible examples in the notes include respiration involving oxygen and haemoglobin, CO2 formation in soda, and formation of ammonia.

mcqs.q: Which changes can affect equilibrium, according to the opening of this lesson?
options: Only changes in the colour of reactants
Changes in temperature, pressure and concentration
Only adding a catalyst to a closed system
mcqs.why: The lesson states that equilibrium can be affected by changes in temperature, pressure and concentration in a reversible reaction.

lessons.notes_html:
Chemical equilibrium is the state in a reversible reaction where the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal. At this point, the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant over time. Equilibrium can be affected by changes in temperature, pressure and concentration.

In this unit you learn that reversible reactions are shown by the symbol ⇌ and may not go to completion, that changing the physical conditions can redirect a reversible reaction, and that reversible reactions achieve equilibrium in a closed system when the rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the reverse reaction.

Everyday Example: Soda Bottle

In a sealed bottle of soda, carbon dioxide (CO2) dissolves into the liquid under pressure, while some CO2 remains in the space above the liquid. An equilibrium is established between the dissolved CO2 in the drink and the CO2 gas in the bottle. When the bottle is opened, the pressure drops and the equilibrium is disturbed. CO2 escapes from the liquid to establish a new equilibrium at the lower pressure, so bubbles form and the drink loses its fizz gradually.

8.1.1 Irreversible Reactions

An irreversible reaction proceeds in only one direction, completely converting reactants into products. The reverse reaction may not occur under normal conditions. Such reactions go to completion and are represented by a single-headed arrow (→). Examples: burning of wood, cooking an egg, digestion of food, rusting of iron, and explosion of fireworks.

8.1.2 Reversible Reactions

A reversible reaction is a chemical process that can occur in both the forward and reverse directions. The reactants form products, and the products can also reform the reactants. Such reactions do not go to completion and ultimately attain equilibrium, where the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant. They are represented by double arrows (⇌) pointing in opposite directions.

Everyday examples include respiration (oxygen and haemoglobin), the formation of carbon dioxide in soda, and the formation of ammonia.

Rate of forward reaction = Rate of backward reaction at equilibrium.

Key Points

  • Chemical equilibrium is reached when forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stay constant.
  • Irreversible reactions go in one direction only, go to completion, and are shown by →.
  • Reversible reactions go in both directions, do not go to completion, and are shown by ⇌.
  • Examples of irreversible reactions: burning of wood, rusting of iron, cooking an egg.
  • Examples of reversible reactions: formation of ammonia, CO2 in soda, respiration.
lessons.title: Reversible and Irreversible Reactions

mcqs.q: Dynamic equilibrium is the state in which what occurs?
options: Both forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate
The forward reaction occurs but the reverse reaction has stopped
Concentrations keep increasing for products only
The reaction reaches completion in a closed system
mcqs.why: Dynamic equilibrium is the state in which both the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, and all chemical equilibria are dynamic.

mcqs.q: Once chemical equilibrium is established, how long will it last if conditions remain unchanged?
options: Only until the forward reaction stops
Only for a few seconds at the molecular level
Until all reactants are used up
mcqs.why: The notes state that once the state of chemical equilibrium is established, it will last forever if conditions remain unchanged.

mcqs.q: At the start of a reaction A + B ⇌ C + D, what happens to reactant and product concentrations?
options: Reactant concentrations increase and product concentrations decrease
Both reactant and product concentrations stay constant from the start
Reactant concentrations decrease as they are converted into products, while product concentrations increase
Product concentrations decrease as reverse reaction dominates from the start
mcqs.why: At the start, reactant concentrations decrease as they are converted into products, while product concentrations increase, so the forward reaction then slows.

mcqs.q: As a reversible reaction approaches equilibrium, how do the forward and reverse rates change?
options: Forward reaction speeds up and reverse reaction slows down
Forward reaction slows down and reverse reaction accelerates
Both reactions stop before equilibrium is reached
Both reactions keep accelerating at the same amount
mcqs.why: As products build up, the forward reaction slows down and the reverse reaction accelerates until both reactions occur at the same rate.

mcqs.q: On a concentration-time graph, what happens to all curves as equilibrium is achieved?
options: All curves become horizontal, showing concentrations remain constant
All curves cross zero at equilibrium
mcqs.why: In a concentration versus time graph, reactant curves slope down and product curves slope up, then all curves become horizontal at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: Why does equilibrium need a closed system?
options: A closed system prevents exchange of matter with surroundings, so reactants and products can react and recombine
A closed system allows matter to escape so products cannot return
A closed system stops both reactions at equilibrium
A closed system changes the equilibrium constant continuously
mcqs.why: A closed system prevents exchange of matter with its surroundings, achieving equilibrium where both reactants and products can react and recombine.

mcqs.q: From which direction can equilibrium be attained?
options: Only from a mixture containing no products
From either direction, giving the same equilibrium mixture under identical conditions
mcqs.why: Equilibrium can be attained from either direction; the same equilibrium mixture results under identical conditions regardless of the starting composition.

mcqs.q: At equilibrium, what continues at the molecular level?
options: Changes continue at the molecular level, although overall amounts of reactants and products do not change
Only product molecules continue to change
Reactants continue to disappear with no reverse change
mcqs.why: Although changes continue at the molecular level at equilibrium, the overall amounts of reactants and products do not change because rates are equal.

mcqs.q: In A + B ⇌ C + D, which direction is the forward reaction?
options: To the left, towards A and B
To the right, towards C and D
In both directions at different equations
Towards the side with fewer substances in every case
mcqs.why: For A + B ⇌ C + D, the notes identify the forward reaction as to the right towards products C and D, and the reverse reaction as to the left.

mcqs.q: Why do concentrations remain constant at equilibrium?
options: Because the reaction has stopped completely
Because products are no longer formed from reactants
Because the rates of product formation and reactant consumption are exactly equal
Because a closed system removes all reactants and products
mcqs.why: Concentrations are constant at equilibrium because the rates of product formation and reactant consumption are exactly equal.

lessons.notes_html:
The state in which both the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate is known as dynamic equilibrium. All chemical equilibria are dynamic. Once the state of chemical equilibrium is established, it will last forever if conditions remain unchanged.

Consider a general reaction where A reacts with B to produce C and D:

A + B ⇌ C + D
(Reactants) ⇌ (Products) — forward reaction to the right, reverse reaction to the left.

How Equilibrium is Reached

At the start of the reaction, the concentrations of reactants decrease as they are converted into products, while product concentrations increase. As this occurs, the forward reaction slows down and the reverse reaction accelerates. Eventually, both reactions occur at the same rate; this is the equilibrium point.

At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant because the forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates. Although changes continue at the molecular level, the overall amounts of reactants and products do not change.

Concentration-Time Graph

In a graph of concentration versus time, the reactant curves slope downwards while the product curves slope upwards. As equilibrium is achieved, all curves become horizontal, showing that the concentrations remain constant over time.

Features of the Equilibrium State

  • Equilibrium is dynamic: The reaction has not stopped, but the reverse and forward reactions are still occurring at the same rate.
  • Equilibrium is achieved in a closed system: A closed system prevents the exchange of matter with its surroundings, achieving equilibrium where both reactants and products can react and recombine.
  • Concentrations are constant at equilibrium: The rates of product formation and reactant consumption are exactly equal.
  • Equilibrium can be attained from either direction: The same equilibrium mixture will result under identical conditions, regardless of whether the reaction begins with all reactants, all products, or a combination of both.

Key Points

  • Dynamic equilibrium means forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate.
  • All chemical equilibria are dynamic and last forever if conditions remain unchanged.
  • At equilibrium, concentrations stay constant even though reactions continue at the molecular level.
  • On a concentration-time graph, all curves become horizontal at equilibrium.
  • Equilibrium needs a closed system and can be reached from either direction.
lessons.title: Chemical Equilibrium

mcqs.q: Reversible reactions can achieve equilibrium in a closed system when what condition is met?
options: The rates of the forward and backwards reactions are equal
The concentrations of reactants become zero
mcqs.why: Equilibrium is achieved in a closed system when the rates of the forward and backwards reactions are equal, resulting in no overall change in concentrations.

mcqs.q: Why is a closed system essential for equilibrium?
options: It allows matter to exchange freely with the surroundings
It prevents the exchange of matter with the surroundings, so reactants and products stay in the system
It stops evaporation and condensation completely
It makes a reversible reaction go to completion
mcqs.why: A closed system is essential because it prevents exchange of matter with the surroundings, so reactants and products stay and can react and recombine.

mcqs.q: What are the two essential conditions for equilibrium named in the key points?
options: An open system and an irreversible reaction
A catalyst and a closed container
A reversible reaction and a closed system
mcqs.why: The key points name two essential conditions for equilibrium: a reversible reaction and a closed system.

mcqs.q: In the volatile solvent example, what happens initially in a closed container?
options: Condensation occurs faster than evaporation from the start
The amount of liquid increases as vapour forms
No molecules move between liquid and vapour phases
The solvent evaporates, increasing the number of vapour molecules above the liquid
mcqs.why: Initially the solvent evaporates, increasing the number of vapour molecules above the liquid, before some vapour molecules start to condense back.

mcqs.q: When does dynamic equilibrium form in the volatile solvent example?
options: When evaporation stops and condensation continues
When condensation stops and evaporation continues
When the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation
When all the liquid has evaporated into vapour
mcqs.why: Eventually the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation, establishing a dynamic equilibrium in the closed container.

mcqs.q: At equilibrium in the closed solvent container, what remains constant?
options: The movement of molecules between phases
The amount of liquid and vapour
Only the rate of evaporation, not condensation
The number of molecules that stop moving
mcqs.why: At this stage the amount of liquid and vapour remains constant, even though molecules continue to move between the two phases.

mcqs.q: Why is this equilibrium described as dynamic, not static?
options: Because molecules keep evaporating and condensing, but at equal rates, so there is no overall change
Because the container is open to the surroundings
Because liquid amount keeps changing in one direction
Because vapour pressure rises continuously without limit
mcqs.why: It is dynamic, not static: molecules keep evaporating and condensing, but at equal rates, so there is no overall change.

mcqs.q: At equilibrium, how many molecules continue to react every second, according to the notes?
options: None, because the system is balanced
Only a few molecules in the vapour phase
Billions of molecules, but overall concentrations remain constant
All molecules, so concentrations change every second
mcqs.why: The notes state that at equilibrium billions of molecules continue to react every second, but overall concentrations remain constant.

mcqs.q: In a closed system at equilibrium, the system is described as balanced because what happens?
options: The reaction occurs in both directions at the same rate, resulting in no overall change in concentrations
Only the forward reaction occurs at a constant rate
Reactants and products are removed at the same rate
The amounts of reactants become equal to zero
mcqs.why: At equilibrium the system is balanced because the reaction occurs in both directions at the same rate, so concentrations of reactants and products remain constant over time.

mcqs.q: Which example is used in this lesson to show dynamic equilibrium in a closed system?
options: Formation of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen
Vapour pressure of a volatile solvent in a closed container
mcqs.why: The lesson uses the vapour pressure of a volatile solvent in a closed container, where evaporation and condensation reach dynamic equilibrium.

lessons.notes_html:
Reversible reactions can achieve equilibrium (a state of balance) in a closed system when the rates of the forward and backwards reactions are equal. This indicates that the reaction occurs in both directions at the same rate, resulting in no overall change in the concentrations (amounts) of the reactants and products.

At equilibrium, the system is balanced, and the concentrations of the reactants and products remain constant over time. A closed system is essential because it prevents the exchange of matter with the surroundings, so reactants and products stay in the system and can react and recombine.

Example: Vapour Pressure of a Volatile Solvent

Consider the vapour pressure of a volatile solvent in a closed container. Initially, the solvent evaporates, increasing the number of vapour molecules above the liquid. As more vapour forms, some molecules start to condense back into the liquid.

Eventually, the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation, establishing a dynamic equilibrium. At this stage, the amount of liquid and vapour remains constant, even though molecules continue to move between the two phases.

This is dynamic, not static: molecules keep evaporating and condensing, but at equal rates, so there is no overall change. At equilibrium, billions of molecules continue to react every second, but overall concentrations remain constant.

Key Points

  • Equilibrium is achieved in a closed system when forward and backward rates are equal.
  • In a closed system there is no exchange of matter with the surroundings.
  • Evaporation and condensation in a closed container reach dynamic equilibrium.
  • At equilibrium the amounts of liquid and vapour stay constant, but molecules keep moving between phases.
  • Two essential conditions for equilibrium: a reversible reaction and a closed system.
lessons.title: Dynamic Equilibrium in Closed Systems

mcqs.q: For A + B ⇌ C + D, what happens if the concentration of a reactant A or B is increased?
options: The reaction shifts backward to form more reactants
The reaction shifts forward to produce more products
No shift occurs because concentrations do not affect equilibrium
mcqs.why: If the concentration of any reactant A or B is increased, the reaction shifts forward to produce more products, according to the notes.

mcqs.q: For A + B ⇌ C + D, what happens if the concentration of a product C or D is increased?
options: The reaction shifts forward to produce more products
The reaction shifts backward to form more reactants
The reaction shifts towards fewer gas moles
The equilibrium constant decreases in every case
mcqs.why: Increasing any product C or D shifts the reaction backwards to form more reactants, while decreasing products shifts it forward to restore equilibrium.

mcqs.q: For A + B ⇌ C + D, decreasing a product will shift the reaction in which direction?
options: Towards the side with more gas moles only
It will change the equilibrium constant only
Forward, towards products, to restore equilibrium
mcqs.why: Decreasing products shifts the reaction forward to restore equilibrium; conversely, decreasing reactants shifts the reaction backwards.

mcqs.q: If the pressure of an equilibrium mixture of gases is increased, the reaction shifts towards which side?
options: The side with more moles of gas molecules
The side with fewer moles of gas molecules, to reduce pressure
The reactant side in every gas reaction
The side that changes the equilibrium constant
mcqs.why: Increasing pressure by decreasing volume shifts the reaction towards the side with fewer moles of gas molecules to reduce pressure.

mcqs.q: In N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), why does increased pressure favour ammonia formation?
options: Reactants have fewer gas moles than products
Products and reactants have equal gas moles
Reactants total more gas moles than the product side
Ammonia formation is endothermic in the forward direction
mcqs.why: Working: reactant gas moles are 1 + 3 = 4, while product gas moles are 2, so increased pressure shifts towards the side with fewer moles, ammonia.

mcqs.q: If pressure is reduced for PCl5(g) ⇌ PCl3(g) + Cl2(g), why does dissociation increase?
options: The product side has more moles of gas than the reactant side
The reactant side has more moles of gas than the product side
Both sides have exactly the same moles of gas
PCl5 dissociation is favoured only by a catalyst
mcqs.why: Working: one mole of PCl5 breaks into product moles totalling 1 + 1 = 2, so reduced pressure shifts towards the side with a greater number of gas moles.

mcqs.q: Raising the temperature shifts equilibrium towards which direction?
options: The endothermic direction, favouring the reaction that absorbs heat
The exothermic direction, favouring the reaction that releases heat
The direction with fewer gas moles in every reaction
The backward direction in every reaction
mcqs.why: Raising the temperature shifts equilibrium towards the endothermic direction, favouring the reaction that absorbs heat; a decrease favours exothermic reactions.

mcqs.q: For N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), the forward reaction is endothermic. What does an increase in temperature favour?
options: Formation of reactants N2 and O2
No change, because temperature affects only the constant
mcqs.why: In nitric oxide formation the forward reaction is endothermic, so an increase in temperature favours formation of products, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: For ammonia formation, the forward reaction is exothermic. What does increasing temperature do?
options: Shifts equilibrium to the right and increases ammonia
Favours ammonia production more than lowering temperature
Shifts equilibrium to the left, causing ammonia to decompose
Changes only the pressure, not the equilibrium position
mcqs.why: In ammonia formation the forward reaction is exothermic, so increasing temperature shifts equilibrium to the left, causing ammonia to decompose; lowering temperature favours ammonia.

mcqs.q: Which change alone alters the equilibrium constant?
mcqs.why: Changes in concentration, pressure or volume influence equilibrium position but do not alter the equilibrium constant, which is only changed by temperature variations.

lessons.notes_html:
Changing the physical conditions of a system at equilibrium can shift the equilibrium towards the formation of either reactants or products.

8.4.1 Effect of Concentration

Consider a system in equilibrium: A + B ⇌ C + D. If the concentration of any reactant (A or B) is increased, the reaction shifts forward to produce more products, while increasing any product (C or D) shifts the reaction backwards to form more reactants. Conversely, decreasing reactants shifts the reaction backwards, and decreasing products shifts it forward to restore equilibrium.

8.4.2 Effect of Pressure

If the pressure of an equilibrium mixture of gases is increased by decreasing the volume at constant temperature, the reaction shifts towards the side with fewer moles of gas molecules to reduce pressure. Example — formation of ammonia, where 4 moles of gas react to form 2 moles:

N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g)

Conversely, if the pressure is reduced by increasing the volume, the reaction shifts towards the side with a greater number of moles of gas, as observed in the dissociation of PCl5, where 1 mole breaks down into 2 moles:

PCl5(g) ⇌ PCl3(g) + Cl2(g)

Pressure or volume changes significantly affect equilibrium only when the number of moles of gas differs on each side of the equation.

8.4.3 Effect of Temperature

Changes in concentration, pressure or volume influence the equilibrium position but do not alter the equilibrium constant, which is only changed by temperature variations.

In the formation of nitric oxide, the forward reaction is endothermic, so an increase in temperature favours the formation of products:

N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g) — ΔH = +180.5 kJ/mol (forward: endothermic, reverse: exothermic)

In ammonia formation, the forward reaction is exothermic, so lowering the temperature favours ammonia production:

N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) — ΔH = -46.2 kJ/mol (forward: exothermic, reverse: endothermic)

Increasing the temperature shifts this equilibrium to the left, causing ammonia to decompose. Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium towards the endothermic direction, favouring the reaction that absorbs heat. A decrease in temperature favours exothermic reactions.

Condition ChangedChangeEquilibrium Shifts
ConcentrationReactant increased / product decreasedForward, towards products
ConcentrationProduct increased / reactant decreasedBackward, towards reactants
Pressure (gases)Pressure increasedTowards side with fewer moles of gas
Pressure (gases)Pressure decreasedTowards side with more moles of gas
TemperatureTemperature increasedTowards endothermic direction
TemperatureTemperature decreasedTowards exothermic direction

Key Points

  • Increasing a reactant shifts equilibrium forward; increasing a product shifts it backward.
  • Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles, e.g. towards NH3 in N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.
  • Decreasing pressure favours the side with more gas moles, e.g. dissociation of PCl5.
  • Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction; decreasing temperature favours the exothermic direction.
  • Only temperature changes the equilibrium constant.
lessons.title: Effect of Physical Conditions on Equilibrium

mcqs.q: When a hydrated compound is heated, what happens to its water molecules?
options: They are removed, shifting equilibrium towards formation of the anhydrous form
They increase, shifting equilibrium towards the hydrated form
They remain fixed and the colour always stays blue
They turn the anhydrous compound into a gas
mcqs.why: When a hydrated compound is heated, water molecules can be removed, causing equilibrium to shift towards formation of the anhydrous form of the compound.

mcqs.q: What is the appearance of hydrated copper(II) sulphate, CuSO4.5H2O?
mcqs.why: Hydrated copper(II) sulphate is blue crystals; on heating it forms anhydrous copper(II) sulphate, which is a white powder.

mcqs.q: What is the appearance of anhydrous copper(II) sulphate, CuSO4?
mcqs.why: Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate is a white powder, formed when blue hydrated crystals lose their water of crystallisation on heating.

mcqs.q: Why does the blue colour of CuSO4.5H2O change to white on heating?
options: Because copper is removed from the compound
Because water is added during heating
Because the compound becomes hydrated cobalt chloride
Because the water of crystallisation is released
mcqs.why: The blue colour changes to white because the water of crystallisation is released when hydrated copper(II) sulphate is heated.

mcqs.q: How many water molecules are released when one formula unit of CuSO4.5H2O is heated to form CuSO4?
mcqs.why: The equation in the notes shows CuSO4.5H2O forming CuSO4 plus 5H2O, so five water molecules are released from the hydrated compound.

mcqs.q: The dehydration of CuSO4.5H2O on heating is which type of reaction?
options: Exothermic, favoured by a decrease in temperature
Irreversible in both directions under all conditions
A reaction that releases heat as water is removed
Endothermic, favoured by an increase in temperature
mcqs.why: Heating blue CuSO4.5H2O to give white anhydrous CuSO4 is described as an endothermic reaction, favoured by an increase in temperature.

mcqs.q: What happens when water is added to anhydrous copper(II) sulphate?
options: White powder becomes blue crystals as hydrated CuSO4.5H2O forms and heat is released
Blue crystals become white powder and heat is absorbed
No colour change occurs because water shifts equilibrium left
Pink CoCl2.6H2O forms instead of a copper compound
mcqs.why: Adding water to anhydrous CuSO4 shifts equilibrium right, favouring hydrated CuSO4.5H2O; the white powder becomes blue crystals and heat is released.

mcqs.q: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride, CoCl2, has which colour, and what colour is its hydrated form?
options: Anhydrous is pink and hydrated is blue
Anhydrous is blue and hydrated is pink
Anhydrous is white and hydrated is blue
Both forms are pink in the notes
mcqs.why: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue; the hydrated form CoCl2.6H2O is pink, so on hydration the colour changes from blue to pink.

mcqs.q: How many water molecules are shown combining with CoCl2 to form its hydrated compound in the notes?
mcqs.why: The equation in the notes shows CoCl2 combining with 6H2O to form CoCl2.6H2O, the pink hydrated form of cobalt(II) chloride.

mcqs.q: What safety precautions are given for handling copper sulphate and cobalt chloride?
options: No precautions are needed because both are harmless
Wear safety glasses and gloves, work under a teacher's supervision, and ensure proper containment and disposal
Handle them only with bare hands in an unsupervised area
Heat them without safety glasses to see the colour change clearly
mcqs.why: The safety note says copper sulphate and cobalt chloride are hazardous: wear safety glasses and gloves, work only under a teacher's supervision, and ensure proper containment and disposal.

lessons.notes_html:
8.4.4 Effect of Heat on Hydrated Compounds

A decrease in temperature favours exothermic reactions, whereas an increase in temperature favours endothermic reactions. When a hydrated compound is heated, the water molecules can be removed, causing the equilibrium to shift towards the formation of the anhydrous form of the compound.

Hydrated Compound + Heat ⇌ Anhydrous Compound + Water

For example, when CuSO4.5H2O is heated, the water molecules are removed, causing the equilibrium to shift towards the formation of CuSO4:

CuSO4.5H2O(s) + Heat → CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(g)

Hydrated copper(II) sulphate is blue crystals. On heating it forms anhydrous copper(II) sulphate, a white powder. The blue colour changes to white because the water of crystallisation is released. This is an endothermic reaction, favoured by an increase in temperature. Book activity: heat blue CuSO4.5H2O crystals in a test tube — they turn white; add water again, and the blue colour returns.

8.4.5 Addition of Water to Anhydrous Substances

Adding water to anhydrous substances can shift the equilibrium towards the formation of the hydrated form, while removing water shifts the equilibrium in the opposite direction.

Copper(II) sulphate: Adding water to anhydrous copper(II) sulphate (CuSO4) shifts the equilibrium to the right, favouring the formation of the hydrated form, CuSO4.5H2O. Conversely, removing water shifts the equilibrium to the left.

CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l) → CuSO4.5H2O(s) + Heat — white powder becomes blue crystals.

Cobalt(II) chloride: Adding water to anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride (CoCl2) shifts the equilibrium to the right, favouring the formation of the hydrated form, CoCl2.6H2O. Conversely, removing water shifts the equilibrium to the left.

CoCl2(s) + 6H2O(l) → CoCl2.6H2O(s) + Heat — anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue; the hydrated form is pink, so on hydration the colour changes from blue to pink.

Safety note from the book: Copper sulphate and cobalt chloride are hazardous compounds. Always wear safety glasses and gloves when handling these substances, perform tasks only under the supervision of a teacher, and ensure proper containment and disposal.

Key Points

  • Heating a hydrated compound removes its water and shifts equilibrium towards the anhydrous form.
  • Heating blue CuSO4.5H2O gives white anhydrous CuSO4 + 5H2O; this dehydration is endothermic.
  • Adding water to anhydrous CuSO4 reforms blue CuSO4.5H2O and releases heat.
  • Adding water to blue anhydrous CoCl2 forms pink CoCl2.6H2O.
  • Adding water promotes hydrated forms; removal of water shifts equilibrium in the opposite direction.
lessons.title: Effect of Heat on Hydrated Compounds and Addition of Water to Anhydrous Substances

mcqs.q: According to the Bronsted-Lowry concept, what is an acid?
options: A substance that accepts a proton
A substance that donates a proton (H+)
A substance that releases hydroxide ions only
A substance that neither gains nor loses protons
mcqs.why: The Bronsted-Lowry concept defines an acid as a proton donor, that is, a substance that gives away an H+ ion to another substance.

mcqs.q: In the Bronsted-Lowry concept, a base is a substance that can:
mcqs.why: A Bronsted-Lowry base accepts a proton, as ammonia does when it takes H+ from water and forms the ammonium ion NH4+.

mcqs.q: Who proposed the Bronsted-Lowry concept, and in which year?
options: Johannes Bronsted and Thomas Martin Lowry, in 1923
mcqs.why: The notes state that the proton-transfer concept was proposed by Johannes Bronsted and Thomas Martin Lowry in 1923.

mcqs.q: What are the products when hydrogen chloride reacts with water, HCl + H2O?
mcqs.why: HCl donates its proton to water, giving the hydronium ion H3O+ and the chloride ion Cl-, as shown in the equation in the notes.

mcqs.q: Ammonia reacts with water as NH3 + H2O. What does this reaction produce?
mcqs.why: Ammonia accepts a proton from water, so the products are the ammonium ion NH4+ and the hydroxide ion OH-, in an equilibrium reaction.

mcqs.q: Acetic acid is the acid found in which common substance?
mcqs.why: The notes list acetic acid as the acid found in vinegar, while malic acid is in apples and carbonic acid is in carbonated drinks.

mcqs.q: Citric acid and ascorbic acid (vitamin C) are found in:
mcqs.why: The notes say citric acid and ascorbic acid, which is vitamin C, occur in citrus fruits and give them their sour taste.

mcqs.q: Sulphuric acid is used in which of the following?
mcqs.why: The notes list sulphuric acid as being used in batteries, fertilisers and explosives, while sodium hydroxide is used in soaps.

mcqs.q: In aqueous solution, alkalis release which ions into the water?
mcqs.why: Alkalis release hydroxide ions OH- in aqueous solution, and this is what gives the solution its alkaline nature and lets it neutralise acids.

mcqs.q: From the equation H2SO4 + 2H2O -> 2H3O+ + SO4 2-, how many hydronium ions are formed from one formula unit of sulphuric acid?
mcqs.why: The coefficient in front of H3O+ in the equation is 2, so the working is simply: hydronium ions formed = coefficient of H3O+ = 2.

lessons.notes_html:
Acids, bases and salts are used in daily life and in industry. Acetic acid is found in vinegar, citric acid and ascorbic acid (vitamin C) in citrus fruits, malic acid in apples and carbonic acid in carbonated drinks. Sulphuric acid is used in batteries, fertilisers and explosives. Sodium hydroxide, a base, is used in soaps and detergents, ammonia in household cleaners, and magnesium hydroxide as an antacid.

9.1 Bronsted-Lowry Concept

This concept describes acids and bases in terms of proton transfer. It was proposed by Johannes Bronsted and Thomas Martin Lowry in 1923.

An acid is a substance that donates a proton (H+). Examples: HCl, HNO3, H2SO4 and CH3COOH.

HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl- (acid + water → hydronium ion + chloride ion)

A base is a substance that can accept a proton (H+ ion). Examples: NH3, OH- and CH3COO-.

NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH- (ammonia + water ⇌ ammonium ion + hydroxide ion)

Lemon juice contains citric acid, which gives it a sour taste. Your stomach produces hydrochloric acid (HCl) to help digest food and kill microbes.

9.2 Aqueous Solutions of Acids

In aqueous solution, acids release hydrogen ions (H+) into the water, making the solution acidic. This release of H+ ions is a fundamental property of acids.

H2SO4 + 2H2O → 2H3O+ + SO4 2- (sulphuric acid + water → hydronium ions + sulphate ion)

9.2.1 Aqueous Solutions of Alkalis

In aqueous solution, alkalis release hydroxide ions (OH-) into the water, which gives the solution its alkaline nature. This release of OH- ions enables alkalis to neutralise acids.

NaOH + H2O ⇌ Na+ + OH- (sodium hydroxide + water ⇌ sodium ion + hydroxide ion)

Key Points

  • Bronsted-Lowry acid = proton donor; base = proton acceptor (1923).
  • Aqueous solutions of acids contain H+ ions.
  • Aqueous solutions of alkalis contain OH- ions.
  • Citric and ascorbic acids give citrus fruits their sour taste.
lessons.title: Bronsted-Lowry Concept and Aqueous Solutions

mcqs.q: What does a strong acid do in aqueous solution?
options: It does not dissociate at all
It forms an equilibrium with many unionised molecules
mcqs.why: A strong acid completely dissociates into ions in aqueous solution, which gives a high concentration of hydrogen ions.

mcqs.q: A weak acid in aqueous solution:
options: Gives a high concentration of H+ ions
Is shown by a single-headed arrow
mcqs.why: A weak acid only partially dissociates, so it gives a low concentration of hydrogen ions and stays in equilibrium with its unionised form.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a strong acid?
mcqs.why: The notes name hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid and nitric acid as strong acids, whereas acetic acid is the weak acid example.

mcqs.q: Which acid is given in the notes as the example of a weak acid?
mcqs.why: Acetic acid, CH3COOH, is the weak acid example; it reacts with water in an equilibrium to give H3O+ and CH3COO- ions.

mcqs.q: Which pair are both strong bases?
options: Ammonia and sodium hydroxide solution only when dilute
mcqs.why: Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are the strong bases in the notes because they completely dissociate to give a high concentration of OH- ions.

mcqs.q: Ammonia is classified as a weak base because it:
options: Gives a high concentration of OH- ions
Partially dissociates, giving a low concentration of OH- ions
mcqs.why: Ammonia only partially dissociates in water, NH3 + H2O giving NH4+ and OH- in equilibrium, so the hydroxide ion concentration stays low.

mcqs.q: In an equation, a single-headed arrow for dissociation shows that the acid or base is:
mcqs.why: A single-headed arrow shows complete dissociation, which is the behaviour of a strong acid or a strong base in aqueous solution.

mcqs.q: The double arrows in the dissociation of acetic acid show:
options: That the reaction is very fast
An equilibrium between the unionised and ionised forms
mcqs.why: Double arrows show a weak acid: only some molecules ionise, so unionised and ionised forms exist together in equilibrium.

mcqs.q: Why are strong acids good conductors of electricity in aqueous solution?
options: They give many free ions in solution
mcqs.why: Complete dissociation produces many free ions in the solution, and these moving ions are what carry the electric current.

mcqs.q: Sulphuric acid dissociates as H2SO4(aq) -> 2H+(aq) + SO4 2-(aq). How many H+ ions come from each H2SO4 unit?
mcqs.why: The coefficient before H+ is 2, so the working is: number of H+ ions = coefficient of H+ in the equation = 2 per H2SO4 unit.

lessons.notes_html:
The strength of an acid or base is related to its degree of dissociation in water. The extent of dissociation distinguishes strong from weak acids and bases.

9.3.1 Strong and Weak Acids

Strong acids completely dissociate into ions in aqueous solution. This gives a high concentration of hydrogen ions. Examples: hydrochloric acid (HCl), sulphuric acid (H2SO4) and nitric acid (HNO3).

HCl(aq) → H+(aq) + Cl-(aq)

H2SO4(aq) → 2H+(aq) + SO4 2-(aq)

HNO3(aq) → H+(aq) + NO3-(aq)

Weak acids partially dissociate into ions in aqueous solution. This gives a low concentration of hydrogen ions. Example: acetic acid.

CH3COOH + H2O ⇌ H3O+(aq) + CH3COO-(aq)

A strong acid is shown by a single-headed arrow (complete dissociation). A weak acid is shown by double arrows, an equilibrium between the unionised and ionised forms. Strong acids are good conductors in aqueous solution because they give many free ions.

9.3.2 Strong and Weak Bases

Strong bases completely dissociate into ions in aqueous solution. This gives a high concentration of hydroxide ions. Examples: sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide.

NaOH(aq) → Na+(aq) + OH-(aq)

KOH(aq) + H2O → K+(aq) + OH-(aq)

Weak bases partially dissociate into ions in aqueous solution. This gives a low concentration of hydroxide ions. Example: ammonia.

NH3(g) + H2O ⇌ NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq)

TypeDissociationIon concentrationExample
Strong acid / baseCompleteHigh H+ or OH-HCl, NaOH, KOH
Weak acid / basePartialLow H+ or OH-CH3COOH, NH3

Key Points

  • Strong = completely dissociates; weak = partially dissociates.
  • Strong acids: HCl, H2SO4, HNO3. Weak acid: CH3COOH.
  • Strong bases: NaOH, KOH. Weak base: NH3.
  • Single arrow = strong; double arrows ⇌ = weak.
lessons.title: Strong and Weak Acids and Bases

mcqs.q: Bases are typically which kinds of substances?
mcqs.why: The notes describe bases as typically the oxides or hydroxides of metals, such as sodium oxide, calcium oxide and sodium hydroxide.

mcqs.q: An alkali is best defined as:
options: A base that dissolves in water to form hydroxide ions
A metal oxide that never reacts with water
mcqs.why: An alkali is a water-soluble base; when it dissolves it forms hydroxide ions OH- in solution, which give the basic properties.

mcqs.q: Which statement about bases and alkalis is correct?
options: All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis
mcqs.why: Every alkali is a soluble base, but insoluble bases such as copper(II) oxide are bases without being alkalis, so the two groups are not identical.

mcqs.q: Copper(II) oxide is a base but not an alkali because it:
options: Reacts with water to form an acid
mcqs.why: Copper(II) oxide does not dissolve in water, so it cannot form hydroxide ions in solution and therefore counts as a base only, not an alkali.

mcqs.q: Calcium hydroxide is generally considered a weak alkali because it is:
mcqs.why: Calcium hydroxide dissolves only slightly, so only a small amount of hydroxide ions forms in solution, making it a weak alkali.

mcqs.q: Why is potassium hydroxide classed as an alkali?
options: Because of its high solubility in water
mcqs.why: Potassium hydroxide is highly soluble, and in water it gives K+ and OH- ions, which is exactly what makes a soluble base an alkali.

mcqs.q: When a base neutralises an acid, the products are:
mcqs.why: Neutralisation of an acid by a base forms a salt and water only, for example NaOH + HCl gives NaCl and H2O.

mcqs.q: Why do farmers add lime, Ca(OH)2, to their fields?
options: To make the soil more acidic
To neutralise acidic soil and improve crop growth
To add nitrogen to the soil
To kill microbes in the stomach
mcqs.why: Lime is calcium hydroxide, a base, so it neutralises excess acid in acidic soil and this improves the growth of crops.

mcqs.q: Which basic metal oxide reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide?
mcqs.why: The notes give CaO(s) + H2O -> Ca(OH)2(aq): calcium oxide reacts with water to form the hydroxide, calcium hydroxide.

mcqs.q: In the reaction Na2O + H2O -> 2NaOH(aq), how many formula units of sodium hydroxide are produced?
mcqs.why: The coefficient in front of NaOH is 2, so the working is: NaOH produced = coefficient of NaOH in the balanced equation = 2 formula units.

lessons.notes_html:
Bases are substances that can accept protons (H+). A base is a proton acceptor. Bases are typically oxides or hydroxides of metals.

Metal oxides include sodium oxide (Na2O), calcium oxide (CaO) and copper(II) oxide (CuO). Basic metal oxides react with water to form hydroxides:

Na2O + H2O → 2NaOH(aq)

CaO(s) + H2O → Ca(OH)2(aq)

Bases neutralise acids to form salt and water:

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O

Ca(OH)2(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + 2H2O

Real life: farmers add lime, Ca(OH)2, to acidic soil to improve crop growth.

Bases and Alkalis

Bases can be soluble or insoluble in water. Sodium hydroxide dissolves in water, whereas copper(II) oxide does not.

An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to form hydroxide ions in solution. The solubility of a base decides whether it is an alkali. Examples of alkalis: sodium hydroxide (NaOH), potassium hydroxide (KOH) and calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)2).

KOH(aq) → K+(aq) + OH-(aq)

Hydroxide ions (OH-) are responsible for the basic properties of aqueous solutions. Potassium hydroxide is an alkali due to its high solubility. Calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble, so it is generally considered a weak alkali. Copper(II) hydroxide is insoluble in water, so it is a base, not an alkali.

BaseSoluble in water?Alkali?
NaOH, KOHYesYes
Ca(OH)2SlightlyYes, weak alkali
CuO, copper(II) hydroxideNoNo, base only

Key Points

  • Bases are oxides or hydroxides of metals and accept protons.
  • An alkali is a water-soluble base that produces OH- ions.
  • All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis.
  • Bases neutralise acids to form salt and water.
lessons.title: Differences Between Bases and Alkalis

mcqs.q: Which physical property is characteristic of acids?
options: They taste sour, like lemon juice and vinegar
They turn red litmus paper blue
mcqs.why: Acids taste sour, as in lemon juice and vinegar; bitter taste and a slippery feel are properties of bases, not acids.

mcqs.q: What happens to blue litmus paper in an acid?
mcqs.why: Acids turn blue litmus paper red; bases do the opposite and turn red litmus paper blue.

mcqs.q: The pH value of an acid is:
mcqs.why: Acids have a pH value less than 7, while bases have a pH value greater than 7, as listed in the properties in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why do acids conduct electricity in aqueous solution?
options: Because of the presence of H+ ions
Because they are soluble in metals
mcqs.why: In aqueous solution acids produce hydrogen ions H+, and these free ions move through the solution and carry the electric current.

mcqs.q: An acid reacting with a reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium produces:
mcqs.why: The general reaction is acid plus reactive metal gives a salt and hydrogen gas, for example 2K + 2HCl gives 2KCl + H2.

mcqs.q: When an acid reacts with a carbonate, the products are:
mcqs.why: Acid plus carbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide; the carbon dioxide appears as fizzing during the reaction.

mcqs.q: How is the carbon dioxide from an acid-carbonate reaction recognised in the notes?
options: It extinguishes a lit splint and is seen as fizzing
mcqs.why: The gas is seen as fizzing in the mixture, and carbon dioxide extinguishes a lit splint, which is how it is identified.

mcqs.q: The reaction between an acid and a base is called:
mcqs.why: Acid plus base gives salt and water, and this particular reaction between an acid and a base is named neutralisation.

mcqs.q: Soft drinks contain carbonic acid, H2CO3. What does it do?
options: It gives the drinks their fizz but can erode tooth enamel
mcqs.why: Carbonic acid gives soft drinks their fizz, but the notes warn that drinking them excessively gradually erodes tooth enamel.

mcqs.q: In 2K(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> 2KCl(aq) + H2(g), how many molecules of hydrogen are formed for every 2 molecules of HCl used?
mcqs.why: Reading the coefficients: 2 HCl produce 1 H2, so the working is hydrogen formed = coefficient of H2 = 1 molecule for 2 HCl molecules.

lessons.notes_html:
9.5.1 Physical Properties

  • They taste sour, similar to lemon juice and vinegar.
  • They turn blue litmus paper red.
  • They have a pH value less than 7.
  • They corrode metals and other materials.
  • They are soluble in water.
  • They conduct electricity in aqueous solution due to the presence of H+ ions.

9.5.2 Chemical Properties

i) They react with reactive metals (like sodium, potassium, zinc or magnesium) to produce salt and hydrogen gas.

2K(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + H2(g)

Note: reactions of nitric acid with metals tend to differ and form other products.

ii) They react with carbonates to produce salt, water and carbon dioxide. The CO2 is seen as fizzing and it extinguishes a lit splint.

CaCO3(s) + 2HNO3(aq) → Ca(NO3)2(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O

iii) They react with bases to produce salt and water. This reaction between an acid and a base is called neutralisation.

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O

Ca(OH)2(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + 2H2O

Acid reacts withProducts
Reactive metalSalt + hydrogen
CarbonateSalt + water + carbon dioxide
Base (neutralisation)Salt + water

9.5.3 Uses of Acids

Acids are found in cleaning products, food preservation, batteries, metal processing and various industrial applications. They are commonly used as laboratory chemicals.

Not all acids are dangerous. Citric acid gives fruits their tangy flavour, ascorbic acid is vitamin C, crucial for immunity, and acetic acid is commonly consumed in vinegar. Soft drinks contain carbonic acid (H2CO3), which gives them their fizz, but it gradually erodes tooth enamel if consumed excessively.

Key Points

  • Acids: sour taste, pH less than 7, turn blue litmus red.
  • Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas.
  • Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
  • Acid + base → salt + water (neutralisation).
lessons.title: Characteristic Properties and Uses of Acids

mcqs.q: Which physical property belongs to bases?
options: Bitter taste and a slippery feel
mcqs.why: Bases have a bitter taste and feel slippery to touch, the opposite of acids, which taste sour and turn blue litmus red.

mcqs.q: What happens to red litmus paper in a base or alkali?
mcqs.why: Bases turn red litmus paper blue, just as acids turn blue litmus paper red; the notes give this as the litmus test for a base.

mcqs.q: The pH value of a base is:
mcqs.why: Bases have a pH value greater than 7, whereas acids have a pH value less than 7, according to the comparison table in the notes.

mcqs.q: Bases conduct electricity in solution because of the presence of:
mcqs.why: In solution a base provides hydroxide ions OH-, and these free ions carry the electric current through the solution.

mcqs.q: Zinc reacts with sodium hydroxide to produce:
mcqs.why: The equation in the notes is Zn + 2NaOH -> Na2ZnO2 + H2, so the products are sodium zincate and hydrogen gas.

mcqs.q: When a base reacts with a non-metal oxide such as carbon dioxide, the products are:
mcqs.why: Base plus non-metal oxide gives a salt and water; for example CO2 + Ca(OH)2 gives calcium carbonate and water.

mcqs.q: Heating or reacting a base with an ammonium salt produces which gas?
mcqs.why: Base plus ammonium salt gives a salt, water and ammonia gas, as in NaOH + NH4Cl giving NaCl, H2O and NH3.

mcqs.q: Magnesium hydroxide, a weak alkali, is used in milk of magnesia to:
options: Relieve heartburn and indigestion by neutralising excess stomach acid
mcqs.why: Milk of magnesia contains magnesium hydroxide, which neutralises excess acid in the stomach and so relieves heartburn and indigestion.

mcqs.q: Which statement about using bases at home is correct?
options: Strong sodium hydroxide is safe to handle at home
Only weak bases such as baking soda are safe to use at home
mcqs.why: Strong bases such as sodium hydroxide are highly corrosive and can cause serious burns, so only weak bases like baking soda are safe at home.

mcqs.q: In Ca(OH)2(s) + (NH4)2SO4(aq) -> CaSO4(aq) + 2H2O + 2NH3(g), how many ammonia molecules are released?
mcqs.why: The coefficient in front of NH3 is 2, so the working is: ammonia released = coefficient of NH3 in the equation = 2 molecules.

lessons.notes_html:
9.6.1 Physical Properties

  • They have a bitter taste.
  • They feel slippery to touch.
  • Strong bases can be corrosive.
  • They turn red litmus paper blue.
  • They have a pH value greater than 7.
  • They conduct electricity in solution due to the presence of OH- ions.
TestAcidBase / Alkali
LitmusBlue litmus → redRed litmus → blue
pHLess than 7Greater than 7
Taste / feelSourBitter, slippery

9.6.2 Chemical Properties

i) They react with metals to produce salt and hydrogen gas.

Zn(s) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na2ZnO2(aq) + H2(g) (zinc + sodium hydroxide → sodium zincate + hydrogen)

ii) They react with non-metal oxides to produce salt and water.

CO2(g) + Ca(OH)2(aq) → CaCO3(aq) + H2O (carbon dioxide + calcium hydroxide → calcium carbonate + water)

iii) They react with acids to produce salt and water.

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O

iv) They react with ammonium salts to produce salt, water and ammonia gas.

NaOH(aq) + NH4Cl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O + NH3(g)

Ca(OH)2(s) + (NH4)2SO4(aq) → CaSO4(aq) + 2H2O + 2NH3(g)

9.6.3 Uses of Bases

Bases are found in cleaning agents, soap and detergent production, paper manufacturing, water treatment and various industrial processes. They are commonly used as laboratory chemicals and play an important role in neutralising acids.

Magnesium hydroxide, a weak alkali, is used in milk of magnesia to relieve heartburn and indigestion. It neutralises excess stomach acid. Strong bases such as sodium hydroxide are highly corrosive and can cause serious burns; only weak bases such as baking soda are safe to use at home.

Key Points

  • Bases: bitter taste, slippery feel, pH greater than 7, turn red litmus blue.
  • Base + acid → salt + water.
  • Base + ammonium salt → salt + water + ammonia gas.
  • Bases are used in cleaning agents, soaps, detergents and neutralising acids.
lessons.title: Characteristic Properties and Uses of Bases

mcqs.q: In the modern periodic table, the groups are:
mcqs.why: Groups are the vertical columns of the table and there are 18 of them; the horizontal rows are the periods, and there are 7 periods.

mcqs.q: Why do elements in the same group have similar chemical and physical properties?
options: They have the same atomic number
They have the same number of shells
They have identical valence electron configurations
mcqs.why: Group members share the same number of electrons in the valence shell, and this identical outer configuration gives them similar properties.

mcqs.q: The period of an element is given by:
options: The highest shell (principal quantum number n) that contains electrons
The subshell of its last electron
mcqs.why: The period number equals the highest occupied shell; sodium has electrons up to the third shell, so sodium is in Period 3.

mcqs.q: Sodium has configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1. In which period is sodium?
mcqs.why: The highest energy level containing electrons in sodium is n = 3 (the 3s1 electron), so sodium belongs to Period 3.

mcqs.q: Chlorine ends in the 3p subshell, so chlorine belongs to which block?
mcqs.why: The block is decided by the subshell into which the last electron enters; for chlorine that is the 3p subshell, so it is a p-block element.

mcqs.q: Iron has configuration [Ar] 4s2 3d6 and is placed in the:
mcqs.why: Iron's last electrons fill the 3d subshell, and the block is named after that subshell, so iron is a d-block element.

mcqs.q: Period 1 is the shortest period. Which elements does it contain?
mcqs.why: The notes list Period 1 as the shortest period with just 2 elements, hydrogen and helium, while Periods 2 and 3 have 8 each.

mcqs.q: Periods 6 and 7 are described as the longest periods because each contains:
mcqs.why: Periods 6 and 7 each contain 32 elements including the lanthanides and actinides, more than the 18 in Periods 4 and 5.

mcqs.q: For s-block elements, the group number equals:
options: The electrons in the outermost s subshell
mcqs.why: For the s-block, ns1 means Group 1 and ns2 means Group 2, so the group number is simply the number of electrons in the outer s subshell.

mcqs.q: An element ends in ns2np5. Using the p-block rule in the notes, what is its group number?
mcqs.why: For p-block elements add the outer s and p electrons and then add 10. The working is 2 + 5 + 10 = 17, so the element is in Group 17.

lessons.notes_html:
The periodic table is a systematic arrangement of elements in order of increasing proton number (atomic number), arranged in periods and groups. Groups are numbered 1 to 18, also written I to VIII. Elements in the same group have similar chemical and physical properties because they have identical valence electron configurations. This lets us predict the behaviour of an unfamiliar element from its position.

Groups

The columns of elements are called groups. There are 18 groups in the modern periodic table. All elements in a group have the same number of electrons in the valence (outermost) shell. Group 1 (IA), the alkali metals, have one valence electron, while Group 17 (VIIA) have seven valence electrons. The atomic number increases as you move down a group.

The group is found from the outer configuration. For s-block elements, the group number equals the electrons in the outermost s subshell: ns1 is Group 1 and ns2 is Group 2. For p-block elements, add the outermost s and p electrons and then add 10: ns2np5 gives 2 + 5 + 10 = Group 17. For d-block elements, the group number is the sum of the electrons in the outermost s subshell and the (n-1)d subshell.

Periods

The rows of elements are called periods. There are seven periods. Moving left to right across a period, the atomic number increases and the elements show a gradual change in properties. The period of an element is given by the highest shell (principal quantum number, n) that contains electrons. Sodium has configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1, so its highest energy level is 3 and sodium is in Period 3.

PeriodTypeElements
1Shortest2 elements: hydrogen and helium
2 and 3Short8 each: lithium to neon; sodium to argon
4 and 5Long18 each: potassium to krypton; rubidium to xenon
6 and 7Longest32 each, including lanthanides and actinides

Blocks

All elements are divided into four blocks, based on the subshell into which the last electron enters: s-block, p-block, d-block and f-block. Chlorine has configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5; its last electron occupies the 3p subshell, so chlorine is a p-block element. Iron has configuration [Ar] 4s2 3d6; its last electrons fill the 3d subshell, so iron is a d-block element.

Key Points

  • Groups are columns (18 in total); periods are rows (7 in total).
  • Same group means the same number of valence electrons and similar properties.
  • The highest occupied shell gives the period number.
  • The subshell of the last electron gives the block: s, p, d or f.
lessons.title: Groups, Periods and Blocks in the Periodic Table

mcqs.q: An element in Group 1 typically forms an ion with which charge?
mcqs.why: Group 1 elements lose their single valence electron to reach a noble gas configuration, so they form cations with a +1 charge, like Na+.

mcqs.q: Magnesium is in Group 2. The ion it forms is:
mcqs.why: Group 2 elements lose two electrons, so magnesium forms Mg2+, an ion with a complete outer shell like a noble gas.

mcqs.q: Elements in Group 13 typically form ions with a charge of:
mcqs.why: Groups 1, 2 and 13 lose electrons to form +1, +2 and +3 ions respectively, so a Group 13 element forms a +3 ion.

mcqs.q: Chlorine is in Group 17, so the chloride ion has the charge and symbol:
mcqs.why: Group 17 elements gain one electron to complete their outer shell, giving a -1 charge, so chlorine forms the Cl- ion.

mcqs.q: Elements in Group 16 commonly gain electrons to form ions with which charge?
mcqs.why: On the right of the table, Groups 15, 16 and 17 form -3, -2 and -1 ions respectively, so Group 16 gives a -2 charge.

mcqs.q: A Group 15 element typically forms an anion with a charge of:
mcqs.why: Group 15 elements gain three electrons to complete their outer shell, so the ions they form carry a -3 charge.

mcqs.q: Why do the noble gases in Group 18 generally not form ions?
options: They already possess a complete outer shell
mcqs.why: Group 18 elements already have a complete outer shell like the stable noble gas arrangement, so they have no need to gain or lose electrons.

mcqs.q: Transition metals in Groups 3 to 12 differ from main group elements because they:
options: Form ions with a fixed +18 charge
mcqs.why: Because of their complex electron configurations, transition metals can show variable oxidation states rather than one fixed ion charge.

mcqs.q: Lanthanides and actinides, although formally part of Group 3, commonly form which ions?
mcqs.why: The notes state that lanthanides and actinides commonly form M3+ ions, that is, ions carrying a +3 charge.

mcqs.q: Group 14 elements tend to show which charges?
mcqs.why: The table in the notes gives Group 14 a typical charge of +4 or -4, sitting between the electron-losing left side and the electron-gaining right side.

lessons.notes_html:
The charge of the ion formed by an element is closely linked to its group number, because elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons. When elements form ions, they gain or lose electrons to achieve a stable electron configuration similar to that of the noble gases.

Elements in Groups 1, 2 and 13, on the left side of the table, typically lose electrons to form cations (positive ions) with +1, +2 and +3 charges respectively. Group 14 elements tend to show +4 or -4 charges. On the right side, elements in Groups 15, 16 and 17 commonly gain electrons to form anions (negative ions) with -3, -2 and -1 charges respectively. Noble gases in Group 18 possess a complete outer shell and generally do not form ions.

Transition metals in Groups 3 to 12 can show variable oxidation states due to their complex electron configurations. Although lanthanides and actinides are formally part of Group 3, they commonly form M3+ ions.

GroupTypical chargeGroupTypical charge
Group 1+1Group 16-2
Group 2+2Group 17-1
Group 13+3Group 18none
Group 14+4 / -4Transition metalsvariable
Group 15-3Lanthanides / actinides+3

So sodium in Group 1 forms Na+, magnesium in Group 2 forms Mg2+, and chlorine in Group 17 forms Cl-. In each case the ion formed has a complete outer shell, like a noble gas.

Key Points

  • Group number and ion charge are linked through the valence electrons.
  • Groups 1, 2 and 13 lose electrons: +1, +2 and +3 ions.
  • Groups 15, 16 and 17 gain electrons: -3, -2 and -1 ions.
  • Group 18 noble gases form no ions; transition metals have variable charges.
lessons.title: Group Number and the Charge of Ions

mcqs.q: How does atomic radius change down a group?
options: It decreases because nuclear charge increases
It increases because the number of shells increases
It decreases because shells are lost
mcqs.why: Going down a group adds more electron shells, so the outermost electron is farther from the nucleus and the atomic radius increases.

mcqs.q: Across a period, the atomic radius:
options: Increases, because more shells are added
Decreases, because the nuclear charge increases and pulls electrons closer
mcqs.why: Across a period the shell number stays the same but nuclear charge rises, pulling the electrons closer to the nucleus, so the radius decreases.

mcqs.q: Ionisation energy is the energy required to:
options: Add an electron to a gaseous atom
Remove a valence electron from a gaseous atom
Attract a shared pair of electrons
Break a solid into ions in water
mcqs.why: Ionisation energy is defined by M(g) -> M+(g) + e-, the energy needed to remove a valence electron from a gaseous atom.

mcqs.q: How does ionisation energy change across a period and down a group?
options: It increases across a period and decreases down a group
It decreases across a period and increases down a group
mcqs.why: Ionisation energy increases across a period as nuclear charge rises, and decreases down a group as the atomic radius increases.

mcqs.q: Electron affinity is the energy change when:
options: An electron is removed from a gaseous atom
One mole of electrons is added to one mole of neutral gaseous atoms
A bond pair is shared in a molecule
mcqs.why: Electron affinity is written X(g) + e- -> X-(g): it is the energy released or absorbed when gaseous atoms gain electrons to form negative ions.

mcqs.q: Electronegativity is an atom's ability to:
options: Attract a shared pair of electrons towards itself in a molecule
Gain a full mole of electrons
mcqs.why: Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom attracts the bond pair towards itself; fluorine attracts bonding electrons strongly and has a high value.

mcqs.q: Which element is the most electronegative, and which is the least electronegative?
options: Sodium is most, fluorine is least
Fluorine is most, caesium is least
Caesium is most, fluorine is least
Chlorine is most, hydrogen is least
mcqs.why: The notes name fluorine as the most electronegative element and caesium as the least electronegative element in the periodic table.

mcqs.q: Using the values in the notes, Na = 495.8 kJ/mol and Mg = 737.7 kJ/mol, by how much is magnesium's ionisation energy higher?
mcqs.why: Subtract the two first ionisation energies: 737.7 - 495.8 = 241.9, so magnesium's value is higher by 241.9 kJ/mol, matching the rise across a period.

mcqs.q: Chlorine's electron affinity is -349 kJ/mol and hydrogen's is -73 kJ/mol. What is the difference between their magnitudes?
mcqs.why: Compare the sizes of the energy releases: 349 - 73 = 276, so chlorine releases 276 kJ/mol more energy than hydrogen when gaining an electron.

mcqs.q: The notes give 1 angstrom = 10^-10 m and 1 pm = 10^-12 m. How many picometres are there in 1 angstrom?
mcqs.why: Divide the two lengths: 10^-10 / 10^-12 = 10^2 = 100, so one angstrom contains 100 picometres.

lessons.notes_html:
The physical and chemical properties of elements are fixed by their electronic configuration, which changes gradually across the table. Down a group the number of electrons increases but the outer shell configuration stays the same, so group members have similar properties. Across a period the valence configuration changes step by step. This recurring pattern of properties at regular intervals is called the periodicity of properties.

Atomic Radius

The atomic radius is the average distance from the centre of the nucleus to the outermost electron shell, or half the distance between two identical bonded atoms. A large radius means the nucleus is far from the last electron, so the attraction is weaker and the electron is given up more easily, increasing reactivity. Atomic radius is expressed in nanometres, angstroms or picometres (1 nm = 10-9 m, 1 angstrom = 10-10 m, 1 pm = 10-12 m). It increases down a group because the number of shells increases, and decreases across a period because the nuclear charge increases and pulls the electrons closer.

Ionisation Energy

Ionisation energy is the amount of energy required to remove a valence electron from a gaseous atom: M(g) → M+(g) + e-. For example, Na(g) → Na+(g) + e-, delta H = 495.8 kJ/mol, and Mg(g) → Mg+(g) + e-, delta H = 737.7 kJ/mol. It is measured in kJ/mol or kcal/mol. Ionisation energy decreases down a group because the atomic radius increases, and increases across a period because the nuclear charge increases.

Electron Affinity

Electron affinity is the amount of energy released (or absorbed) when one mole of electrons is added to one mole of neutral gaseous atoms to form negative ions: X(g) + e- → X-(g). For example, H(g) + e- → H-(g), delta H = -73 kJ/mol, and Cl(g) + e- → Cl-(g), delta H = -349 kJ/mol. It decreases down a group due to the increase in the number of shells, and increases across a period due to the increase in nuclear charge.

Electronegativity

Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract a shared pair (bond pair) of electrons towards itself within a molecule. Fluorine attracts bonding electrons strongly and has a high value; sodium has a low value. Electronegativity decreases down a group due to the increase in atomic size, and increases across a period due to the increase in the number of protons (nuclear charge). Fluorine is the most electronegative element and caesium is the least electronegative. Electronegativity, electron affinity and ionisation energy show similar trends in the periodic table.

PropertyDown a groupAcross a period
Atomic radiusIncreasesDecreases
Ionisation energyDecreasesIncreases
Electron affinityDecreasesIncreases
ElectronegativityDecreasesIncreases

Key Points

  • Atomic radius increases down a group and decreases across a period.
  • Ionisation energy is the energy to remove an electron from a gaseous atom.
  • Electron affinity is the energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron.
  • Electronegativity increases across a period; fluorine is the highest, caesium the lowest.
lessons.title: Periodic Trends: Atomic Radius, Ionisation Energy, Electron Affinity and Electronegativity

mcqs.q: Metallic character is an element's tendency to:
options: Gain electrons and form negative ions
Lose electrons and form positive ions
Share electrons in covalent bonds only
mcqs.why: Metallic character means losing electrons to form positive ions; metals have low ionisation energies and readily lose their valence electrons.

mcqs.q: How does metallic character change across a period?
mcqs.why: Across a period atomic size decreases and nuclear charge increases, so valence electrons are held more tightly and metallic character decreases.

mcqs.q: Down a group, metallic character:
options: Increases, because atomic size increases and electrons are less tightly bound
Stays the same for all elements
mcqs.why: Down a group the extra shells make the atom bigger, so the outer electrons are less tightly bound and are lost more easily, increasing metallic character.

mcqs.q: Metal reactivity down a group:
options: Increases, because atomic size increases and electrons are lost more easily
mcqs.why: As atomic size increases down a group, losing electrons and forming cations becomes easier, so the reactivity of metals increases.

mcqs.q: The reactivity of nonmetals generally:
options: Increases across a period and decreases down a group
Decreases across a period and increases down a group
mcqs.why: The notes state that nonmetal reactivity generally increases across a period and decreases down a group, the reverse pattern to metal reactivity down a group.

mcqs.q: Density is defined as:
mcqs.why: Density is mass per unit volume, which is why the values in the notes are given in grams per cubic centimetre, g/cm3.

mcqs.q: Which is the least dense naturally occurring element, and which are the densest?
options: Hydrogen is least dense; osmium and iridium are densest
Lithium is least dense; gold is densest
Osmium is least dense; hydrogen is densest
Lead is least dense; platinum is densest
mcqs.why: The notes say hydrogen is the least dense naturally occurring element, whereas iridium and osmium are the densest natural elements.

mcqs.q: Osmium has density 22.59 g/cm3 and iridium 22.56 g/cm3. How much denser is osmium?
mcqs.why: Subtract the two densities: 22.59 - 22.56 = 0.03, so osmium is denser than iridium by only 0.03 g/cm3.

mcqs.q: Density in the periodic table typically:
options: Decreases down a group and towards the centre
Is highest at the start of every period
Increases down a group and towards the centre of the table
Is the same for all transition metals
mcqs.why: Density typically increases down a group and towards the centre of the table, especially among the transition metals; period ends tend to be less dense.

mcqs.q: An element sits lower in its group than a known element. What can be predicted about it?
options: Smaller atomic radius and higher ionisation energy
Larger atomic radius, lower ionisation energy and stronger metallic character
