Higher electronegativity and weaker metallic character
mcqs.why: Lower group members generally have larger atomic radii, lower ionisation energies, reduced electronegativities and stronger metallic character.

lessons.notes_html:
Metallic Character

The metallic character of an element is its tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions. The non-metallic character is the tendency to gain or share electrons to form negative ions or covalent bonds. Metals have low ionisation energies and readily lose valence electrons, forming positively charged cations. Metallic character decreases across a period: as atomic size decreases, the valence electrons become more tightly bound because of the increase in nuclear charge. Metallic character increases down a group: as atomic size increases, the electrons become less tightly bound because of the increase in the number of shells.

Reactivity

Reactivity is the ability of an element to combine with another element to form a compound. Elements on the left of the table are metals and those on the right are nonmetals. Group 1 (IA) alkali metals are renowned for their high reactivity, particularly with water. Group 17 (VIIA) halogens are highly reactive nonmetals; they react with metals, especially alkali metals, to form ionic compounds, also known as salts.

Reactivity of nonmetals generally increases across a period and decreases down a group. Metal reactivity typically decreases from left to right across a period, because ionisation energy rises as nuclear charge increases, making it harder for metals to lose electrons. Metal reactivity increases down a group, as atomic size increases, which makes the loss of electrons and the formation of cations easier.

Density

Density is mass per unit volume. Heavier elements are not always denser. The least dense naturally occurring element is hydrogen, whereas iridium and osmium are the densest. Osmium has a density of about 22.6 g/cm3. Synthetic elements such as meitnerium are believed to be even denser (predicted around 37.4 g/cm3), but only limited quantities exist for accurate measurement, so this is only an estimate.

ElementDensity (g/cm3)ElementDensity (g/cm3)
H0.0000899Au19.32
Li0.534Pt21.45
Pb11.34Os22.59
U19.05Ir22.56

Density typically increases down a group and towards the centre of the periodic table, especially among the transition metals. Elements at the beginning and end of periods tend to have lower densities.

Predicting the Properties of Elements

Because periodic trends are consistent within groups and periods, the properties of an element can be predicted reliably from its position. Elements lower in a group generally have larger atomic radii, lower ionisation energies, reduced electronegativities, stronger metallic character and increased metallic reactivity. Non-metals higher in a group tend to be more reactive because of their greater ability to gain electrons. Oxidation states can also be predicted: Group 1 elements form +1 ions, Group 2 form +2 ions and Group 17 form -1 ions. The behaviour of an element can therefore be predicted by comparing it with other members of its group or period.

Key Points

  • Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group.
  • Metal reactivity increases down a group; nonmetal reactivity decreases down a group.
  • Density increases down a group and towards the centre of the table.
  • Hydrogen is the least dense element; osmium and iridium are the densest natural elements.
  • Position in the table is used to predict properties of unknown elements.
lessons.title: Periodic Trends: Metallic Character, Reactivity, Density and Predicting Properties

mcqs.q: The alkali metals form which family, and what is their behaviour?
options: Group 1; highly reactive and readily lose one electron
mcqs.why: Alkali metals are the Group 1 family, Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs and Fr; they are highly reactive because they readily lose their one outer electron.

mcqs.q: Alkaline earth metals are in Group 2. How do they compare with alkali metals?
options: More reactive than alkali metals and form +1 ions
Less reactive than alkali metals and form +2 ions
They are nonmetals that gain electrons
mcqs.why: The family table lists Group 2 as Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba and Ra: less reactive than the alkali metals, and they form +2 ions.

mcqs.q: Halogens, the Group 17 family, are described as:
options: Highly reactive nonmetals that gain one electron and form salts with metals
Elements with variable oxidation states only
mcqs.why: Halogens F, Cl, Br, I and At are highly reactive nonmetals; they gain one electron and react with metals to form salts.

mcqs.q: The noble gas family in Group 18 is characterised by:
options: A complete duplet or octet, making them stable and unreactive
mcqs.why: Noble gases He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe and Rn have a complete duplet or octet in the outer shell, so they are stable and unreactive.

mcqs.q: Transition metals, in Groups 3 to 12, are known for:
options: Variable oxidation states and coloured compounds
mcqs.why: The d-block transition metals such as Fe, Cu, Zn, Ag and Au show variable oxidation states and form coloured compounds.

mcqs.q: Uranium (U) and plutonium (Pu) belong to which family, and what is their key feature?
options: Actinides; radioactive and used in nuclear technology
mcqs.why: The notes place uranium and plutonium in the actinide f-block family, which is radioactive and used in nuclear technology.

mcqs.q: An unknown element is shiny, conducts well and is malleable. This suggests it is:
mcqs.why: Shiny appearance, good conductivity and malleability are the physical signs of a metallic nature listed in the notes for identifying unknown elements.

mcqs.q: An unknown element is dull, a poor conductor and brittle. It is most likely:
mcqs.why: Dull appearance, poor conductivity and brittleness indicate non-metallic character, the opposite of the shiny, conducting, malleable metal pattern.

mcqs.q: An unknown element has a low ionisation energy, so it loses electrons readily. It is probably:
options: A halogen or oxygen group non-metal
An alkali metal or an alkaline earth metal
An element at the top right of the table
mcqs.why: Low ionisation energy means electrons are lost easily, which the notes link to alkali metals or alkaline earth metals on the left of the table.

mcqs.q: A high electronegativity in an unknown element suggests it is:
options: A non-metal, possibly in the halogen or oxygen group
A noble gas with a full shell
An element low down in a group
mcqs.why: Higher electronegativity points to a non-metal that attracts electrons strongly, possibly in the halogen or oxygen group of the table.

lessons.notes_html:
The periodic table is divided into groups or families, each with its own specific characteristics.

FamilyGroupMain features
Alkali metalsGroup 1 (IA)Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr; highly reactive, readily lose one electron
Alkaline earth metalsGroup 2 (IIA)Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra; less reactive than alkali metals, form +2 ions
HalogensGroup 17 (VIIA)F, Cl, Br, I, At; highly reactive nonmetals, gain one electron, form salts with metals
Noble gasesGroup 18 (VIIIA)He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn; complete duplet or octet, stable and unreactive
Transition metalsGroups 3 to 12 (d-block)Fe, Cu, Zn, Ag, Au and others; variable oxidation states, coloured compounds
Lanthanidesf-blockFrom cerium (Ce) to lutetium (Lu); shiny metals, used in electronics and catalysis
Actinidesf-blockInclude uranium (U) and plutonium (Pu); radioactive, used in nuclear technology

Determining the Nature, Position and Identity of Unknown Elements

From given properties of an unknown element — physical state, colour, lustre, density, melting and boiling points, reactivity, specific reactions, valence electrons, ionisation energy, electronegativity and formation of compounds — we can deduce its nature, possible position and even its identity.

Physical properties analysis: a shiny appearance, good conductivity and malleability suggest a metallic nature. A dull appearance, poor conductivity and brittleness indicate non-metallic character.

Chemical properties examination: study the reactivity with water, acids or other elements, and the ionisation energy and electronegativity. A lower ionisation energy suggests the element loses electrons readily, possibly an alkali metal or alkaline earth metal. Higher electronegativity suggests a non-metal, possibly in the halogen or oxygen group.

Position determination: a larger atomic radius and lower ionisation energy may indicate a lower position in a group. Trends in known group characteristics narrow down the possible positions.

Comparison with known elements: similarities in atomic radius, electronegativity and chemical reactivity give clues about the group or period. For example, if the unknown element matches known elements in Group 17 (the halogens), the possible elements would be fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), iodine (I) and astatine (At).

Key Points

  • Each family has its own group number and characteristic properties.
  • Shine, conductivity and malleability point to a metal; dull and brittle points to a non-metal.
  • Low ionisation energy points to Groups 1 or 2; high electronegativity points to a reactive non-metal.
  • Comparing an unknown element with known elements narrows down its identity.
lessons.title: Families of Elements and Finding Unknown Elements

mcqs.q: The word alkali in alkali metals comes from an Arabic word meaning:
mcqs.why: Alkali comes from an Arabic word meaning ashes, because compounds of sodium and potassium were isolated from wood ashes by early chemists.

mcqs.q: Why are alkali metals stored in oil such as kerosene?
options: To prevent reactions with oxygen and water in the air
mcqs.why: They are the most reactive metals in the table, so oil keeps them away from the oxygen and water in air that they would react with.

mcqs.q: What is the valence shell configuration of the alkali metals, and what ion do they form?
options: ns1, forming M+ ions with a +1 oxidation state
mcqs.why: Group 1 atoms have one outer electron, ns1; losing it gives a monovalent M+ ion and the stable configuration of a noble gas, an oxidation state of +1.

mcqs.q: Why are alkali metals soft enough to be cut with a knife?
options: Their metallic bonding is weak because the single outer electron is far from the nucleus
They contain water inside the metal
mcqs.why: The one outer electron is far from the nucleus, so attraction is weak and the metallic bonding is weak, letting layers of cations glide past each other.

mcqs.q: Down Group 1, atomic radius increases. The reason given is:
options: Nuclear charge decreases down the group
Extra energy levels (shells) are added down the group
Electrons are lost down the group
mcqs.why: Each element down the group has an extra electron shell, so the atoms get bigger: lithium is 152 pm and caesium is 262 pm in the table.

mcqs.q: Ionisation energy decreases down Group 1 because:
options: The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and easier to remove
mcqs.why: As atomic size grows, the outermost electron sits farther from the nucleus, is held less strongly and is easier to remove, so less energy is needed.

mcqs.q: Melting points fall from lithium 180.5 C to caesium 28.4 C. What is the size of this fall?
mcqs.why: Subtract the two melting points: 180.5 - 28.4 = 152.1, so the melting point falls by 152.1 C from lithium to caesium.

mcqs.q: Density generally increases down Group 1, but which element is the exception to that trend?
mcqs.why: The notes say density is expected to increase down the group with the exception of potassium, whose value, 0.86, sits below sodium's 0.97.

mcqs.q: Which alkali metal reacts explosively with water, and which is the least reactive?
options: Lithium is explosive; caesium is least reactive
Caesium reacts explosively; lithium is least reactive
Sodium is explosive; francium is least reactive
Potassium is explosive; rubidium is least reactive
mcqs.why: Reactivity increases down the group: lithium, the smallest with the highest ionisation energy, is least reactive, while caesium reacts explosively with water.

mcqs.q: When an alkali metal reacts with water, the products are:
options: The metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas
mcqs.why: The equations in the notes, such as 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2, show every alkali metal giving its hydroxide plus hydrogen gas with water.

lessons.notes_html:
Group 1 (IA) elements — lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium — are known as alkali metals. The term alkali comes from an Arabic word meaning ashes, because compounds of sodium and potassium were isolated from wood ashes by early chemists. They are the most reactive metals in the periodic table and must be stored in oil (such as kerosene) to prevent reactions with oxygen and water in the air.

Their valence shell electronic configuration is ns1. They are excellent reducing agents, forming monovalent positive ions (M+) by losing one valence electron and achieving the stable electronic configuration of noble gases. They show an oxidation state of +1.

Why Alkali Metals Are Soft

Alkali metals are soft and can be cut with a knife at room temperature. Their single outer electron is far from the nucleus, so the attraction to the nucleus is weak. This gives weak metallic bonding: layers of metal cations glide past one another with minimal force, making the metal soft and malleable. Down the group the atoms get bigger, the outer electron becomes more diffuse and the attraction weakens further, so melting points decrease and softness increases. Their low melting points also come from weak metallic bonding and large atomic size.

Trends Down Group 1

ElementAtomic radius (pm)Ionisation energy (kJ/mol)Density (g/cm3)
Li1525200.53
Na1864960.97
K2314190.86
Rb2444031.53
Cs2623761.90

Atomic size increases down the group because extra energy levels (shells) are added. Ionisation energy decreases down the group because the electrons are located farther from the nucleus, so the outermost electron is easier to remove. Density is expected to increase down the group, with the exception of potassium. Melting and boiling points decrease down the group, because the forces holding the metal atoms together weaken as atomic size increases: melting points fall from Li 180.5 C to Cs 28.4 C, and boiling points from Li 1330 C to Cs 671 C.

Reactivity Trend

Reactivity increases down the group, because atomic size increases and the outermost electron is lost more easily. Lithium is the least reactive, with the smallest size and highest ionisation energy. Sodium is more reactive than lithium, potassium more than sodium, and rubidium more than potassium. Caesium is the most reactive, reacting explosively with water because of its large size and exceptionally low ionisation energy. Francium is predicted to be the most reactive of all, but this is hard to observe because it is scarce and radioactive.

Reactions with water give the metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas: 2Li + 2H2O → 2LiOH + H2; 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2; 2K + 2H2O → 2KOH + H2.

Key Points

  • Alkali metals have one outer electron (ns1) and form +1 ions.
  • They are soft, with low melting points, because their metallic bonding is weak.
  • Down the group: atomic radius and density increase; ionisation energy and melting point decrease.
  • Reactivity increases down the group: lithium is least reactive, caesium reacts explosively with water.
  • They are stored in oil to keep them away from air and water.
lessons.title: Group 1: The Alkali Metals

mcqs.q: Halogens are called salt formers because:
options: They are found in sea water only
All of them react directly with metals to produce salts
mcqs.why: Halogen comes from the Greek halos and genes, meaning salt formers, because each halogen reacts directly with metals to produce salts.

mcqs.q: How many electrons do halogens have in their outermost shell?
options: 7 electrons, two in ns and five in np
mcqs.why: Add the outer subshell electrons: 2 in the ns orbital plus 5 in the np orbital gives 2 + 5 = 7 electrons in the outermost shell.

mcqs.q: At room temperature, bromine is:
mcqs.why: The physical properties table lists bromine as a reddish brown liquid, while fluorine and chlorine are gases and iodine is a violet-black solid.

mcqs.q: In what form do the halogens exist as elements?
options: As diatomic molecules such as F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2
mcqs.why: The notes state that halogens exist as diatomic molecules, F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2, and that they are all coloured, poisonous and corrosive.

mcqs.q: Fluorine is the most reactive non-metal known. This is due to:
options: Its large size and low electronegativity
Its small size and high electronegativity
It being a solid at room temperature
mcqs.why: Fluorine's small atomic size and high electronegativity let it accept one electron very easily to complete its octet, making it the most reactive non-metal.

mcqs.q: What is the correct order of halogen reactivity?
mcqs.why: Reactivity decreases down the group as atomic size increases and electronegativity falls, giving the order F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.

mcqs.q: Density increases from the top to the bottom of Group 17 mainly because:
options: Of the rise in atomic mass rather than the change in atomic size
mcqs.why: The notes explain that halogen density rises down the group mainly because atomic mass increases, rather than because of the change in atomic size.

mcqs.q: Which hydrogen halide is the most thermally stable, and why?
options: HI, because its bond is weakest
HF, because the H-F bond is the strongest
HBr, because it is in the middle
mcqs.why: HF has the highest electronegativity difference and the strongest bond, 565 kJ/mol, so it is the most stable with negligible dissociation at high temperatures.

mcqs.q: The H-F bond strength is 565 kJ/mol and the H-I bond strength is 299 kJ/mol. By how much is the H-F bond stronger?
mcqs.why: Subtract the bond strengths: 565 - 299 = 266, so the H-F bond is stronger than the H-I bond by 266 kJ/mol, which matches the falling stability down the group.

mcqs.q: In Cl2 + 2KI -> 2KCl + I2, chlorine displaces iodine. In this redox reaction chlorine acts as:
options: A reducing agent, oxidised from 0 to -1
An oxidising agent, reduced from 0 to -1 by gaining electrons
A catalyst that does not change
mcqs.why: Chlorine gains electrons from the iodide ions and its oxidation state falls from 0 to -1, so chlorine is reduced and therefore acts as the oxidising agent.

lessons.notes_html:
Group 17 (VIIA) elements — fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine — are collectively known as halogens. The word halogen derives from the Greek halos and genes, meaning salt formers, because all of these elements react directly with metals to produce salts. They have seven electrons in their outermost shells: two electrons in the ns orbital and five electrons in the np orbital. They mostly show a -1 oxidation state.

Physical Properties

The halogens exist as diatomic molecules (F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2) and they are all coloured. They are all poisonous and corrosive. At room temperature and pressure, fluorine is a pale-yellow gas, chlorine is a yellow-green (greenish yellow) gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid and iodine is a grey-black (lustrous violet-black) solid.

ElementStateColourDensity (g/cm3)
F2GasPale yellow0.0017
Cl2GasGreenish yellow0.0032
Br2LiquidReddish brown3.122
I2SolidLustrous violet black4.933

Trends in Reactivity and Density

Halogens are the most reactive non-metals, and fluorine is the most reactive non-metal known, due to its small size and high electronegativity. They can easily accept one electron to complete their octet. Reactivity decreases down the group, mainly due to the increase in atomic size and the corresponding decrease in electronegativity: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. Density generally increases from top to bottom in the group, mainly because of the rise in atomic mass rather than the change in atomic size.

Thermal Stabilities of Hydrogen Halides (HX)

Thermal stability depends on the electronegativity difference between hydrogen and the halogen. HF shows the highest difference, giving the strongest H-F bond and the greatest stability, with negligible dissociation at high temperatures. Stability falls down the group as the bond weakens.

Hydrogen halideBond strength (kJ/mol)Thermal stabilityDissociation at high temperature
HF565HighestNegligible
HCl432HighModerate
HBr366ModerateSignificant
HI299LowestExtensive

Halogen Displacement Reactions

In a displacement reaction, a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from its salt solution. For example: Cl2 + 2KI → 2KCl + I2. Here the more reactive halogen (chlorine) displaces the less reactive halogen (iodine) from potassium iodide solution, forming the salt of the more reactive halogen (KCl) and the diatomic molecule of the less reactive halogen (I2).

These are redox reactions. The chlorine atoms are reduced from 0 to -1 oxidation state by gaining electrons from the iodide ions, so chlorine acts as an oxidising agent. The iodine atoms are oxidised from -1 to 0 as they lose electrons. This dual role, acting as both oxidising and reducing agents, is a characteristic feature of redox reactions.

Key Points

  • Halogens are diatomic, coloured, poisonous non-metals with 7 outer electrons.
  • Fluorine is a pale-yellow gas, chlorine yellow-green gas, bromine a red-brown liquid, iodine a grey-black solid.
  • Reactivity decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2; density increases.
  • Hydrogen halide stability decreases HF > HCl > HBr > HI as the bond weakens.
  • A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from its salt solution.
lessons.title: Group 17: The Halogens

mcqs.q: Transition elements are the elements found in:
options: Groups 3 to 12, in the centre of the periodic table
The f-block below the table only
mcqs.why: Transition elements occupy Groups 3 to 12 between Groups 2 and 13 in the centre of the table; examples are chromium, iron, cobalt, silver, copper and gold.

mcqs.q: Metals conduct heat and electricity well and are malleable and ductile because:
options: They have covalent bonds between individual atoms
They have a sea of free electrons and atoms in a regular structure that can slide
They have complete outer shells like noble gases
They have weak forces that break easily

mcqs.q: Compared with metals, non-metals generally:
options: Are excellent conductors with high melting points
Are poor conductors, brittle, with low melting and boiling points
Have a sea of free electrons

lessons.notes_html:
Transition Elements

The elements in Groups 3 to 12 are called transition elements. They are located in the centre of the periodic table, between Groups 2 (IIA) and 13 (IIIA). Examples include chromium, iron, cobalt, silver, copper and gold. Gold is the only metal that naturally shows a yellow hue, whereas most other metals appear silvery or grey.

General features of transition elements:

  • They are all metals, including common ones such as iron, copper, silver and gold.
  • They are good conductors of heat and electricity.
  • They have high melting and boiling points and high densities.
  • Most show more than one oxidation state (variable oxidation state), ranging from +2 to +7; the most frequent oxidation states are +2 and +3. For example, Fe shows +2 and +3, Cu shows +1 and +2, and Mn shows +2, +3, +4, +6 and +7.
  • Most of their compounds are coloured in the solid state or in solution, for example CuSO4 (blue), NiSO4 (green) and cobalt chloride (pink).
  • Most transition elements (Fe, Ni, Pt) and their compounds (V2O5, MnO2, CuCl2) are used as catalysts.
CatalystUse
FeFinely divided iron in the Haber-Bosch process for making ammonia
NiRaney nickel in the hydrogenation of vegetable oil to form ghee
CuOxidation of alcohols to produce aldehydes
PtFormerly used in the Contact process for producing sulphuric acid
V2O5Oxidation of SO2 to SO3 needed for H2SO4 in the Contact process
MnO2Decomposition of KClO3 to produce O2 gas

Group 18: Noble Gases

The elements in Group 18 (VIIIA) — helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon — are called noble gases. They occur naturally in the atmosphere in very small quantities and are characterised by extremely low chemical reactivity. They are unreactive, monatomic elements: they exist as single atoms rather than as molecules. Because they do not readily combine with other elements, they are also known as inert gases.

Their inertness is due to their electronic configuration. Helium contains two electrons filling its only shell, while all the other noble gases — neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon — have eight electrons in their outermost shell, a complete octet. With complete outer shells, they usually do not gain, lose or share electrons, so they show minimal chemical reactivity under normal conditions.

Helium, neon and argon are completely inert and form no naturally occurring compounds. Krypton and xenon can form a few rare compounds with highly reactive elements such as oxygen and fluorine, for example xenon hexafluoride (XeF6), only under specific conditions. When electricity passes through neon in a tube, its electrons become excited and give the bright red-orange glow of neon signboards. Helium fills balloons and airships because it is non-flammable and less dense than air.

Difference in Physical Properties between Metals and Non-metals

These differences arise from structure and bonding. Metals have a metallic bond, a sea of free electrons shared by the metal atoms. Non-metals typically have covalent bonds, the sharing of electrons between individual atoms.

PropertyMetalsNon-metals
Thermal conductivityExcellent; free electrons transfer thermal energy efficientlyPoor; they lack free electrons
Electrical conductivityExcellent; electrons move freely, carrying chargePoor; charges cannot move to carry a current
Malleability and ductilityMalleable (hammered into sheets) and ductile (drawn into wires); atoms in a regular structure slide past one anotherBrittle; irregular arrangement and weak forces break easily under stress
Melting and boiling pointsHigh; strong metallic bonds need a lot of energy to breakLow; weaker forces of attraction need less energy to overcome

Key Points

  • Transition elements are hard, dense metals with variable oxidation states and coloured compounds.
  • Transition elements and their compounds are widely used as catalysts, e.g. Fe in the Haber process and Ni in making ghee.
  • Noble gases are monatomic and unreactive because they have complete outer shells.
  • Helium, neon and argon form no natural compounds; krypton and xenon form a few rare compounds.
  • Metals conduct heat and electricity and are malleable and ductile; non-metals are poor conductors and brittle.
lessons.title: Transition Elements, Noble Gases and Metals vs Non-metals

lessons.notes_html:
The atmosphere is the protective layer of gases surrounding the Earth. It sustains life, shields the Earth from dangerous cosmic rays, filters harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, and maintains the heat balance by absorbing infrared radiation. Its thickness is approximately 500 km above the surface of the Earth.

Human activities release pollutants such as carbon monoxide and sulphur dioxide into the atmosphere. These threaten air quality, cause air pollution and climate change, and harm human health and ecosystems. Water is also essential for all living beings. It helps in digestion, keeps us cool, and transports nutrients around the body. Most of the Earth's water is salty or frozen, so only a small amount is fresh and drinkable.

Composition of Clean, Dry Air

ComponentFormulaPercentage (%)Significance
NitrogenN278.00A major component of the atmosphere
OxygenO221.00Supports respiration and combustion
ArgonAr0.93Chemically inert; used in lighting and industry
Carbon dioxideCO20.03Greenhouse gas; essential for photosynthesis
Trace gasesNe, He, CH4, Kr, Xe~0.01Present in minute quantities

Nitrogen is used by certain bacteria that convert it into useful compounds for plants, and by industries to produce ammonia for fertilisers. Oxygen is essential for the survival of living organisms. Carbon dioxide is necessary for plants to carry out photosynthesis. The atmosphere also acts as a carrier of water from the oceans to the land. Without the ozone layer, life on Earth would be impossible. Stratospheric ozone absorbs up to 99% of the harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

Key Points

  • The atmosphere protects life and is about 500 km thick.
  • Clean, dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.
  • Argon is 0.93% and carbon dioxide is 0.03% of clean, dry air.
  • Oxygen supports respiration and combustion; CO2 is needed for photosynthesis.
lessons.title: The Atmosphere and the Composition of Clean, Dry Air

lessons.notes_html:
Pollutants are substances in the air that have a harmful effect on living organisms or their environment.

Carbon Dioxide, CO2

CO2 is colourless and typically odourless at low concentrations, with a sharp, acidic smell at higher levels. It is soluble in water. Major sources are burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas for electricity and transportation. These fuels undergo complete combustion: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. Other sources are industrial processes, deforestation, and combustion of biomass and waste. Higher levels of CO2 cause global warming and climate change, melting of polar ice caps and glaciers, rising sea levels, coastal flooding, heatwaves, droughts, floods and wildfires.

Carbon Monoxide, CO

CO is a colourless, odourless and tasteless gas, produced by the incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels, mainly from vehicles. Other sources are petroleum refining, the paper industry, coal mining, furnaces, forest fires and incineration of biomass. It is extremely toxic and causes suffocation if inhaled. High exposure causes headache, fatigue, unconsciousness and death. CO binds with haemoglobin in the blood, preventing oxygen transport.

Particulates

Particulates (soot, dust, smoke) are tiny solid or liquid particles suspended in the air. Natural sources are dust storms, forest fires, volcanic eruptions and sea spray. Human-made sources are burning fossil fuels in vehicles, power stations and industry. They irritate the respiratory system, worsen asthma and bronchitis, and prolonged exposure is linked to lung cancer and cardiovascular diseases. They also reduce visibility and cause haze.

Methane, CH4

Methane is a saturated hydrocarbon, the main component of natural gas, and a colourless, odourless gas. It comes mainly from agriculture, wetlands, landfills and flooded rice paddies. Ruminant animals like cattle, sheep, cows and goats produce methane during digestion. Wetlands, landfills and rice paddies generate methane by anaerobic decomposition of organic matter by bacteria: Cattle Waste → CO2 + CH4. Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas causing global warming and climate change.

Key Points

  • CO2 forms by complete combustion and is the main cause of global warming.
  • CO forms by incomplete combustion and is extremely toxic.
  • Particulates irritate lungs and reduce visibility as haze.
  • CH4 comes from agriculture, livestock digestion, wetlands and landfills.
lessons.title: Major Air Pollutants: Carbon Dioxide, Carbon Monoxide, Particulates and Methane

lessons.notes_html:
Oxides of Nitrogen, NOx

The three oxides are N2O, NO and NO2. Nitrous oxide, N2O, is not generally regarded as a pollutant. Nitric oxide, NO, and nitrogen dioxide, NO2, are the significant pollutants, together called NOx. NO is colourless and odourless, whereas NO2 has a reddish-brown colour and a pungent, suffocating odour. The major man-made source is gasoline and diesel vehicles: N2 + O2 → 2NO and 2NO + O2 → 2NO2. NOx irritate the airways and lungs and help form fine particulate matter and ground-level ozone. In the atmosphere they form acid rain: 2NO2 + H2O → HNO3 + HNO2. Acid rain harms aquatic ecosystems, forests, crops, buildings and infrastructure.

Oxides of Sulphur, SOx

Sulphur dioxide, SO2, is a colourless, pungent gas. Sulphur trioxide, SO3, is a colourless solid. Both are highly reactive and can irritate or suffocate at higher concentrations. They form during combustion of sulphur-containing fossil fuels in power plants and petroleum industries: S + O2 → SO2 and SO2 + O2 → SO3. SO2 irritates the eyes, nose, throat and lungs. With water vapour they form sulphurous acid and sulphuric acid, the major components of acid rain: SO2 + H2O → H2SO3 and SO3 + H2O → H2SO4. Acid rain acidifies soils, rivers, lakes and streams, harms aquatic life, damages plants and forests, and damages steel, paint, cement, limestone and marble. With fine particulate matter it forms haze.

Ground-Level Ozone, O3

Ozone is an allotrope of oxygen, a pale-yellow gas, slightly soluble in water. In the stratosphere it protects the Earth from harmful UV radiation. In the biosphere it acts as a pollutant. Ground-level ozone forms from reactions between nitrogen oxides from car engines and volatile organic compounds in the presence of sunlight. It damages humans, plants and animals, causing eye irritation, throat discomfort, coughing and asthma. It reduces agricultural productivity and weakens paints and fabrics. The word smog was first introduced in 1905 for the combination of fog and smoke over London.

Key Points

  • NO2 is reddish-brown with a pungent smell; NO is colourless.
  • NOx come mainly from vehicle engines and form acid rain and smog.
  • SO2 and SO3 come from sulphur-containing fossil fuels and form H2SO4 in acid rain.
  • Ground-level O3 forms from NOx and VOCs in sunlight and harms lungs and crops.
lessons.title: Oxides of Nitrogen, Oxides of Sulphur and Ground-Level Ozone

lessons.notes_html:
Role of Ozone in the Atmosphere

Ozone, O3, occurs in the stratosphere, forming a protective layer about 16-50 km above the Earth's surface: O2 → O + O (by UV) and O + O2 → O3. The ozone layer acts as a shield, absorbing most of the Sun's harmful rays. This prevents genetic mutations, skin cancers and eye cataracts in humans, and protects animals and plants from radiation damage.

Harmful Effects of Ozone Depletion

A decrease in stratospheric ozone below its normal level is called ozone depletion. More ultraviolet radiation then reaches the surface.

  • Human health: increased risk of skin cancer, cataracts, immune system issues and respiratory problems.
  • Ecosystems: damages phytoplankton, disturbs food chains and alters biochemical cycles.
  • Agriculture and materials: hinders plant growth and reduces yields; damages tyres, rubber and asphalt.

Greenhouse Effect

The greenhouse effect is the process by which thermal infrared radiation from the Earth is trapped by gases such as carbon dioxide, water vapour, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone, preventing heat from escaping back into space. This natural process maintains the average temperature of the planet and keeps it warm.

Global Warming

Global warming, also called climate change, is the gradual increase in the average temperature of the Earth's atmosphere from the accumulation of heat-trapping greenhouse gases. Contributions to the greenhouse effect are: CO2 about 76% (65% from fossil fuel and industrial processes and 11% from forestry and other land use), methane 16%, nitrous oxide 6% and fluorinated gases 2%. Melting glaciers in northern Pakistan, in the Karakoram and Himalayan ranges, leads to Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs).

Mechanism of Global Warming

  • Absorption: greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface.
  • Reflection: they reflect this energy back towards the Earth.
  • Emission: they re-emit the absorbed energy in all directions, including back to the surface, raising the temperature.
  • They also reduce thermal energy loss to space. Plants remove CO2 by absorption, so removing CO2 reduces the greenhouse effect.

Key Points

  • The ozone layer lies 16-50 km up and absorbs harmful UV rays.
  • Ozone depletion increases skin cancer, cataracts and damage to crops.
  • Greenhouse gases trap infrared radiation and warm the Earth.
  • CO2 contributes about 76%, CH4 16% and N2O 6% to the greenhouse effect.
lessons.title: Role of Ozone, Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming

lessons.notes_html:
Acid rain mainly forms when sulphur dioxide, SO2, and nitrogen oxides, NO and NO2, are released into the atmosphere from power stations, vehicles and industrial processes. These gases undergo chemical changes in the presence of oxygen and water vapour, producing strong acids that return to the surface as acidic precipitation, which includes rain, snow, fog, dew and even dry particles.

Formation of Sulphuric Acid, H2SO4

SO2 reacts with oxygen and water in the atmosphere to form sulphuric acid: SO2 + H2O → H2SO3 and SO3 + H2O → H2SO4.

Formation of Nitric Acid, HNO3

Nitric oxide, NO, is produced during high-temperature combustion. In the atmosphere it oxidises to nitrogen dioxide: 2NO + O2 → 2NO2. Nitrogen dioxide further reacts with water and oxygen to form nitric acid: 4NO2 + 2H2O + O2 → 4HNO3.

Catalytic Role of Nitrogen Oxides

Nitrogen oxides not only produce nitric acid but also catalyse the oxidation of sulphur dioxide, increasing acid rain formation. NO2 oxidises SO2 to SO3, which then reacts with water to form sulphuric acid: SO2 + NO2 → SO3 + NO and SO3 + H2O → H2SO4. The NO produced is re-oxidised to NO2 by atmospheric oxygen, so the catalytic cycle continues: 2NO + O2 → 2NO2.

Environmental Impacts of Acid Rain

ImpactEffect
Acidification of aquatic ecosystemsRaises acidity of rivers, lakes and oceans; kills fish, invertebrates and other aquatic animals; damages vegetation
Soil degradationLeaches essential nutrients from soil, decreasing fertility and plant growth
Vegetation damageCauses leaf loss and bark damage, slows tree growth, weakens forests and decreases biodiversity
Infrastructure corrosionDamages buildings, monuments and stone sculptures; erodes steel bridges and towers, especially limestone, marble and concrete
Human healthAirborne particles cause respiratory issues; children and people with asthma are especially at risk

Key Points

  • Acid rain forms from SO2 and NOx reacting with oxygen and water vapour.
  • Its main acids are sulphuric acid, H2SO4, and nitric acid, HNO3.
  • NO2 also acts as a catalyst for the oxidation of SO2 to SO3.
  • Acid rain acidifies water and soil and corrodes limestone and marble buildings.
lessons.title: Acid Rain: Formation and Environmental Impact

mcqs.q: Approximately how many trees does deforestation destroy every minute worldwide, according to the notes?

options: Oxidises CO to CO2, reduces NO and NO2 to N2 and O2, oxidises unburnt hydrocarbons
mcqs.why: The three-way converter (i) oxidises CO to CO2, (ii) reduces NO and NO2 to N2 and O2, (iii) oxidises unburnt hydrocarbons to CO2 and water.

mcqs.q: Which equation is a catalytic converter reaction in the notes?
mcqs.why: Converter reactions listed are 2CO + O2 -> 2CO2, 2NO -> N2 + O2, and 2CO + 2NO -> 2CO2 + N2.

mcqs.q: Flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) in power stations uses what to eliminate SO2?
mcqs.why: FGD using calcium oxide is used in power stations to eliminate sulphur dioxide from flue gases before release.

mcqs.q: Using low sulphur fuels reduces emissions of which gas?
mcqs.why: Using low sulphur fuels also reduces SO2 emissions, as stated alongside catalytic converters in reducing acid rain.

mcqs.q: Which indoor pollutants are listed as causing asthma, allergies and lung cancer?
options: Radon gas, tobacco smoke, mould spores and household chemicals
mcqs.why: Indoor pollutants listed are radon gas, tobacco smoke, mould spores and household chemicals, which can cause asthma, allergies and lung cancer.

mcqs.q: Allergens such as pollen, dust mites and animal dander can lead to what?
mcqs.why: Allergens: pollen, dust mites and animal dander can lead to allergic rhinitis and asthma, according to the health risks section.

lessons.notes_html:
Reducing Climate Change

  • Planting trees: deforestation destroys approximately 2,000 trees every minute worldwide. Dead trees no longer absorb CO2, and their decay or combustion releases stored carbon as CO2. In photosynthesis, carbon dioxide and water react in the presence of chlorophyll and light energy to produce glucose and oxygen: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2.
  • Reduction in livestock farming: cattle release methane during digestion and manure decomposition. Installing biogas plants reduces methane emissions.
  • Decreasing use of fossil fuels: shift from coal, oil and natural gas to solar, wind, geothermal and hydropower.
  • Increasing use of hydrogen: hydrogen is a clean-burning fuel that produces only water vapour. Hydrogen fuel cells can be used in vehicles and industries.
  • Renewable energy: wind and solar energy generate electricity without greenhouse gas emissions.

Reducing Acid Rain

Catalytic converters in vehicles reduce harmful emissions and promote complete combustion. A three-way catalytic converter: (i) oxidises CO to CO2, (ii) reduces NO and NO2 to N2 and O2, (iii) oxidises unburnt hydrocarbons to carbon dioxide and water. Reactions: 2CO + O2 → 2CO2, 2NO → N2 + O2, 2CO + 2NO → 2CO2 + N2. Using low sulphur fuels also reduces SO2 emissions. Flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) using calcium oxide is used in power stations to eliminate sulphur dioxide from flue gases before release.

Environmental Risks and Long-Term Respiratory Health

  • Indoor pollutants: radon gas, tobacco smoke, mould spores and household chemicals can cause asthma, allergies and lung cancer.
  • Outdoor air pollution: from vehicles and industries, it leads to asthma, bronchitis, reduced lung function and lung cancer.
  • Smoking and secondhand smoke: smoking is a major risk factor for lung cancer and chronic bronchitis; non-smokers exposed to smoke also face higher risk.
  • Allergens: pollen, dust mites and animal dander can lead to allergic rhinitis and asthma.
  • Climate change: poor air quality, higher pollen levels and extreme weather affect respiratory health over time.

Key Points

  • Planting trees removes CO2 by photosynthesis.
  • Catalytic converters change CO to CO2 and NOx to N2.
  • Flue gas desulphurisation with calcium oxide traps SO2 in power stations.
  • Long-term exposure to smoke, allergens and polluted air damages the lungs.
lessons.title: Strategies to Reduce Environmental Problems and Respiratory Health Risks

mcqs.q: Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate changes from what to what in the presence of water?
mcqs.why: Anhydrous CuSO4 is white; in hydration it absorbs water and changes into blue hydrated copper sulphate, CuSO4.5H2O.

mcqs.q: Which equation shows hydration of anhydrous copper(II) sulphate?
mcqs.why: The test is CuSO4 + 5H2O -> CuSO4.5H2O, described as white -> blue in the test for water section.

mcqs.q: What does 'anhydrous' mean in the notes?
mcqs.why: Anhydrous means without water; anhydrous copper(II) sulphate is white before it absorbs water.

mcqs.q: What percentage of Earth's water is in seas and oceans?
mcqs.why: The water distribution table gives seas and oceans as 97.2%, saltwater covering 71% of Earth's surface.

mcqs.q: Fresh liquid water (lakes, rivers and groundwater) makes up what percentage?
mcqs.why: Fresh liquid water is 0.63% in the table, while polar ice caps and glaciers are 2.15% and water vapour is 0.001%.

mcqs.q: Polar ice caps and glaciers plus fresh liquid water together make up what percentage?
mcqs.why: Working: polar ice caps and glaciers 2.15% + fresh liquid water 0.63% = 2.78% of Earth's water.

mcqs.q: Pure water melts and boils at which temperatures under standard atmospheric pressure?
mcqs.why: Pure water melts at 0°C (32°F) and boils at 100°C (212°F) under standard atmospheric pressure; impurities change these points.

mcqs.q: Impurities typically do what to water's melting and boiling points?
options: Reduce melting point and increase boiling point
mcqs.why: Typically, impurities reduce the melting point and increase the boiling point, so deviation indicates impurities.

mcqs.q: Distilled water is described as having what?
mcqs.why: The tap vs distilled table says distilled water has virtually none (impurities), lacks minerals, and is used in laboratories, steam irons and batteries.

mcqs.q: Which is listed as a harmful substance in natural water?
options: Nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers and detergents contributing to algae blooms
mcqs.why: Harmful substances include nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers and detergents, which contribute to algae blooms and water pollution.

lessons.notes_html:
Test for Water Using Anhydrous Copper(II) Sulphate

This test is frequently used in laboratories to identify the presence of water. Anhydrous means without water. Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate is white. In hydration it absorbs water and changes into blue hydrated copper sulphate: CuSO4 + 5H2O → CuSO4.5H2O (white → blue). Procedure: place a small amount in a test tube, add a few drops of the substance being tested, and shake. If the crystals turn blue, water is present; if they stay white, there is low or no water. Note: alcohols can also turn it blue.

Water Distribution on Earth

Water TypePercentageExplanation
Seas and oceans97.2%Saltwater covering 71% of Earth's surface
Polar ice caps and glaciers2.15%Frozen freshwater reserves
Fresh liquid water0.63%Lakes, rivers and groundwater
Water vapour0.001%Water in the atmosphere

Although 71% of the Earth's surface is covered with water, less than 1% is readily accessible freshwater fit for drinking.

Testing Purity by Melting and Boiling Points

Pure water melts at 0°C (32°F) and boils at 100°C (212°F) under standard atmospheric pressure. Any significant deviation indicates impurities. Typically, impurities reduce the melting point and increase the boiling point.

Tap Water and Distilled Water

FeatureTap WaterDistilled Water
ImpuritiesVaries: minerals, chemicals, microorganismsVirtually none
MineralsMay contain beneficial mineralsLacks minerals
DrinkingGenerally safe, depending on qualityNot recommended for long-term consumption
Common usesDrinking, cooking, cleaning, bathingLaboratory experiments, steam irons, batteries

Substances in Water from Natural Sources

Beneficial: dissolved oxygen, essential for aquatic life; and minerals such as calcium, sodium, potassium, iron and magnesium, important for human health. Harmful: metal compounds, toxic at high concentrations; plastics, which harm wildlife and marine life; sewage, containing harmful bacteria, viruses and organic matter; harmful microbes that cause waterborne diseases; and nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers and detergents, which contribute to algae blooms and water pollution.

Key Points

  • White anhydrous CuSO4 turns blue in the presence of water.
  • 97.2% of Earth's water is in seas and oceans; only 0.63% is fresh liquid water.
  • Pure water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C.
  • Distilled water has virtually no minerals and is used in laboratories.
lessons.title: Testing Water and Substances in Natural Water

mcqs.q: In domestic water treatment, what is the first step (pretreatment)?
options: Screens remove large debris such as leaves and sticks
mcqs.why: Step (i) pretreatment: screens remove large debris such as leaves and sticks, before coagulation and later steps.

mcqs.q: Coagulation in water treatment uses what to make small particles clump together?
mcqs.why: Step (ii) coagulation: aluminium sulphate or potash alum makes small particles clump together, before sedimentation.

mcqs.q: During sedimentation, what happens?
options: Water rests in tanks so heavy particles settle out
mcqs.why: Step (iii) sedimentation: water rests in tanks so heavy particles settle out, followed by filtration through sand and gravel.

mcqs.q: Disinfection of domestic water uses what to kill microorganisms?
mcqs.why: Step (vi) disinfection: chlorine kills bacteria, viruses and other harmful microorganisms, making water fit for drinking.

mcqs.q: Carbon adsorption in water treatment uses activated charcoal to remove what?
mcqs.why: Step (v) carbon adsorption: activated charcoal removes tastes, odours and organic contaminants from the water.

mcqs.q: Which pair is described as the most common waterborne diseases killing thousands each year?
mcqs.why: Waterborne diseases include cholera and diarrhoea (the most common, killing thousands each year), hepatitis, GIT worms and typhoid fever.

mcqs.q: A person needs a minimum of how much water per day for hygiene, cooking and drinking (United Nations)?
mcqs.why: Water scarcity section states a person needs a minimum of 50 litres per day for hygiene, cooking and drinking (United Nations).

mcqs.q: Pakistan ranks where among the 17 extremely high-water risk countries?
mcqs.why: Pakistan ranks 14th among the 17 extremely high-water risk countries, and over 80% of its population suffers severe scarcity at least one month a year.

mcqs.q: Urea fertiliser contains what percentage of nitrogen?
mcqs.why: The fertiliser table gives urea as 46% nitrogen, a white crystalline solid, most concentrated and most widely used in Pakistan.

mcqs.q: Leaching of fertilisers means what?
options: Water washes nitrates from the root zone into groundwater and surface water, polluting it
mcqs.why: Leaching is when water washes nitrates from the root zone into groundwater and surface water, polluting it, as defined in the fertilisers section.

lessons.notes_html:
Treatment of Domestic Water

Water treatment makes water fit for drinking by removing impurities. Steps: (i) Pretreatment: screens remove large debris such as leaves and sticks. (ii) Coagulation: aluminium sulphate or potash alum makes small particles clump together. (iii) Sedimentation: water rests in tanks so heavy particles settle out. (iv) Filtration: through sand and gravel to remove fine particles and microorganisms. (v) Carbon adsorption: activated charcoal removes tastes, odours and organic contaminants. (vi) Disinfection: chlorine kills bacteria, viruses and other harmful microorganisms.

Waterborne Diseases

Waterborne diseases are caused by consuming or contacting contaminated water. They include cholera and diarrhoea (the most common, killing thousands each year), hepatitis (a viral disease of the liver), GIT worms such as roundworms, hookworms, tapeworms, pinworms and whipworms, and typhoid fever (a bacterial disease).

Water Pollution: Effects and Prevention

Contaminated water spreads diseases and causes poisoning from pesticides, mercury and arsenic, and can disrupt hormone function. Pollutants harm aquatic organisms, disrupt ecosystems, food chains and biodiversity. Excess nutrients cause algal blooms and dead zones, and toxic pollutants accumulate in fish and shellfish. Prevention includes effective water treatment, good hygiene and sanitation, regulations on industrial waste disposal, public education, investment in water infrastructure, and conservation of water sources.

Water Scarcity

Water scarcity is insufficient freshwater to meet the needs of people and ecosystems. A person needs a minimum of 50 litres per day for hygiene, cooking and drinking (United Nations). Pakistan ranks 14th among the 17 extremely high-water risk countries. Over 80% of its population suffers severe scarcity for at least one month each year, groundwater is severely overdrawn for irrigation, and over 80% of freshwater is used in agriculture, with inefficient irrigation wasting nearly half of it. Causes: rapid population growth and urbanisation; climate change; poor agricultural practices (rice, wheat, sugarcane and cotton consume over 80% of water resources but contribute only 5% to GDP); inefficient irrigation infrastructure; water pollution; and inter-provincial distribution disputes. Solutions include good governance, improved water management, conservation and efficient farming, diversifying sources (rainwater harvesting, wastewater reuse, desalination), recycling wastewater, climate adaptation, and fair inter-provincial distribution.

Fertilisers

FertiliserNitrogenKey Fact
Urea46%White crystalline solid; most concentrated and most widely used in Pakistan; readily soluble
Ammonium salts21-33%e.g. ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulphate; used for many crops except paddy rice
Nitrates13-16%e.g. calcium nitrate Ca(NO3)2, potassium nitrate KNO3; highly soluble but prone to leaching

Fertilisers provide essential nutrients and increase crop production. Leaching is when water washes nitrates from the root zone into groundwater and surface water, polluting it.

Key Points

  • Treatment steps: pretreatment, coagulation, sedimentation, filtration, carbon adsorption, disinfection.
  • Cholera, diarrhoea, hepatitis and typhoid are common waterborne diseases.
  • Pakistan is a high water-risk country; agriculture uses over 80% of its freshwater.
  • Urea has 46% nitrogen; ammonium salts 21-33%; nitrates 13-16%.
lessons.title: Water Treatment, Waterborne Diseases, Pollution, Scarcity and Fertilisers

mcqs.q: Organic chemistry is the branch that studies what?
options: Carbon-based compounds, their structure, properties and reactions
mcqs.why: Organic chemistry studies carbon-based compounds, their structure, properties and reactions, and explains life processes such as photosynthesis and respiration.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT organic, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: Carbonates, bicarbonates, carbides, cyanides, CO, CO2 and CS2 are not organic, so sodium carbonate is not an organic compound.

mcqs.q: Hydrocarbons contain which elements only?
mcqs.why: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen; they are the simplest organic compounds and the main part of petrol, diesel and natural gas.

mcqs.q: n-Butane, CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3, is an example of which type of molecule?
mcqs.why: Straight-chained molecules have carbons in one continuous line, e.g. n-butane CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3 and n-pentane.

mcqs.q: Isobutane and neopentane are given as examples of which type?
mcqs.why: Branched molecules have a main chain with one or more branches, e.g. isobutane and neopentane, as listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: Cyclopropane, cyclobutane and benzene, C6H6, are examples of which type?
mcqs.why: Cyclic molecules have carbons joined in a closed ring, e.g. cyclopropane, cyclobutane and benzene C6H6.

mcqs.q: Organic compounds may contain carbon along with which other elements listed?
options: Hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens
mcqs.why: Organic compounds contain carbon along with other elements such as hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens.

mcqs.q: Which life processes are explained by organic chemistry in the notes?
options: Photosynthesis, respiration and making of proteins, lipids and nucleic acids
mcqs.why: It explains life processes such as photosynthesis, respiration and the making of proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

mcqs.q: Many medicines listed as organic compounds include which set?
mcqs.why: Many medicines, such as antibiotics, analgesics, anaesthetics and antivirals, are organic compounds, according to the introduction.

mcqs.q: Why is a systematic method of naming organic compounds necessary?
options: So every compound has one clear name
So only living organisms can make them
mcqs.why: A systematic method of naming is necessary so that every compound has one clear name, as stated in the lesson.

lessons.notes_html:
Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies carbon-based compounds, their structure, properties and reactions. It explains life processes such as photosynthesis, respiration and the making of proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. Many medicines, such as antibiotics, analgesics, anaesthetics and antivirals, are organic compounds. It is also used to make plastics, rubbers, fibres, fuels, dyes, agrochemicals and fragrances.

Organic compounds contain carbon along with other elements such as hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens. Carbon is the primary element and is essential to life. Examples are methane, acetylene, benzene, carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

A few carbon compounds are not organic: carbonates, bicarbonates, carbides, cyanides, cyanates, CO, CO2 and CS2. So sodium carbonate is not an organic compound. Chemists can also synthesise organic compounds in laboratories; they are not made only by living organisms. A systematic method of naming is necessary so that every compound has one clear name.

Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. They are the simplest organic compounds and are the main part of petrol, diesel and natural gas.

Three Types of Molecules

  • Straight-chained: carbons in one continuous line, e.g. n-butane, CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3, and n-pentane, CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3.
  • Branched: a main chain with one or more branches, e.g. isobutane and neopentane.
  • Cyclic: carbons joined in a closed ring, e.g. cyclopropane, cyclobutane and benzene, C6H6. Each carbon in the ring is bonded to at least two other atoms.

Key Points

  • Organic compounds contain carbon; carbonates, CO and CO2 are not organic.
  • Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen.
  • Molecules are straight-chained, branched or cyclic.
  • Carbon is essential to life; all living organisms are made of carbon compounds.
lessons.title: Organic Compounds and Classification of Organic Molecules

mcqs.q: Saturated hydrocarbons contain which bonds between carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single bonds between carbon atoms; they are also called alkanes, the simplest family.

mcqs.q: What is the general formula of alkanes?
mcqs.why: Saturated alkanes have general formula CnH2n+2 and their names end in -ane, as given in the saturated hydrocarbons section.

mcqs.q: Using CnH2n+2, what is the formula of propane with n = 3?
mcqs.why: Working: for n = 3, H = 2n + 2 = 2 x 3 + 2 = 8, so propane is C3H8, matching the alkane table in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the general formula of alkenes?
mcqs.why: Alkenes contain one or more C=C double bonds and have general formula CnH2n; ethylene (ethene) is the first member.

mcqs.q: Using CnH2n, what is the formula of propene with n = 3?
mcqs.why: Working: for n = 3, H = 2n = 2 x 3 = 6, so propene is C3H6, matching the alkene table CH2=CH-CH3.

mcqs.q: What is the general formula of alkynes?
mcqs.why: Alkynes contain one or more carbon-carbon triple bonds and have general formula CnH2n-2, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Using CnH2n-2, what is the formula of butyne with n = 4?
mcqs.why: Working: for n = 4, H = 2n - 2 = 2 x 4 - 2 = 6, so butyne is C4H6, matching 1-butyne and 2-butyne in the table.

mcqs.q: Ethylene gas released during ripening of bananas does what?
mcqs.why: Ethylene gas is released during the ripening of bananas and speeds up ripening, as noted in the alkenes section.

mcqs.q: The simplest alkane and main component of natural gas is what?
mcqs.why: The simplest alkane is methane, the main component of natural gas; petroleum and natural gas are mostly alkanes.

mcqs.q: Why are unsaturated hydrocarbons able to add more atoms?
options: Their valencies are not fully satisfied, so other atoms can be added at the double or triple bond
mcqs.why: Unsaturated hydrocarbons have at least one double or triple bond; valencies are not fully satisfied, so other atoms can be added.

lessons.notes_html:
Hydrocarbons are the most basic organic compounds, made of carbon and hydrogen only, joined by covalent bonds. Examples are methane (CH4), ethylene (C2H4), acetylene (C2H2) and benzene (C6H6). They are divided into saturated and unsaturated types by the bonds present.

Saturated Hydrocarbons — Alkanes

Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single bonds between carbon atoms. They are also called alkanes, the simplest family of organic compounds. Petroleum and natural gas are mostly alkanes. The simplest alkane is methane, the main component of natural gas. Saturated means the four valencies of carbon are fully satisfied, so no more atoms can be added. Their general formula is CnH2n+2 and their names end in -ane.

NameC AtomsMolecular FormulaStructural Formula
Methane1CH4CH4
Ethane2C2H6CH3-CH3
Propane3C3H8CH3-CH2-CH3
Butane4C4H10CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3

Unsaturated Hydrocarbons

Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one double or triple bond between two carbon atoms. The valencies are not fully satisfied, so other atoms can be added. They include alkenes and alkynes.

Alkenes contain one or more C=C double bonds. General formula: CnH2n. Ethylene (ethene) is the first member. Ethylene gas is released during the ripening of bananas and speeds up ripening.

AlkeneC AtomsFormulaStructural Formula
Ethene2C2H4CH2=CH2
Propene3C3H6CH2=CH-CH3
1-Butene4C4H8CH2=CH-CH2-CH3
2-Butene4C4H8CH3-CH=CH-CH3

Alkynes contain one or more carbon-carbon triple bonds. General formula: CnH2n-2. Alkynes are less common in nature than alkenes, but more than a thousand have been isolated from natural sources.

AlkyneC AtomsFormulaStructural Formula
Ethyne2C2H2CH≡CH
Propyne3C3H4CH≡C-CH3
1-Butyne4C4H6CH≡C-CH2-CH3
2-Butyne4C4H6CH3-C≡C-CH3

Key Points

  • Saturated = only single bonds; these are alkanes, CnH2n+2.
  • Alkenes have a C=C double bond; general formula CnH2n.
  • Alkynes have a triple bond; general formula CnH2n-2, e.g. C4H6 is an alkyne.
  • Unsaturated compounds can add more atoms at the double or triple bond.
lessons.title: Saturated and Unsaturated Hydrocarbons

mcqs.q: A structural formula shows what that a molecular formula does not fully show?
options: The arrangement and connectivity of atoms and chemical bonds
mcqs.why: A structural formula clearly shows arrangement and connectivity of atoms and bonds; a molecular formula only gives the number of atoms.

mcqs.q: Ethene, C2H4, has which structural formula in the notes?
mcqs.why: The table gives ethene C2H4 as CH2=CH2, while ethyl alcohol is CH3-CH2-OH and methyl acetate is CH3-C(=O)-OCH3.

mcqs.q: Members of a homologous series differ from the next by which group?
mcqs.why: A homologous series is a group where each member differs from the next by a methylene group, -CH2-; members are homologues.

mcqs.q: Each successive homologue differs in molecular mass by how much?
mcqs.why: Working: -CH2- mass = 12 + 2 x 1 = 14, so each successive member differs by -CH2- and molecular mass differs by 14.

mcqs.q: Butane and pentane are homologues; pentane's formula in the alkane table is what?
mcqs.why: Working: pentane n = 5, H = 2n + 2 = 2 x 5 + 2 = 12, so C5H12, matching CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3 in the table.

mcqs.q: Hexane with n = 6 has which formula using CnH2n+2?
mcqs.why: Working: for n = 6, H = 2n + 2 = 2 x 6 + 2 = 14, so hexane is C6H14, as listed in the alkane table.

mcqs.q: All members of a homologous series share what?
options: The same general formula and same functional group
mcqs.why: All members have the same functional group and share the same general formula, giving similar chemical properties.

mcqs.q: Why do physical properties change gradually along a homologous series?
options: Molecular masses differ, so physical properties show a gradual trend
mcqs.why: They have distinct physical properties because their molecular masses differ, and physical properties show a gradual trend.

mcqs.q: What is the general formula for alcohols given in this lesson?
mcqs.why: General formulae listed: alkanes CnH2n+2, alkenes CnH2n, alkynes CnH2n-2 and alcohols CnH2n+1OH, where n is carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: Heptane in the alkane table has how many carbon and hydrogen atoms?
mcqs.why: Working: heptane n = 7, H = 2n + 2 = 2 x 7 + 2 = 16, so C7H16, matching the table entry for heptane.

lessons.notes_html:
Structural Formula

A structural formula is a two-dimensional representation of a three-dimensional molecule. It clearly shows the arrangement and connectivity of atoms and chemical bonds in the molecule. It is an unambiguous description of how the atoms are arranged, so it shows more than the molecular formula, which only gives the number of atoms.

CompoundMolecular FormulaStructural Formula
EtheneC2H4CH2=CH2
Ethyl alcoholC2H6OCH3-CH2-OH
Methyl acetateC3H6O2CH3-C(=O)-OCH3

Homologous Series

A homologous series is a group of organic compounds in which each member differs from the next by a methylene group, -CH2-. The members are called homologues. All members are represented by the same general formula. For example, butane (CH3CH2CH2CH3) and pentane (CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3) are homologues. General formulae: alkanes CnH2n+2, alkenes CnH2n, alkynes CnH2n-2 and alcohols CnH2n+1OH, where n is the number of carbon atoms.

AlkaneC AtomsFormulaCondensed Formula
Methane1CH4CH4
Ethane2C2H6CH3CH3
Propane3C3H8CH3CH2CH3
Butane4C4H10CH3CH2CH2CH3
Pentane5C5H12CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3
Hexane6C6H14CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2CH3
Heptane7C7H16CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2CH2CH3

General Characteristics of a Homologous Series

  • All members have the same functional group.
  • All members share the same general formula.
  • They have similar chemical properties because of the identical functional group.
  • They have distinct physical properties because their molecular masses differ, and physical properties show a gradual trend.
  • Each successive member differs by a -CH2- group, so the molecular mass differs by 14.
  • Every compound in the series contains the same type of elements.

Key Points

  • A structural formula shows how atoms are arranged and bonded.
  • Homologues differ from each other by one -CH2- unit only.
  • Same general formula and same functional group give similar chemical properties.
  • Physical properties change gradually along the series.
lessons.title: Structural Formula and Homologous Series

mcqs.q: A functional group determines what about an organic molecule?
mcqs.why: A functional group is an atom or group in a molecule that determines its chemical properties and reactivity; it is the reactive part.

mcqs.q: Methanol, ethanol and propanol have similar properties because they all contain what?
mcqs.why: Methanol CH3OH, ethanol CH3CH2OH and propanol all contain the hydroxyl group -OH, so they have similar properties as alcohols.

mcqs.q: The functional group of alkenes is what?
mcqs.why: The class table gives alkenes the functional group C=C, example ethene CH2=CH2; alkynes are C triple bond C.

mcqs.q: Ethanol, CH3CH2OH, belongs to which class?
mcqs.why: The table lists alcohols with functional group -OH and example ethanol CH3CH2OH, distinct from aldehydes -CHO and ketones -CO-.

mcqs.q: Acetic acid, CH3COOH, has which functional group?
mcqs.why: Carboxylic acids have functional group -COOH, example acetic acid CH3COOH in the functional groups table.

mcqs.q: Using CnH2n+2, butane with n = 4 has how many hydrogens?
mcqs.why: Working: butane n = 4, H = 2n + 2 = 2 x 4 + 2 = 10, giving C4H10, as worked in the reading the formulae section.

mcqs.q: For ethanol, the notes calculate hydrogens (excluding OH) as what?
options: 2 x 2 + 1 = 5 hydrogen atoms, plus the OH group
mcqs.why: Working: ethanol n = 2, 2 x 2 + 1 = 5 hydrogen atoms plus the OH group, using alcohols formula CnH2n+1OH.

mcqs.q: The functional group of amines is what?
mcqs.why: The table lists amines with functional group -NH2, example methylamine CH3NH2; halides are -X and nitriles are -C triple bond N.

mcqs.q: Chloromethane, CH3Cl, is an example of which class?
mcqs.why: Halides (alkyl halides) have functional group -X (F, Cl, Br, I), example chloromethane CH3Cl, in the class table.

mcqs.q: If one functional group is replaced by another, what happens?
options: The chemical behaviour of the molecule changes
The hydrocarbon chain becomes reactive only
mcqs.why: If one functional group is replaced by another, the chemical behaviour changes; e.g. methanol and methanoic acid differ because their functional groups differ.

lessons.notes_html:
Functional Groups

A functional group is an atom or a specific group of atoms in an organic molecule that determines its chemical properties and reactivity. It is the reactive part of the compound, while the hydrocarbon chain remains comparatively inert. Compounds with the same functional group show similar chemical properties and belong to the same homologous series. Double and triple bonds also act as functional groups. If one functional group is replaced by another, the chemical behaviour of the molecule changes.

For example, methanol (CH3OH), ethanol (CH3CH2OH) and propanol (CH3CH2CH2OH) have similar properties because they all contain the hydroxyl group, -OH. Methanol (CH3OH) and methanoic acid (HCOOH) have different properties because their functional groups are different. This idea helps in the classification and naming of organic compounds, such as alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, phenols, carboxylic acids, amines, esters and amides.

Reading the General Formulae

  • Alkanes, CnH2n+2: n is the number of carbon atoms and (2n+2) is the number of hydrogen atoms. Butane has n = 4, so H = 2 x 4 + 2 = 10, giving C4H10.
  • Alcohols, CnH2n+1OH: ethanol (CH3CH2OH) has n = 2 and 2 x 2 + 1 = 5 hydrogen atoms, plus the OH group.
  • Carboxylic acids, CnH2n+1COOH: ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) has n = 2, plus the carboxyl (COOH) group.

The general formulae show the ratio of carbon to hydrogen atoms and help us understand the similarities and differences within a homologous series.

Key Points

  • The functional group decides the chemical properties of a compound.
  • Methanol and ethanol share the -OH group, so both are alcohols.
  • Same functional group means similar chemical properties.
  • General formulae: alkanes CnH2n+2, alcohols CnH2n+1OH, carboxylic acids CnH2n+1COOH.
lessons.title: Functional Groups and General Formulae

mcqs.why: Alkanes are called paraffins, from Latin parum (little) and affin (affinity), meaning little affinity or least reactive.

lessons.notes_html:
Isomerism

Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae are known as isomers, and the phenomenon is called isomerism. For example, ethyl alcohol and dimethyl ether both have the molecular formula C2H6O but different structural formulae. The number of isomers increases as the number of carbon atoms in the molecule increases.

Structural Isomers

Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae; they differ in the arrangement of atoms within the molecule. Examples:

  • n-butane, CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3, and isobutane — both are C4H10.
  • 1-butene, CH3-CH2-CH=CH2, and 2-butene, CH3-CH=CH-CH3 — both are C4H8, differing in the position of the double bond (the functional group).

Isomers have different physical, chemical and biological properties.

Alkanes

Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with single bonds between their carbon atoms. They are also called paraffins, from the Latin parum (little) and affin (affinity), meaning little affinity or least reactive. In alkanes the four valencies of carbon are fully satisfied, so no further atom can bond without removing hydrogen atoms. They have no functional group. Examples are methane, ethane, propane and butane. Their general formula is CnH2n+2.

AlkaneLine Formula
MethaneCH4
EthaneCH3-CH3
PropaneCH3-CH2-CH3
ButaneCH3-CH2-CH2-CH3

Alkanes are used to produce liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and petrol for vehicles. Solid alkanes are used in waxy coatings on fruits and vegetables to prevent loss of water, improve appearance and slow down degradation by microbes.

Key Points

  • Isomers: same molecular formula, different structural formulae.
  • Butane and 2-methylpropane (isobutane) are structural isomers, both C4H10.
  • Alkanes are paraffins — saturated, single bonds, no functional group.
  • Alkanes follow CnH2n+2 and are used as LPG and petrol.
lessons.title: Isomerism in Organic Compounds and Alkanes

mcqs.q: Thermal cracking involves heating to about what temperature in the absence of oxygen?
mcqs.why: Thermal cracking: heating to about 700-900°C in the absence of oxygen, e.g. C10H22 -> C8H18 + C2H4.

mcqs.why: Catalytic cracking is at lower temperature 450-550°C with a zeolite or aluminosilicate catalyst, giving more branched and cyclic alkanes for petrol.

mcqs.why: Catalytic cracking example: C16H34 (hexadecane) -> C8H18 (octane) + 2C4H8 (butene), with zeolite at 500°C.

mcqs.q: Hydrogenation of alkenes commonly uses which catalyst?
mcqs.why: Alkenes add hydrogen with a catalyst - nickel, platinum or palladium - to form alkanes; nickel is the catalyst commonly used.

mcqs.q: Reduction of alkyl halides in the notes uses which reducing agent example?
options: Zinc metal, e.g. ethyl chloride + 2[H] -> ethane + HCl with Zn/HCl
mcqs.why: Alkyl halides are reduced easily at room temperature with zinc metal: ethyl chloride + 2[H] -> ethane + HCl, with Zn/HCl.

mcqs.q: Complete combustion of methane releases approximately how much heat per mole?
options: 890 kJ, ΔH = -890.3 kJ/mol in the equation
mcqs.why: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, ΔH = -890.3 kJ/mol; one mole of methane releases nearly 890 kJ, enough to heat about 30 litres of water to boiling.

mcqs.q: Incomplete combustion of alkanes (insufficient oxygen) gives what products in the example?
options: Carbon monoxide, carbon soot and water: 3CH4 + 4O2 -> 2CO + C + 6H2O
mcqs.why: Incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide, carbon soot and water: 3CH4 + 4O2 -> 2CO + C + 6H2O; it is less efficient and CO is toxic.

mcqs.q: Why are alkanes generally unreactive?
options: Their C-C and C-H sigma bonds are stable and non-polar
mcqs.why: Alkanes are generally unreactive because their C-C and C-H sigma bonds are stable and non-polar; they react mainly in combustion and chlorination.

mcqs.q: Halogenation of alkanes is which type of reaction and needs what condition?
options: Substitution, needs ultraviolet light or high temperature
mcqs.why: Halogenation is a substitution reaction where H atoms are replaced by halogen atoms; it needs ultraviolet light or high temperature, e.g. CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl (UV).

mcqs.q: The products of halogenation of alkanes are called what?
options: Chloroalkanes, also called alkyl halides (for chlorine example)
mcqs.why: Products are chloroalkanes, also called alkyl halides, e.g. CH3Cl from methane and CH3CH2Cl from ethane under UV light.

lessons.notes_html:
Preparation of Alkanes

1. Cracking of larger hydrocarbons: Cracking breaks larger hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful alkanes and alkenes.

  • Thermal cracking: heating to about 700-900°C in the absence of oxygen. C10H22 (decane) → C8H18 (octane) + C2H4 (ethylene).
  • Catalytic cracking: at lower temperature, 450-550°C, with a zeolite or aluminosilicate catalyst. It gives more branched and cyclic alkanes for petrol. C16H34 (hexadecane) → C8H18 (octane) + 2C4H8 (butene), with zeolite at 500°C.

2. Hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes: Hydrogenation is the addition of hydrogen. Alkenes and alkynes add hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst — nickel, platinum or palladium — to form alkanes. Nickel is the catalyst commonly used. CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3-CH3 (Ni at 200-250°C, or Pt/Pd at 25°C). Alkynes react in two steps: ethyne → ethene → ethane (Pd at 25°C).

3. Reduction of alkyl halides: Alkyl halides are more reactive, so this reaction is easy at room temperature with a reducing agent such as zinc metal. Ethyl chloride + 2[H] → ethane + HCl, with Zn/HCl.

Chemical Properties of Alkanes

Alkanes are generally unreactive because their C-C and C-H sigma bonds are stable and non-polar. They react mainly in combustion and chlorination.

Combustion: Alkanes burn in oxygen to give carbon dioxide, water vapour and much heat energy. Complete combustion (excess oxygen): CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O, ΔH = -890.3 kJ/mol. The heat of combustion is the heat released when one mole of a hydrocarbon is completely combusted. One mole of methane releases nearly 890 kJ, enough to heat about 30 litres of water from 25°C to boiling point. Incomplete combustion (insufficient oxygen) gives carbon monoxide, carbon soot and water: 3CH4 + 4O2 → 2CO + C + 6H2O. It is less efficient and carbon monoxide is a toxic air pollutant. Alkanes are widely used as fuels: cheap, easily obtained from crude oil and natural gas, and giving much heat per unit mass. Methane, propane and butane are used for cooking, heating and power generation.

Substitution (Halogenation): In a substitution reaction, one atom or group is replaced by another. In halogenation, one or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms, usually chlorine or bromine. The reaction needs ultraviolet light or high temperature. CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl (UV light). CH3CH3 + Cl2 → CH3CH2Cl + HCl (UV light). The products are chloroalkanes, also called alkyl halides.

Key Points

  • Alkanes are prepared by cracking, hydrogenation and reduction of alkyl halides.
  • Hydrogenation uses a nickel (or Pt/Pd) catalyst.
  • Complete combustion of methane gives CO2 and water; incomplete gives CO and soot.
  • Halogenation is a substitution reaction and needs UV light.
lessons.title: Preparation and Chemical Properties of Alkanes

mcqs.why: Monosaccharides are simple sugars, and the notes list galactose, fructose and glucose as examples, so glucose is a monosaccharide.

mcqs.why: The notes state that oligosaccharides on hydrolysis yield 2-10 monosaccharides, with sucrose, lactose and raffinose as examples.

mcqs.why: The notes state that by photosynthesis plants convert over 100 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrates annually.
