lessons.notes_html:
Biochemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the composition, structure and properties of matter found in living organisms. The most common compounds in living organisms are carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids and vitamins. Biochemistry helps us improve quality of life, fight diseases and develop new crop varieties by genetic engineering. In this unit you will explain the importance of nutrition and healthy eating, recognise the main biomolecules with their sources and required daily intake for young adults, and identify carbohydrates as a source of energy.

What are Carbohydrates?

Carbohydrates are biomolecules composed of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, typically in a 1:2:1 ratio, with general formula (Cn(H2O)n). They are the most abundant class of biomolecules on Earth and a primary energy source for most living organisms. They provide energy, store energy and form structural parts of cells and tissues. By photosynthesis, plants convert over 100 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrates annually. The human brain alone uses about 120 grams of glucose daily, nearly 60% of the body's total glucose consumption.

Main Classes of Carbohydrates

  • Monosaccharides: simple sugars. Examples: galactose, fructose, glucose.
  • Oligosaccharides: on hydrolysis yield 2-10 monosaccharides. Examples: sucrose, lactose, raffinose.
  • Polysaccharides: complex and abundant in nature. Examples: starch, glycogen, cellulose.

Sources of Carbohydrates

Main dietary sources are cereal grains (wheat, rice, maize, barley, oats), starchy vegetables (potatoes, sweet potatoes, corn, peas), fruits (bananas, apples, oranges, grapes), legumes (beans, lentils, peas) and dairy products (milk, yoghurt).

CarbohydrateSources
GlucoseFruits, vegetables and honey
FructoseFruits, honey and some vegetables
Sucrose (Table Sugar)Sugarcane, sugar beet, fruits and vegetables
LactoseMilk and other dairy products
StarchPotato, cereals like wheat, rice and maize
GlycogenAnimal liver

Recommended Daily Intake

For young adults: 225-325 grams per day, making up 45-65% of a 2,000-calorie diet. The World Health Organisation (WHO) recommends that daily caloric intake from sucrose should not exceed 5%, as excess added sugars can lead to obesity and dental caries. Recommended daily fibre intake is 21-25 grams for women and 30-38 grams for men.

Carbohydrates as a Source of Energy

Carbohydrates provide about 4 kcal/g. They are broken down into simple sugars, mainly glucose, by digestive enzymes. The small intestine absorbs glucose into the bloodstream, which carries it to body cells, where it produces energy through respiration. Excess glucose is converted into glycogen and stored in the liver and muscles as a short-term energy reserve. Unused glucose can be converted into fat and stored in adipose tissue, which can contribute to obesity. In hospitals, 5% glucose solution (5% dextrose) is used in drips for patients who cannot take food.

Key Points

  • Biochemistry studies the matter found in living organisms.
  • Carbohydrates contain C, H and O in a 1:2:1 ratio; formula (Cn(H2O)n).
  • Three classes: monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides.
  • Daily intake for young adults is 225-325 g (45-65% of calories).
  • Carbohydrates give about 4 kcal/g; excess glucose is stored as glycogen.
lessons.title: Biochemistry and Carbohydrates

lessons.notes_html:
The word protein comes from the Greek term proteios, meaning 'first'. Proteins are polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds (-CO-NH-). The human body uses various amino acids to form proteins: ten are synthesised by our body and the remaining ten are obtained from food sources. The amino acids that are essential in our diet are known as essential amino acids.

Functions of Proteins

  • Structure and support: in skin, hair, cartilage, muscles, tendons and ligaments.
  • Enzymes, hormones and antibodies: they catalyse, regulate and protect body chemistry.
  • Transport: haemoglobin, myoglobin and lipoproteins facilitate the transport of oxygen and other substances within the body. Haemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood.

Proteins are vital to every living cell and are found in all forms of life. Plants can produce their own proteins using simple elements, but animals mainly obtain their proteins by consuming amino acids from their food. Animals can synthesise some amino acids on their own.

Sources of Proteins

We can obtain the required proteins or amino acids from meat, eggs, beans, fruits, lentils, pulses, dried fruits and seeds. Fish, poultry and dairy products are also good protein sources.

Recommended Daily Intake

The recommended daily protein intake for young adults is approximately 46-56 grams, making up about 10-15% of total daily calories. The exact amount varies with age, gender, body weight, level of physical activity and overall health.

Real-life application: enzymes obtained from bacteria are commonly used in modern detergents to remove protein-based stains, including blood, egg and sweat, from clothes.

Key Points

  • Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
  • Essential amino acids must be obtained through diet.
  • Proteins give structure, work as enzymes, hormones and antibodies, and transport oxygen.
  • Sources include meat, eggs, milk, lentils, beans, nuts and seeds.
  • Daily intake for young adults is 46-56 g (10-15% of total calories).
lessons.title: Proteins

mcqs.why: The notes say healthy fats like omega-3 and omega-6 are vital for proper brain function, heart health and hormone regulation.

lessons.notes_html:
Lipids are esters of fatty acids and glycerol. They form a vital class of biomolecules found across all living organisms. The most well-known lipids are fats and oils, which are triesters of glycerol (also known as triglycerides) and long-chain carboxylic acids, commonly called fatty acids. A triglyceride has three fatty acids and one glycerol. In the general formula of a lipid, R1, R2 and R3 represent hydrocarbon chains of different lengths derived from fatty acids.

Other important types of lipids include phospholipids, steroids, terpenes and waxes. Beeswax is a natural wax made by bees; paraffin wax, used in candles, is a petroleum-derived mixture of alkanes and does not contain the ester functional group.

Fats and Oils

  • Fats: found in animals, solid at normal temperature. Humans consume animal fat, margarine, butter and cream. Fats contain more saturated fatty acids.
  • Oils: unsaturated compounds that are liquid at normal temperatures, usually found in plant products. Oils contain more unsaturated fatty acids.

The lipid layer beneath our skin helps insulate the body against temperature changes. Lipids provide long-term energy storage and store more energy per gram than carbohydrates.

Sources of Lipids

Lipids are obtained from both plants and animals. In animals they are mainly found as fats; in plants they are found as oils.

  • Animal sources: butter, lard, tallow, fish oil and egg yolk.
  • Plant sources: olive oil, coconut oil, sunflower oil, soybean oil, mustard oil and peanut oil (groundnut oil).

These lipids act as concentrated energy sources and are essential for cell structure, insulation and hormone production.

Recommended Daily Intake

Young adults should obtain about 20-35% of their daily calories from fats (45-80 g per day). Not all fats are harmful: healthy fats like omega-3 and omega-6 are vital for proper brain function, heart health and hormone regulation.

Key Points

  • Lipids are esters of fatty acids and glycerol; a triglyceride has 3 fatty acids + 1 glycerol.
  • Fats are solid and mostly from animals; oils are liquid and mostly from plants.
  • Lipids store energy, insulate organs, protect the body and form cell membranes.
  • Sources: butter, fish oil and egg yolk; olive, coconut and sunflower oils.
  • Daily intake is 20-35% of calories (45-80 g per day).
lessons.title: Lipids

lessons.notes_html:
Nucleic acids are essential biopolymers found in all living organisms. They are responsible for heredity and cellular functions. They store and transmit genetic information and direct the synthesis of proteins necessary for all cellular activities. The two main types are DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid) and RNA (Ribonucleic Acid).

Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA)

DNA defines genetic identity and regulates cellular functions. It consists of repeating units called nucleotides, each consisting of a phosphate group, a deoxyribose sugar, and one of four nitrogenous bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G). The sequence of these bases forms the genetic code. DNA is a double-stranded helix, with specific base pairing (A with T, and C with G). It provides the instructions for protein synthesis. Each human being has their own characteristic DNA sequence inherited from their parents, which is matched in a DNA test.

Ribonucleic Acid (RNA)

RNA is a single-stranded nucleic acid with ribose sugar instead of deoxyribose, and uracil (U) replaces thymine. RNA acts most notably as a messenger between DNA and the protein synthesis machinery. It assists in converting the genetic code into proteins and regulates the chemical reactions within cells.

FeatureDNARNA
StrandsDouble-stranded helixSingle-stranded
SugarDeoxyriboseRibose
Special baseThymine (T)Uracil (U)
Main functionStores genetic informationCarries instructions to make proteins

Sources of Nucleic Acids in Diet

  • Animal sources: organ meats (liver, kidney), meat, fish and seafood are rich in DNA and RNA due to their high cellular content.
  • Plant sources: legumes such as beans and lentils, green vegetables like spinach and broccoli, mushrooms and whole grains provide nucleotides in lower, yet beneficial, amounts.
  • Other sources: yeast and yeast extracts are very high in RNA.

The body can synthesise nucleotides; however, dietary intake becomes increasingly important during growth, illness or recovery.

Required Daily Intake

There is no official Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for nucleic acids; however, adults typically consume 300-600 mg of nucleotides daily through a balanced diet. Young adults may benefit from 500-700 mg daily to support growth, immunity and tissue repair. The requirement per kilogram of body weight is higher for infants and young children.

Key Points

  • Nucleic acids store and transmit genetic information; types are DNA and RNA.
  • DNA is double-stranded, has deoxyribose and thymine, and carries the genetic code.
  • RNA is single-stranded, has ribose and uracil, and helps make proteins.
  • Both are built from nucleotides: phosphate group + sugar + nitrogenous base.
  • Rich food sources are organ meats, fish, legumes, green vegetables and yeast.
lessons.title: Nucleic Acids: DNA and RNA

lessons.notes_html:
The general recommendations for daily intake of macronutrients for adults are given in Table 13.2. Individual needs can vary significantly with age, sex, level of physical activity and health conditions. Values are in grams per day.

Lipids20-35% of total calories (45-80 g for adults)Store energy, insulate organs, protect nerves, produce hormonesFatty fish, nuts, seeds, vegetable oils, avocados
Nucleic AcidsSmall amount neededStore and transmit genetic informationDNA and RNA found in all living organisms

Importance of Nutrition and Healthy Eating

Good nutrition and healthy eating are essential for overall health and well-being, preventing chronic diseases and promoting an optimal quality of life.

  • Proper nutrition boosts the immune system, facilitates tissue building and repair, and sustains strong bones and teeth.
  • For children, adolescents and pregnant women, it is vital for healthy growth, development and formation of organs and tissues.
  • Balancing calorie intake with physical activity maintains a healthy weight and body composition.
  • A well-balanced diet can help prevent chronic diseases such as heart disease, diabetes and certain cancers.
  • A diet rich in healthy fats, complex carbohydrates, vitamins and minerals enhances cognitive function, regulates mood and promotes mental health.

Basics of Nutrition and Healthy Eating

  • Eat various foods from all food groups: fruits and vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins (fish, beans, poultry, low-fat dairy) and healthy fats (avocados, nuts, seeds, olive oil).
  • Be mindful of portion sizes to avoid overeating; pay attention to hunger and fullness cues.
  • Drink plenty of water; aim for eight glasses daily, adjusting for individual needs and activity levels.
  • Limit processed foods, sugary drinks and items high in saturated and trans fats.
  • Enjoy treats in moderation; focus on a balanced diet overall and avoid deprivation.
  • Eat a diverse range of foods within each group to obtain all essential vitamins and minerals.
  • Consider age, sex, activity level and health status; consult a healthcare professional or dietitian for personalised advice.

Our diet also requires dietary fibre, which is not digestible. Fibre helps move undigested food through the digestive system; take 20 to 30 grams per day. Sufficient fibre promotes digestive health, prevents constipation and reduces the risk of heart disease, diabetes, weight gain and certain cancers. A deficiency of dietary fibre often results in constipation.

Key Points

  • Adults need carbohydrates 225-325 g, proteins 46-56 g and lipids 45-80 g per day.
  • Needs vary with age, sex, physical activity and health conditions.
  • Good nutrition boosts immunity, growth, healthy weight and mental well-being.
  • Eat varied foods, control portions, drink about eight glasses of water daily.
  • Take 20-30 g of dietary fibre daily for healthy digestion.
lessons.title: Daily Intake of Macronutrients and Healthy Nutrition

lessons.notes_html:
Standardised units help scientists communicate and work together easily worldwide. When everyone uses the same system, such as the International System of Units (SI), they can share data, compare results and repeat experiments without confusion. In chemistry even minor variations in measurements can significantly affect the results.

This unit covers standardised units, SI units, prefixes, practical lab units, accuracy and precision, apparatus, and standard form A × 10^n.

Examples from the Book

  • Mass: if a chemist in Pakistan uses 0.5 kilograms of salt, a chemist in England knows exactly how much salt to use. Pounds and ounces would make results difficult to compare.
  • Volume: 1.0 litre of hydrochloric acid is understood everywhere. Pints and gallons vary by country and would be confusing.
  • Temperature: a reaction at 298K, which is equivalent to 25°C, is clear to everyone.
  • Amount: 2.0 moles of carbon dioxide is precise because a mole is always the same number of particles, about 6.022 × 10^23.

Physical and Abstract Quantities

Physical quantities can be measured directly and possess a physical presence. Examples include length, time and temperature. Abstract quantities, in contrast, cannot be measured directly and lack standardised SI units, as they are often subjective and reliant on interpretation.

In the past people used non-standardised units such as cubit (length of the forearm), foot, and handspan for length, stone and bushel for mass and volume, and sundial and hourglass for time. These were significantly inaccurate, varying widely between individuals and locations, causing confusion in trade and construction. The SI system was established in 1960 to provide a standardised set of units.

QuantitySI UnitSymbol
MassKilogramkg
LengthMeterm
TimeSeconds
TemperatureKelvinK
Amount of SubstanceMolemol
Electric CurrentAmpereA

The book Table 14.1 also lists luminous intensity in candela (cd), electric charge in coulomb (C), force in newton (N), energy in joule (J) and pressure in pascal (Pa).

Key Points

  • Standard units allow chemists worldwide to compare, repeat and trust results.
  • SI is the International System of Units, established in 1960.
  • Physical quantities are measured directly; abstract quantities cannot be measured directly.
  • Old units like cubit, handspan and stone were inaccurate and inconsistent.
  • Key SI units: kg for mass, m for length, s for time, K for temperature, mol for amount of substance.
lessons.title: The Importance of Standard Units and SI Quantities

lessons.notes_html:
Prefixes such as kilo (k), deci (d) and milli (m) are used in the SI system to express quantities more flexibly and efficiently. They help in converting between large and small measurement scales without writing very large or very small numbers.

PrefixSymbolFactorExample
kilo-k10001 kg = 1000 g, 1 km = 1000 m
deci-d0.1 or 10^-11 dm = 0.1 m = 10 cm
milli-m0.001 or 10^-31 mg = 0.001 g, 1 mL = 0.001 L

The word kilo comes from the Greek word khilioi, meaning thousand, and milli derives from the Latin millesimus, meaning thousandth. Examples: a bag of rice weighing 5 kilograms has a mass of 5,000 grams, and a distance of 12 kilometres equals 12,000 metres. If a notebook is 2 decimetres wide, it measures 20 centimetres. A tablet containing 500 milligrams of a substance has a mass of 0.5 grams.

Practical Advantages of cm3, g and s in Chemistry Labs

In chemistry laboratories the choice of units is critical, particularly when working with small quantities of substances. Chemists use cm3, g and s as more practical units for small amounts in the lab.

  • Volume Measurement (cm3): The cm3 is a convenient unit for measuring the volume of liquids. It is especially practical for small quantities, offering a manageable and easily visualised unit.
  • Mass Measurement (g): The gram is a standard unit of measurement for mass in the metric system. When working with small amounts, balances and scales calibrated in grams provide reliable mass determinations.
  • Time Measurement (s): Seconds are a fundamental unit for time and are vital in chemical experiments. Timing is essential for controlling reaction rates, monitoring reaction progress and conducting time-dependent procedures.

Key Points

  • kilo- means 1000 times, deci- means one-tenth, milli- means one-thousandth.
  • Prefixes keep numbers short, avoid confusion and simplify calculations.
  • cm3 is practical for small liquid volumes in the lab.
  • g is practical for small masses; s is practical for timing reactions.
lessons.title: Combining Units with Magnitude Terms and Practical Lab Units

lessons.notes_html:
Accuracy refers to how closely the measured value aligns with the true or accepted value. It indicates the degree of correctness in a measurement. Precision refers to the closeness of multiple (two or more) measurements to one another, irrespective of whether they are close to the true value. It indicates consistency or reproducibility. Measurements can be precise but not accurate.

Accuracy and Precision Illustration

A dartboard is used as a visual tool, with the bullseye representing the true value.

  • No Accuracy, No Precision: darts land away from the bullseye and far apart from each other.
  • High Precision, Low Accuracy: darts land close to one another but far from the bullseye.
  • Low Precision, High Accuracy: darts are dispersed around the bullseye but generally close to the centre, so accurate on average but not precise.
  • High Precision, High Accuracy: all darts land near the centre and close to one another.

Tools for Accurate Measurement

ApparatusUseBook Facts
BeakerHold, mix, stir liquidsCommonly 50, 100, 500, 1000 mL; markings approximate, not for high-precision tasks
Graduated CylinderMeasure volume of liquidsTypically 10 mL to 1000 mL; not used for weighing, mixing, stirring or heating
Volumetric PipetteMeasure specific liquid volumesCommonly 10 mL and 25 mL; accurate and precise, ideal for preparing solutions and titration; a pipette filler draws liquid in
BuretteTitration, deliver liquid volumes0 mL to 50 mL; greater accuracy than measuring cylinders but less precise than pipettes
Gas SyringeMeasure volume of gasesCollecting and measuring gases produced or consumed in a reaction
BalanceMeasure massTop-loading gives approximate measurements; analytical balance measures small masses, often to 0.0001 g (0.1 mg)
Laboratory ThermometerMeasure temperatureMeasures the precise temperature of substances
StopwatchMeasure timePrecisely measures brief time intervals in experiments

In beverage and perfume industries, pipettes and burettes keep flavour and fragrance precise and consistent in each batch.

Techniques for Accurate Measurement

  • Regular Calibration: compare readings to a known standard, e.g. checking a cylinder measuring 100 mL of water against a standard beaker.
  • Routine Maintenance: cleaning, lubricating moving parts, inspections; a dust-free, well-maintained balance gives precise weights.
  • Choosing the Right Equipment: select the instrument with the highest precision that suits the task.
  • Taking Multiple Measurements: repeating measurements enhances precision and reduces errors, e.g. multiple trials in titration.
  • Minimising Human Error: be attentive and careful; training in consistent practices such as pipetting improves reliability.
  • Understanding Meniscus Reading: a meniscus is the curved surface of liquid in narrow containers, formed due to surface tension. Read the bottom of the meniscus in graduated cylinders for an accurate measurement.

Key Points

  • Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated measurements to each other.
  • An analytical balance measures small masses to 0.0001 g.
  • A burette (0-50 mL) is used to deliver precise volumes during titration.
  • Calibration, maintenance, correct apparatus, repeated readings and correct meniscus reading improve accuracy and precision.
lessons.title: Accuracy, Precision and Tools for Accurate Measurement

mcqs.q: In standard form A x 10^n, A must satisfy what condition?

A is greater than or equal to 1 and less than 10
mcqs.why: The notes define standard form as A x 10^n where A is a number greater than or equal to 1 and less than 10, and n is an integer.

mcqs.q: The large number 235,000,000 written in standard form is what?
mcqs.why: Working: moving the decimal point 8 places to the left gives A = 2.35 and n = 8, so 235,000,000 = 2.35 x 10^8.

mcqs.q: For a very small number such as 9.11 x 10^-29, the exponent is negative because what happened?
options: The decimal point was not moved
The number became smaller after shifting
Shifting the decimal point to the right made the written number larger
mcqs.why: The notes explain the decimal point is shifted right and counted, so n becomes -29, negative because the number has increased in written form.

mcqs.why: Working: shifting the decimal point 23 places until a number between 1 and 10 remains gives 6.022 x 10^23, as shown in the notes.

mcqs.q: When multiplying values in standard form, what happens to the exponents?
mcqs.why: The notes state that in multiplication exponents are added while multiplying, and in division exponents are subtracted.

mcqs.why: Working: 4.5 x 1.2 = 5.4 and 3 + 5 = 8, so the product is 5.4 x 10^8, exactly the example given in the notes.

mcqs.why: Working: 3.2 / 2.5 = 1.28 and 7 - 3 = 4, so the quotient is 1.28 x 10^4, exactly the division example in the notes.

mcqs.why: The notes state the human body contains about 3 x 10^13 cells, and scientists use scientific notation to express such large numbers easily.

mcqs.q: To convert 6.625 x 10^-34 out of exponential form, the decimal point is shifted how?
options: To the left by 34 places, filling vacant spaces with zeros
It is not moved at all
mcqs.why: With a negative exponent, the notes say to move the decimal point to the left by the absolute value of the exponent, here 34 places.

mcqs.q: In A x 10^n, the parts A, 10 and n are called what?
options: A is the exponent, 10 is the coefficient, n is the base
A is the base, 10 is the exponent, n is the coefficient
A is the unit, 10 is the prefix, n is the factor
A is the coefficient, 10 is the base and n is the exponent
mcqs.why: The notes name the parts of standard form directly: A is the coefficient, 10 is the base and n is the exponent.

lessons.notes_html:
The standard form, expressed as A × 10^n, represents numbers, particularly those that are very large or very small, in a concise manner. In this form, A is a number greater than or equal to 1 and less than 10, while n is an integer that can be either positive or negative. A is the coefficient, 10 is the base and n is the exponent. Standard notation enhances communication and data comparison among scientists.

Large and Small Numbers

  • Large Number: 235,000,000 can be written as 2.35 × 10^8. Move the decimal point to the left and count the places moved. A becomes 2.35 and n is 8, positive because the number became smaller.
  • Small Number: 0.00000000000000000000000000000911 can be expressed as 9.11 × 10^-29. Shift the decimal point to the right and count the places moved. A is 9.11 and n becomes -29, negative because the number has increased.

The human body contains about 3 × 10^13 cells, and scientists use scientific notation to express such large numbers easily.

Conversion into Scientific Notation

Avogadro's number (602200000000000000000000) can be easily expressed in exponential form. Shift the decimal point until we arrive at a number between 1 and 10. Count the number of places the decimal point is moved, and that count will become the exponent. The number can be written as 6.022 × 10^23.

Conversion out of Scientific Notation

To convert 6.625 × 10^-34 out of exponential form, shift the decimal point to the left or right according to the value of the exponent. When the exponent is negative, move the decimal point to the left by the absolute value of the exponent: here shift 6.625 by 34 places to the left, filling vacant spaces with zeros, to obtain the standard decimal notation.

Calculations with Values in Standard Form

  • Multiplication: Exponents are added while multiplying. Example: (4.5 × 10^3)(1.2 × 10^5) = 5.4 × 10^(3+5) = 5.4 × 10^8.
  • Division: Exponents are subtracted while dividing. Example: (3.2 × 10^7) ÷ (2.5 × 10^3) = 1.28 × 10^(7-3) = 1.28 × 10^4.

Key Points

  • Standard form is A × 10^n, where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is a positive or negative integer.
  • Large numbers give a positive exponent; small numbers give a negative exponent.
  • To convert in, move the decimal point until one non-zero digit is before it and count the moves.
  • In multiplication exponents are added; in division exponents are subtracted.
lessons.title: Standard Form and Scientific Notation

lessons.notes_html:
Experimental methods are essential in scientific research for studying and understanding various phenomena.

Advantages of Experimental Methods

  • They provide precise control over variables, which allows the establishment of cause-and-effect relationships.
  • The ability to repeat experiments enhances the reliability of results, increasing confidence in scientific conclusions.
  • Experiments offer a level of accuracy and understanding often unattainable through other research approaches.

Disadvantages of Experimental Methods

  • Some experimental conditions may not directly apply to real-world situations.
  • Experiments can be resource-intensive, requiring time, funding and specialised equipment.
  • Not all research questions can be effectively addressed through experimental methods, especially where the complexity of human behaviour or historical context plays a significant role.

Advantages and Disadvantages of Apparatus

ApparatusAdvantagesDisadvantages
StopwatchesProvide precise measurements of time intervalsLimited precision compared to advanced timing devices; susceptible to human error
ThermometersVersatile, measure a wide range of temperatures, easy to useFragile; limitations in measuring extreme temperatures
BalancesHigh-precision measurements for both small and large massesSensitive to external factors such as air currents; require careful handling and calibration
BurettesExcel in precise measurement of liquid volumes during titrationsRequire careful reading; may introduce small errors due to liquid clinging to the walls
Volumetric PipettesHighly accurate for specific liquid volumesFragile and limited to small volumes
Measuring CylindersQuick and versatile for rough measurementsLess precise and accurate for small volumes; reading at the meniscus can be challenging
Gas SyringesEffective in measuring gas volumesLimited to gases; require careful handling to prevent leakage

Meteorologists measure air pressure in pascals and temperature in kelvin to predict weather accurately.

Key Points

  • Experiments give control over variables and repeatable, reliable results.
  • Experiments may not match real-world conditions and need time, funding and specialised equipment.
  • Every apparatus has strengths and limits; choose the apparatus that fits the measurement.
  • Burettes and pipettes are most precise for liquids; measuring cylinders are for rough measurements.

lessons.title: Fundamental Terms in Solutions
lessons.notes_html:
In chemistry, knowing how to prepare solutions and separate their parts is essential for experiments, analysis, and industry. These techniques are vital in pharmaceuticals, environmental science, and food technology.

Key Terms

  • Solvent: a substance, usually a liquid, that dissolves other substances called solutes. It is the main component of a solution and provides the medium for dissolving. Example: water dissolves sugar or salt.
  • Solute: a substance that dissolves in a solvent to form a solution. It can be a solid, liquid, or gas, and is present in a smaller quantity than the solvent. Example: sugar dissolved in water.
  • Solution: a uniform mixture formed by dissolving one or more solutes in a solvent. The solute particles are evenly spread at the molecular level. Example: saltwater, where salt (solute) is dissolved in water (solvent).
  • Saturated solution: a solution containing the maximum quantity of solute that can dissolve under specific conditions. Any extra solute stays undissolved. Example: when no more salt can dissolve in a glass of water at room temperature.
  • Residue: the material that remains after a separation or purification process such as evaporation, distillation, or filtration. Example: after boiling saltwater, the salt crystals left are the residue.
  • Filtrate: the liquid or solution that passes through a filter during filtration, leaving solid particles behind. Example: after filtering sand and water, the clear water collected is the filtrate.

More Useful Terms

  • Dilution: decreasing the concentration of a solute in a solution by adding more solvent.
  • Concentration: the amount of solute in a specific amount of solvent or solution, usually expressed as molarity.
  • Precipitate: a solid formed when a solute comes out of a solution because of a chemical reaction or a change in conditions.
  • Solubility: the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specific temperature and pressure.

Misconception check: adding more solute does not always increase concentration. Once a solution is saturated, extra solute no longer dissolves and settles at the bottom as undissolved particles.

Key Points

  • The solvent is the main component; the solute dissolves in it.
  • A saturated solution holds the maximum solute that can dissolve.
  • Residue stays behind after separation; filtrate passes through a filter.
  • Melting and boiling points are key indicators of purity.

lessons.title: Solvent Extraction and Filtration
lessons.notes_html:
Separation and purification techniques let chemists and industries produce pure substances. Each technique uses different physical or chemical properties of the substances.

Using a Suitable Solvent (Solvent Extraction)

This method uses a solvent in which the desired substance is highly soluble, while the impurities have low solubility in it.

  • First, the impure solute is dissolved in a solvent in which its solubility is low.
  • The mixture is then transferred into another (selected) solvent in which the solute is more soluble.
  • The two solvents are immiscible, or have very limited miscibility (ability to mix).
  • The phase richer in solute is separated with a separating funnel, leaving behind the phase with less solute and more impurity.

Filtration: Separating by Particle Size

Filtration is a physical method used to separate a solid that does not dissolve in a liquid.

  • The mixture is poured through a filter made of porous material such as filter paper, cloth, or mesh.
  • The filter lets the liquid pass through its small holes or pores.
  • The undissolved solid particles are too large to pass, so they are trapped on the surface of the filter as the residue.
  • This method is very effective for removing insoluble solids like sand from water.

Sand remains on the filter paper because its particles are larger than the pores, while dissolved salt passes through with the water.

Key Points

  • Solvent extraction moves a solute into a solvent where it is more soluble.
  • The two solvents in extraction are immiscible and are separated with a separating funnel.
  • Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid by particle size.
  • The solid trapped on the filter is the residue; the liquid through it is the filtrate.

mcqs.q: Solvent extraction uses a solvent in which:
options: Both the desired substance and the impurities are insoluble
The desired substance is highly soluble, while the impurities have low solubility
The impurities are highly soluble and the desired substance is insoluble
Every substance in the mixture dissolves equally well
mcqs.why: The notes state that this method uses a solvent in which the desired substance is highly soluble, while the impurities have low solubility in it, so the desired substance can be moved into that solvent.

The second solvent evaporates faster than the first
The second solvent changes the solute into a solid
The first solvent must be heated to boiling
mcqs.why: The notes describe first dissolving the impure solute in a solvent in which its solubility is low, then transferring the mixture into another selected solvent in which the solute is more soluble.

mcqs.q: The two solvents used in solvent extraction must be:
options: Immiscible, or have very limited miscibility with each other
mcqs.why: The notes state that the two solvents are immiscible, or have very limited miscibility (ability to mix), which is what allows the two phases to be separated afterwards.

mcqs.q: Which apparatus is used to separate the phase richer in solute in solvent extraction?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the phase richer in solute is separated with a separating funnel, leaving behind the phase with less solute and more impurity.

mcqs.why: Filtration is a physical method used to separate a solid that does not dissolve in a liquid, and the notes give removing insoluble solids like sand from water as its use.

mcqs.why: The notes state that the mixture is poured through a filter made of porous material such as filter paper, cloth or mesh, which lets the liquid pass through its small holes or pores.

mcqs.why: The notes state that the undissolved solid particles are too large to pass through the filter, so they are trapped on its surface as the residue, while the liquid through it is the filtrate.

mcqs.why: The notes explain that sand remains on the filter paper because its particles are larger than the pores, while water passes through; filtration separates by particle size.

options: Passes through the filter with the water

mcqs.why: The notes state that the phase richer in solute is separated with a separating funnel, leaving behind the phase with less solute and more impurity.

lessons.title: Crystallisation: Purification through Crystal Formation
lessons.notes_html:
Crystallisation is a separation and purification technique used to obtain pure solid crystals from a solution.

How It Works

  • Prepare a saturated solution at high temperature, so no more solute can dissolve at that temperature.
  • Filter the solution while hot to remove undissolved impurities.
  • Allow the solution to cool slowly.
  • As the temperature decreases, the solubility of the solute also decreases, so the dissolved substance forms solid crystals.
  • Separate the crystals from the remaining liquid, which usually contains the dissolved impurities.

Crystallisation is especially useful for producing highly pure solids, because the impurities stay in the solution while the pure crystals are collected.

Interesting fact: the ancient Egyptians first used crystallisation to purify natural salts from desert lakes.

Key Points

  • Crystallisation gives pure solid crystals from a solution.
  • A hot saturated solution is filtered, then cooled slowly.
  • Cooling lowers solubility, so pure crystals form.
  • Impurities remain dissolved in the leftover liquid.

mcqs.q: Crystallisation is a technique used to obtain:
options: Pure solid crystals from a solution
A pure liquid from a mixture of gases
An insoluble solid from a liquid by filtering
Two separated liquids from a mixture
mcqs.why: The notes define crystallisation as a separation and purification technique used to obtain pure solid crystals from a solution.

mcqs.q: The first step in crystallisation is to prepare:
options: A very dilute solution at room temperature
A saturated solution at high temperature, so no more solute can dissolve at that temperature
A mixture of two immiscible solvents
A solution that has already cooled to form crystals
mcqs.why: The notes state that crystallisation begins by preparing a saturated solution at high temperature, so no more solute can dissolve at that temperature.

mcqs.q: Why is the hot saturated solution filtered during crystallisation?
options: To cool the solution down quickly
To dissolve more solute in the solution
To remove undissolved impurities from the solution
To separate the crystals that have already formed
mcqs.why: The notes state that the solution is filtered while hot to remove undissolved impurities, before it is allowed to cool and form crystals.

mcqs.q: After filtering, the hot saturated solution should be:
options: Boiled until all the liquid evaporates
mcqs.why: The notes state that after hot filtration the solution is allowed to cool slowly, and during this cooling the dissolved substance forms solid crystals.

mcqs.q: Crystals form during cooling because, as the temperature decreases:
options: The solubility of the solute also decreases, so the dissolved substance forms solid crystals
The solubility of the solute increases without limit
The solvent changes into a solid
The impurities turn into crystals first
mcqs.why: The notes explain that as the temperature decreases, the solubility of the solute also decreases, so the dissolved substance can no longer stay dissolved and forms solid crystals.

mcqs.q: During crystallisation, where do the impurities mainly end up?
options: Inside the pure crystals that are collected
In the remaining liquid, where they usually stay dissolved
On the filter paper used for the hot filtration only, in every case
mcqs.why: The notes state that the crystals are separated from the remaining liquid, which usually contains the dissolved impurities, so the impurities stay in the solution while the pure crystals are collected.

mcqs.q: After the crystals have formed, they are separated from:

mcqs.why: The notes list separating the crystals from the remaining liquid as the final step of crystallisation, leaving the dissolved impurities behind in that liquid.

options: Large amounts of impure solid very quickly

Highly pure solids, because the impurities stay in the solution
mcqs.why: The notes state that crystallisation is especially useful for producing highly pure solids, because the impurities stay in the solution while the pure crystals are collected.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, who first used crystallisation to purify natural salts from desert lakes?
mcqs.why: The interesting fact in the notes states that the ancient Egyptians first used crystallisation to purify natural salts from desert lakes.

options: The solute has all turned into crystals
mcqs.why: The notes describe preparing a saturated solution at high temperature, so no more solute can dissolve at that temperature; cooling then lowers solubility further and crystals form.

lessons.title: Simple Distillation and Fractional Distillation
lessons.notes_html:
Simple distillation purifies a liquid using the difference in boiling points between substances in a mixture.

  • The mixture is heated in a distillation apparatus.
  • The component with the lower boiling point vaporises first.
  • The vapour passes through a condenser, where it cools and turns back into a liquid called the distillate, which is collected separately.
  • The substance with the higher boiling point remains in the flask.
  • It works best when the boiling points differ by at least 70°C.

Simple distillation is used to obtain pure water from saltwater in desert regions and in the production of alcohol. Distillation is also used to purify water, extract perfumes, and produce fuels.

Fractional Distillation

Fractional distillation separates liquids in a mixture with closely related boiling points.

  • Like simple distillation, the mixture is heated and the lower boiling point component vaporises first.
  • A fractionating column is placed between the flask and the condenser.
  • The column allows repeated condensation and vaporisation of the rising vapours, so the liquids separate more precisely.
  • Each component rises in the column according to its boiling point: the lower the boiling point, the higher it rises.
  • It is particularly effective when the difference in boiling points is less than 70°C.

Oil refineries use large fractional distillation towers to separate crude oil into petrol, diesel, and kerosene. Other fractions include refinery gas, petroleum ether, light naphtha, fuel oil, lubricating oil, and asphalt.

Key Points

  • Simple distillation: one vaporisation and condensation; best for boiling point differences of at least 70°C.
  • The liquid collected after condensation is the distillate.
  • Fractional distillation uses a fractionating column for repeated condensation and vaporisation.
  • Fractional distillation separates liquids with close boiling points, such as the fractions of crude oil.

mcqs.q: Simple distillation separates substances using the difference in their:
mcqs.why: The notes state that simple distillation purifies a liquid using the difference in boiling points between substances in a mixture, so the component with the lower boiling point vaporises first.

mcqs.q: When a mixture is heated in simple distillation, which component vaporises first?
options: The component with the lower boiling point
The component with the higher boiling point
All components at exactly the same time
mcqs.why: The notes state that the mixture is heated in a distillation apparatus and the component with the lower boiling point vaporises first, while the substance with the higher boiling point remains in the flask.

mcqs.q: In distillation, the vapour turns back into a liquid in the:
mcqs.why: The notes state that the vapour passes through a condenser, where it cools and turns back into a liquid called the distillate, which is collected separately.

mcqs.q: The liquid collected after condensation in distillation is called the:
mcqs.why: The notes name the liquid formed when the vapour cools in the condenser as the distillate, and it is collected separately in the distillate flask.

options: Vaporises first and is collected first

mcqs.why: The notes state that the component with the lower boiling point vaporises first, and the substance with the higher boiling point remains in the flask during simple distillation.

mcqs.why: The key points state that simple distillation involves one vaporisation and condensation and works best for boiling point differences of at least 70°C.

options: Obtaining pure water from saltwater in desert regions

mcqs.why: The notes state that simple distillation is used to obtain pure water from saltwater in desert regions and in the production of alcohol; distillation is also used to purify water, extract perfumes and produce fuels.

options: Filter paper between the flask and the condenser

mcqs.why: The notes state that in fractional distillation a fractionating column is placed between the flask and the condenser, allowing repeated condensation and vaporisation of the rising vapours.

options: Repeated condensation and vaporisation, so the liquids separate more precisely

mcqs.why: The notes explain that the fractionating column allows repeated condensation and vaporisation of the rising vapours, so liquids with closely related boiling points separate more precisely.

mcqs.q: Fractional distillation is particularly effective when the difference in boiling points is:
options: Less than 70°C, as with the fractions of crude oil such as petrol, diesel and kerosene
mcqs.why: The notes state that fractional distillation is particularly effective when the difference in boiling points is less than 70°C, and oil refineries use it to separate crude oil into petrol, diesel and kerosene.

lessons.title: Everyday Separation Techniques: Filtration, Decantation and Crystallisation
lessons.notes_html:
Filtration: Separation of Salt and Sand Mixture

The principle is that the solute (salt) dissolves in a solvent (water), while the insoluble substance (sand) does not.

  • Mix the salt and sand with water to dissolve the salt.
  • Pour the mixture onto a filter paper or filter funnel.
  • The water containing dissolved salt passes through the filter, leaving the sand as a residue on the filter paper.
  • The collected filtrate can be processed further by evaporation to obtain pure salt.

Chemistry in your body: your kidneys act like natural filters, removing waste and maintaining ionic balance, similar to filtration in a laboratory.

Decantation: Separating Oil and Water

Decantation separates oil and water based on their differing densities and the inability of oil to mix with water. Oil is less dense and does not mix with water, so it floats on top of the water.

  • Allow the oil-water mixture to stand undisturbed.
  • The less dense oil forms a distinct layer on top of the water.
  • Carefully pour off the upper layer containing the oil, leaving the water behind.
  • This method is simple, but it may not suit emulsified mixtures where oil and water form a stable suspension.

Crystallisation: Purification of Sugar

  • Dissolve impure sugar in hot water to create a concentrated solution.
  • Allow the solution to cool slowly. As it cools, sugar molecules come together and form crystals.
  • Separate the crystals from the remaining liquid by filtration or decantation.
  • This gives high-purity sugar, leaving the impurities in the liquid phase.

Key Points

  • Salt and sand: dissolve the salt, filter off the sand, then evaporate the filtrate.
  • Decantation pours off one layer of liquids with different densities, like oil on water.
  • Decantation does not work well for emulsified mixtures.
  • Impure sugar is purified by crystallisation from hot water.

options: Salt and sand have different boiling points

Sand dissolves in water, while the salt does not

mcqs.why: The notes state the principle directly: the solute (salt) dissolves in a solvent (water), while the insoluble substance (sand) does not, so the sand can be filtered off.

mcqs.q: When the salt and sand mixture is filtered, the sand is left as:
options: The residue on the filter paper

mcqs.why: The notes state that the water containing dissolved salt passes through the filter, leaving the sand as a residue on the filter paper.

mcqs.q: How is pure salt obtained from the filtrate collected after filtering off the sand?
options: By decantation of the top layer
By adding more sand to it
By processing it further by evaporation
By cooling it until crystals of sand form
mcqs.why: The notes state that the collected filtrate can be processed further by evaporation to obtain pure salt, since the filtrate is water containing dissolved salt.

mcqs.q: Which organs in the human body act like natural filters, removing waste and maintaining ionic balance?
mcqs.why: The notes state that your kidneys act like natural filters, removing waste and maintaining ionic balance, similar to filtration in a laboratory.

mcqs.q: Decantation separates oil and water based on:
options: Their differing densities and the inability of oil to mix with water
The different sizes of their particles
The solubility of oil in water
mcqs.why: The notes state that decantation separates oil and water based on their differing densities and the inability of oil to mix with water.

mcqs.q: In an oil and water mixture left to stand, the oil forms a layer on top because oil:
options: Is less dense than water and does not mix with it

mcqs.why: The notes state that oil is less dense and does not mix with water, so it floats on top of the water and forms a distinct layer on top when the mixture stands undisturbed.

mcqs.q: In decantation of oil and water, the separation is completed by:
options: Filtering the whole mixture through paper

Boiling the mixture until the water evaporates
Cooling the mixture until the oil crystallises
mcqs.why: The notes state that after the oil forms a distinct layer on top, you carefully pour off the upper layer containing the oil, leaving the water behind.

mcqs.q: Decantation may not suit emulsified mixtures because in an emulsion:
options: Oil and water have exactly the same boiling point

The water floats on top of the oil
mcqs.why: The notes state that decantation is simple, but it may not suit emulsified mixtures where oil and water form a stable suspension, so no clean separate layer forms to pour off.

mcqs.q: Impure sugar is purified by crystallisation by dissolving it in hot water, cooling slowly, and then:
options: Evaporating all the water at once

mcqs.why: The notes state that as the concentrated sugar solution cools, sugar molecules form crystals, which are separated from the remaining liquid by filtration or decantation, giving high-purity sugar and leaving the impurities in the liquid phase.

lessons.title: Assessing Purity through Melting and Boiling Points
lessons.notes_html:
Analysing the melting and boiling points of substances is an important method for identifying them and assessing their purity. Pure substances show distinct and consistent melting and boiling points, while impurities cause deviations in these points.

Melting Point Analysis

  • Pure substance: has a distinct and sharp melting point. It changes from solid to liquid rapidly at one precise temperature.
  • Effect of impurities: impurities lower and broaden the melting point. They disrupt the regular crystal lattice structure, so melting becomes less precise and occurs over a broader range of temperatures.
  • A significant deviation or a broader melting range suggests the presence of impurities.

Boiling Point Analysis

  • Pure substance: has a specific boiling point at which it changes from liquid to gas, quickly and at a particular temperature.
  • Effect of impurities: impurities can increase the boiling point and widen the range of temperatures at which the substance boils, so reaching the boiling point requires more energy.
  • Compare the observed boiling point with the known value for the pure substance. A significant difference, or a wider range, suggests impurities.
SampleResult in the Book
Pure iceMelts at 0°C
Impure iceMelts at -0.5°C
Pure waterBoils at 100°C
Salt waterBoils at 100.5°C

Key Points

  • A pure substance melts and boils sharply at one fixed temperature.
  • Impurities lower and broaden the melting point.
  • Impurities raise and widen the boiling point.
  • Comparing observed values with known values tests purity.

mcqs.q: A pure substance melts:
options: Over a broad range of temperatures
Sharply, changing from solid to liquid rapidly at one precise temperature
At a lower temperature than an impure sample
Only after its boiling point is reached
mcqs.why: The notes state that a pure substance has a distinct and sharp melting point and changes from solid to liquid rapidly at one precise temperature.

mcqs.q: Impurities affect the melting point of a substance by:
options: Raising it and making it sharper
Lowering it and broadening it, so melting occurs over a broader range of temperatures
mcqs.why: The notes state that impurities lower and broaden the melting point, disrupting the regular crystal lattice structure so melting becomes less precise and occurs over a broader range of temperatures.

mcqs.q: Why do impurities make melting less precise?
options: They disrupt the regular crystal lattice structure of the solid
They increase the mass of the sample
They change the solid into a gas directly
They remove heat from the sample
mcqs.why: The notes explain that impurities disrupt the regular crystal lattice structure, so melting becomes less precise and occurs over a broader range of temperatures instead of at one sharp point.

mcqs.q: A pure substance boils:
options: Over a wide range of temperatures
At a specific boiling point, quickly and at a particular temperature
At a lower temperature when impurities are added
mcqs.why: The notes state that a pure substance has a specific boiling point at which it changes from liquid to gas, quickly and at a particular temperature.

mcqs.q: Pure water, according to the sample results in the book, boils at:
mcqs.why: The sample result table in the notes gives pure water boiling at 100°C, while salt water boils at 100.5°C because the impurity raises and widens the boiling point.

mcqs.q: A significant deviation of the observed melting point from the known value, or a broader melting range, suggests:

The presence of impurities in the substance

Measuring only the colour of the substance

lessons.title: Tests for Ammonia, Carbon Dioxide and Chlorine
lessons.notes_html:
Qualitative analysis means identifying substances from their physical and chemical properties, without measuring their quantities. Gases are identified by distinctive changes in colour, smell, or sound.

Ammonia Gas (NH3)

Ammonia is produced by heating a mixture of solid ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide:

2NH4Cl(s) + Ca(OH)2(s) → CaCl2(s) + 2H2O(l) + 2NH3(g)

It is a colourless gas with a sharp, pungent odour and shows basic properties. Test: hold damp red litmus paper near the mouth of the test tube (not touching the sides). The paper turns blue, confirming ammonia.

Carbon Dioxide Gas (CO2)

Carbon dioxide is produced by reacting calcium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid:

CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)

Test: pass the gas through limewater (an aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide):

Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) → CaCO3(s) + H2O(l)

A white precipitate of calcium carbonate forms and turns the limewater milky, confirming carbon dioxide.

Chlorine Gas (Cl2)

Chlorine is prepared by reacting concentrated hydrochloric acid with manganese dioxide:

MnO2(s) + 4HCl → MnCl2(aq) + 2H2O(l) + Cl2(g)

Chlorine is a powerful bleaching agent that oxidises coloured substances. Test: hold damp blue litmus paper in the gas. First the paper turns red (acidic nature), then it is bleached white as the colour is removed.

GasTestPositive Result
Ammonia, NH3Damp red litmus paperTurns blue
Carbon dioxide, CO2LimewaterTurns milky
Chlorine, Cl2Damp blue litmus paperTurns red, then bleached white

Key Points

  • Ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue.
  • Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky by forming calcium carbonate.
  • Chlorine turns damp blue litmus red, then bleaches it white.

mcqs.q: Qualitative analysis means identifying substances:
options: From their physical and chemical properties, without measuring their quantities
Only by weighing them on a balance
mcqs.why: The notes define qualitative analysis as identifying substances from their physical and chemical properties, without measuring their quantities; gases are identified by distinctive changes in colour, smell or sound.

mcqs.q: Ammonia gas is produced by heating a mixture of:
options: Calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid
Concentrated hydrochloric acid and manganese dioxide
Solid ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide
mcqs.why: The notes state that ammonia is produced by heating a mixture of solid ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide: 2NH4Cl(s) + Ca(OH)2(s) -> CaCl2(s) + 2H2O(l) + 2NH3(g).

options: A colourless gas with a sharp, pungent odour that shows basic properties
A greenish gas that bleaches litmus paper white
A colourless gas with no smell that turns limewater milky

mcqs.why: The notes describe ammonia as a colourless gas with a sharp, pungent odour that shows basic properties, which is why it turns damp red litmus paper blue.

mcqs.q: The test that confirms ammonia gas is that damp red litmus paper:
options: Turns red and is then bleached white
Catches fire with a pop sound
mcqs.why: The notes state that ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue, confirming ammonia, because ammonia shows basic properties.

mcqs.q: When testing for ammonia, the damp red litmus paper should be held:
options: Inside the liquid in the test tube
Near the mouth of the test tube, not touching the sides
At the bottom of the test tube
mcqs.why: The notes instruct to hold damp red litmus paper near the mouth of the test tube, not touching the sides, and the paper turning blue confirms ammonia.

options: Calcium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid

mcqs.why: The notes state that carbon dioxide is produced by reacting calcium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid: CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g).

mcqs.q: The test that confirms carbon dioxide is that limewater:
options: Turns milky as a white precipitate of calcium carbonate forms
mcqs.why: The notes state that carbon dioxide passed through limewater forms a white precipitate of calcium carbonate, Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) -> CaCO3(s) + H2O(l), which turns the limewater milky and confirms carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: The white precipitate formed when carbon dioxide is passed through limewater is:
mcqs.why: The equation in the notes, Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) -> CaCO3(s) + H2O(l), shows that the white precipitate is calcium carbonate, and it is this solid that turns the limewater milky.

mcqs.q: Chlorine gas is prepared by reacting:
options: Dilute hydrochloric acid with calcium carbonate
Concentrated hydrochloric acid with manganese dioxide
mcqs.why: The notes state that chlorine is prepared by reacting concentrated hydrochloric acid with manganese dioxide: MnO2(s) + 4HCl -> MnCl2(aq) + 2H2O(l) + Cl2(g).

mcqs.q: The test that confirms chlorine gas is that damp blue litmus paper:
options: First turns red, showing its acidic nature, then is bleached white as the colour is removed
mcqs.why: The notes state that chlorine first turns damp blue litmus paper red because of its acidic nature, then bleaches it white, because chlorine is a powerful bleaching agent that oxidises coloured substances.

lessons.title: Tests for Hydrogen, Oxygen and Sulphur Dioxide
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrogen Gas (H2)

Hydrogen is a flammable gas that burns in air to produce water:

2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(l)

Test: hold a burning wooden splint near the mouth of the test tube containing the gas. Hydrogen produces a "pop" sound.

Oxygen Gas (O2)

Oxygen supports combustion and acts as an oxidising agent. It can be obtained by the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide in the presence of a catalyst such as manganese dioxide:

2H2O2(aq) → 2H2O(l) + O2(g)  (catalyst MnO2)

Test: light a wooden splint, blow it out until it glows, and hold the glowing splint at the mouth of the test tube. In oxygen, the splint reignites and burns brightly.

Sulphur Dioxide Gas (SO2)

Test: sulphur dioxide is identified by the decolourisation of acidified potassium permanganate (KMnO4) solution. It reacts with potassium permanganate and sulphuric acid to produce potassium sulphate, manganese sulphate, and water, with the loss of the solution's purple colour:

5SO2 + 2KMnO4 + 2H2SO4 → K2SO4 + 2MnSO4 + 2H2O

The purple solution becomes colourless, confirming sulphur dioxide.

GasTestPositive Result
Hydrogen, H2Burning wooden splintPop sound
Oxygen, O2Glowing splintSplint reignites
Sulphur dioxide, SO2Acidified KMnO4 solutionPurple colour is lost (decolourised)

Key Points

  • Hydrogen gives a pop sound with a burning splint.
  • Oxygen relights a glowing splint.
  • Sulphur dioxide decolourises purple acidified potassium permanganate.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen gas is described in the notes as a gas that:

mcqs.why: The notes state that hydrogen is a flammable gas that burns in air to produce water: 2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l), which is linked to its pop test with a burning splint.

mcqs.q: The test that confirms hydrogen gas is that a burning wooden splint produces:

mcqs.q: Oxygen gas is described in the notes as a gas that:
options: Turns damp red litmus paper blue
Supports combustion and acts as an oxidising agent
mcqs.why: The notes state that oxygen supports combustion and acts as an oxidising agent, which is why a glowing splint reignites and burns brightly in it.

mcqs.q: Oxygen can be obtained by the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide in the presence of a catalyst such as:
mcqs.why: The notes state that oxygen can be obtained by the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide in the presence of a catalyst such as manganese dioxide: 2H2O2(aq) -> 2H2O(l) + O2(g).

mcqs.q: The test that confirms oxygen is that a glowing wooden splint:
mcqs.why: The notes state that a glowing splint held at the mouth of a test tube of oxygen reignites and burns brightly, because oxygen supports combustion.

mcqs.q: To prepare a glowing splint for the oxygen test, you should:
options: Light a wooden splint, blow it out until it glows, and hold it at the mouth of the test tube
Dip the splint in limewater first

mcqs.why: The notes describe the oxygen test exactly this way: light a wooden splint, blow it out until it glows, and hold the glowing splint at the mouth of the test tube, where it reignites in oxygen.

mcqs.q: Sulphur dioxide gas is identified by using:
options: Damp red litmus paper, which turns blue

mcqs.why: The notes state that sulphur dioxide is identified by the decolourisation of acidified potassium permanganate (KMnO4) solution, as it reacts with the permanganate and sulphuric acid.

mcqs.q: In the sulphur dioxide test, the purple potassium permanganate solution:
mcqs.why: The notes state that in the reaction 5SO2 + 2KMnO4 + 2H2SO4 -> K2SO4 + 2MnSO4 + 2H2O, the purple colour of the solution is lost, so the purple solution becomes colourless and confirms sulphur dioxide.

mcqs.q: Which splint result belongs to hydrogen rather than oxygen?
options: A glowing splint reignites and burns brightly
A burning splint gives a pop sound

mcqs.why: The notes contrast the two splint tests: hydrogen gives a pop sound with a burning wooden splint, while oxygen makes a glowing splint reignite and burn brightly.

mcqs.q: In the sulphur dioxide reaction with acidified potassium permanganate, the products named in the notes include:
options: Potassium sulphate, manganese sulphate and water
mcqs.why: The notes state that sulphur dioxide reacts with potassium permanganate and sulphuric acid to produce potassium sulphate, manganese sulphate and water, with the loss of the solution's purple colour.

lessons.title: Flame Test for Metal Cations
lessons.notes_html:
The flame test identifies specific metal cations in compounds by observing the colours they emit when introduced to a flame.

Procedure

  • A clean loop of nichrome wire is dipped into the sample compound or salt that contains the metal cation.
  • The wire loop with the sample is then held in the flame of a Bunsen burner or a similar heat source.
  • A clean wire is used to avoid contamination, so the flame colour stays pure.

Why Colours Appear

As the metal cation is heated in the flame, it absorbs energy, causing its electrons to become excited. When the excited electrons return to their ground state, they emit light at specific wavelengths, giving characteristic colours of the flame. The observed colour is compared with known standards to identify the cation present.

Metal IonColour of Flame
Lithium (Li+)Crimson red
Sodium (Na+)Intense yellow
Potassium (K+)Lilac (light purple)
Calcium (Ca2+)Orange-red (brick red)
Barium (Ba2+)Pale green (apple green)
Copper (Cu2+)Blue-green (with blue streaks)

Observations should be made under controlled conditions to identify the characteristic flame colours accurately.

Key Points

  • The flame test identifies metal cations by their flame colours.
  • Use a clean nichrome wire loop in a Bunsen flame.
  • Excited electrons emit light at specific wavelengths when they return to the ground state.
  • Sodium = intense yellow; potassium = lilac; lithium = crimson red.

mcqs.q: The flame test is used to identify:
options: Specific metal cations in compounds, by the colours they emit in a flame
Gases from the sounds they make with a splint
Colourless amino acids on a chromatogram
The boiling points of pure liquids
mcqs.why: The notes state that the flame test identifies specific metal cations in compounds by observing the colours they emit when introduced to a flame, and the observed colour is compared with known standards.

mcqs.q: In the flame test, the sample is carried into the flame on:
options: A clean loop of nichrome wire dipped into the sample compound or salt
A wooden splint soaked in the sample
A capillary tube filled with solvent
mcqs.why: The procedure in the notes is to dip a clean loop of nichrome wire into the sample compound or salt containing the metal cation, then hold the wire loop with the sample in the flame of a Bunsen burner.

mcqs.q: A clean wire loop is used in the flame test in order to:
options: Change the colour given by the cation
Avoid contamination, so the flame colour stays pure
mcqs.why: The notes state that a clean wire is used to avoid contamination, so the flame colour stays pure and can be compared accurately with known standards.

mcqs.q: Flame colours appear because, when the metal cation is heated in the flame:
options: It absorbs energy, causing its electrons to become excited
It reacts with the wire to form a coloured compound
Its nucleus splits into smaller parts
The flame itself changes its own colour permanently
mcqs.why: The notes explain that as the metal cation is heated in the flame, it absorbs energy, causing its electrons to become excited; the colours appear when those electrons later return to their ground state.

mcqs.q: The characteristic flame colour is produced when the excited electrons:
options: Return to their ground state and emit light at specific wavelengths
Move into the nucleus of the atom
Gain even more energy from the wire
mcqs.why: The notes state that when the excited electrons return to their ground state, they emit light at specific wavelengths, giving the characteristic colours of the flame used to identify the cation.

mcqs.why: The flame colour table in the notes gives lithium (Li+) as crimson red; sodium is intense yellow, potassium is lilac and barium is pale green.

mcqs.why: The key points in the notes state that sodium gives an intense yellow flame; lithium is crimson red and potassium is lilac.

mcqs.q: Potassium ions, K+, give which flame colour?
mcqs.why: The flame colour table in the notes gives potassium (K+) as lilac (light purple); calcium is orange-red, barium is pale green and sodium is intense yellow.

options: Calcium (Ca2+) orange-red (brick red) and barium (Ba2+) pale green (apple green)

Calcium (Ca2+) pale green and barium (Ba2+) orange-red
mcqs.why: The flame colour table in the notes gives calcium (Ca2+) as orange-red (brick red) and barium (Ba2+) as pale green (apple green), so this is the correctly matched pair.

mcqs.why: The flame colour table in the notes gives copper (Cu2+) as blue-green (with blue streaks); crimson red is lithium, lilac is potassium and intense yellow is sodium.

lessons.title: Paper Chromatography and Locating Agents
lessons.notes_html:
Paper chromatography is a simple and effective technique used to separate and identify the components of a mixture of soluble substances.

Principle

  • The stationary phase is a piece of filter paper, which stays in place.
  • The mobile phase is a liquid solvent, which moves up through the paper.
  • Different substances have different solubilities and affinities for the paper, so they travel at different rates and separate.
  • How far each component is carried depends on its solubility in the solvent and its interaction with the paper.

Procedure

  • Cut a piece of filter paper and draw a baseline near one end.
  • Spot the sample onto the baseline using a capillary tube or micropipette.
  • Pour the solvent (such as water and ethanol) into a container, keeping the solvent level below the spot on the paper.
  • Place the paper in the container with its lower end in the solvent, not touching the sides.
  • As the solvent moves up, it carries and separates the components.
  • When the solvent reaches near the top, remove the paper and let it dry. The result is the chromatogram.

Words to Know

  • Solvent front: the highest point the solvent reaches as it rises up the paper.
  • Baseline (origin): the starting line near the bottom of the paper where the sample is spotted.
  • Chromatogram: the pattern that develops on the paper, showing the separated spots of the components.

Locating Agents

Locating agents make colourless substances visible when separating mixtures. They react with colourless substances to produce coloured or fluorescent products. Examples: iodine vapour reacts with fats and oils, turning them brown; ninhydrin is often used to detect colourless amino acids in paper chromatography.

Key Points

  • Stationary phase = paper; mobile phase = solvent.
  • Components separate because of different solubility and affinity for the paper.
  • Keep the solvent level below the sample spot.
  • Locating agents reveal colourless substances.

mcqs.q: In paper chromatography, the stationary phase is:
options: The liquid solvent that moves up the paper
A piece of filter paper, which stays in place
The sample spot on the baseline
mcqs.why: The notes state that the stationary phase is a piece of filter paper, which stays in place, while the mobile phase is the liquid solvent that moves up through the paper.

mcqs.q: In paper chromatography, the mobile phase is:
options: A liquid solvent, which moves up through the paper
The dried pattern left on the paper
The baseline drawn near one end
mcqs.why: The notes state that the mobile phase is a liquid solvent, which moves up through the paper and carries the components of the mixture with it at different rates.

mcqs.q: Components of a mixture separate in paper chromatography because they have different:
options: Solubilities and affinities for the paper, so they travel at different rates

mcqs.why: The notes state that different substances have different solubilities and affinities for the paper, so they travel at different rates and separate as the solvent moves up.

mcqs.q: The baseline (origin) in paper chromatography is:
options: The highest point the solvent reaches
The starting line near the bottom of the paper where the sample is spotted
The pattern that develops after drying
The line where two solvents meet
mcqs.why: The words to know in the notes define the baseline (origin) as the starting line near the bottom of the paper where the sample is spotted, while the highest point reached by the solvent is the solvent front.

mcqs.q: The sample is spotted onto the baseline using:
mcqs.why: The procedure in the notes states that the sample is spotted onto the baseline using a capillary tube or micropipette, after a baseline is drawn near one end of the filter paper.

mcqs.q: When the paper is placed in the solvent, the solvent level must be kept:
options: Above the spot on the paper
Below the spot on the paper
At the very top of the paper
mcqs.why: The notes state that the solvent, such as water and ethanol, is poured into the container keeping the solvent level below the spot on the paper, so the sample is carried up by the rising solvent rather than dissolving into the bulk solvent.

mcqs.q: The solvent front is:
options: The starting line where the sample is spotted
The highest point the solvent reaches as it rises up the paper
The coloured spot left by a component
mcqs.why: The words to know in the notes define the solvent front as the highest point the solvent reaches as it rises up the paper; distances for Rf values are measured from the baseline to this front.

mcqs.q: The pattern that develops on the paper, showing the separated spots of the components, is called the:
mcqs.why: The notes define the chromatogram as the pattern that develops on the paper, showing the separated spots of the components, after the paper is removed when the solvent reaches near the top and is left to dry.

mcqs.q: Locating agents are used in chromatography to:
options: Make colourless substances visible, by reacting with them to produce coloured or fluorescent products
Make the solvent rise faster up the paper
