mcqs.why: The notes state that locating agents make colourless substances visible when separating mixtures, because they react with colourless substances to produce coloured or fluorescent products.

mcqs.q: Which locating agent example is given in the notes?
options: Limewater turning milky with a gas
Ninhydrin, often used to detect colourless amino acids in paper chromatography
Acidified permanganate losing its purple colour
mcqs.why: The notes give ninhydrin as a locating agent often used to detect colourless amino acids in paper chromatography, and also give iodine vapour, which reacts with fats and oils and turns them brown.

lessons.title: Chromatogram Analysis and the Rf Value
lessons.notes_html:
A chromatogram shows spots that represent individual components. These spots tell us which substances are present and whether the sample is pure or a mixture. To analyse it, measure the distance each spot travels from the baseline and calculate the Rf value (retention or retardation factor).

Identifying Unknown Substances

  • Compare the chromatogram of the unknown sample with those of known substances.
  • If a spot from the unknown appears at the same height and has the same colour as a spot from a known substance, they are likely the same.
  • If the spot is at a different position or looks different, it is probably a different substance.

Checking Purity

  • A pure substance produces only one spot on the chromatogram, showing it contains just one component.
  • An impure substance gives two or more spots, showing it is a mixture of substances.

The Rf Value

Rf = distance travelled by component from baseline / distance travelled by solvent front from baseline

  • Each substance has its own Rf value when the same solvent and paper are used.
  • Calculate the Rf value of an unknown and compare it with known values to suggest what the unknown might be.
  • If the Rf values match, the substances could be the same, though it is not always certain because minor differences can occur.
  • Example from the exercise: a component travels 6 cm and the solvent front travels 8 cm, so Rf = 6 / 8 = 0.75. Rf has no units and lies between 0 and 1.

Key Points

  • Match spot height and colour with known substances to identify an unknown.
  • One spot = pure substance; two or more spots = mixture.
  • Rf = distance of component / distance of solvent front, both from the baseline.
  • Rf values help identify substances in chromatography.

mcqs.q: The Rf value in paper chromatography is calculated as:
options: Distance travelled by the solvent front divided by distance travelled by the component
Distance travelled by the component from the baseline divided by distance travelled by the solvent front from the baseline
Distance travelled by the component multiplied by distance travelled by the solvent front
Distance travelled by the solvent front minus distance travelled by the component
mcqs.why: The notes give Rf = distance travelled by component from baseline / distance travelled by solvent front from baseline, with both distances measured from the baseline.

mcqs.q: A component travels 6 cm from the baseline and the solvent front travels 8 cm from the baseline. Its Rf value is:
mcqs.why: Working: Rf = distance travelled by component / distance travelled by solvent front = 6 cm / 8 cm = 0.75. This is the example given in the notes, and Rf has no units.

mcqs.q: Which statement about Rf values is correct?
options: Rf can be any number greater than 1
Rf has no units and lies between 0 and 1
Rf is the same for every substance in any solvent
mcqs.why: The notes state that Rf has no units and lies between 0 and 1, and that each substance has its own Rf value when the same solvent and paper are used.

mcqs.q: A pure substance on a chromatogram produces:
options: Only one spot, showing it contains just one component
A spot exactly at the solvent front in every case
mcqs.why: The notes state that a pure substance produces only one spot on the chromatogram, showing it contains just one component, while an impure substance gives two or more spots.

mcqs.q: A sample that gives two or more spots on its chromatogram is:
options: A pure substance with one component
An impure substance, showing it is a mixture of substances
A substance with an Rf value greater than 1
mcqs.why: The notes state that an impure substance gives two or more spots, showing it is a mixture of substances, whereas a pure substance produces only one spot.

mcqs.q: An unknown substance is likely to be the same as a known substance when its spot:
options: Appears at a different height and has a different colour
Is the only spot on the paper
Appears at the same height and has the same colour as the spot from the known substance
Travels further than the solvent front
mcqs.why: The notes state that if a spot from the unknown appears at the same height and has the same colour as a spot from a known substance, they are likely the same; a different position or appearance means it is probably a different substance.

mcqs.q: A component travels 4 cm from the baseline and the solvent front travels 8 cm from the baseline. Its Rf value is:
mcqs.why: Working: Rf = distance travelled by component / distance travelled by solvent front = 4 cm / 8 cm = 0.5. The value has no units and lies between 0 and 1, as the notes require.

mcqs.q: A component travels 3 cm from the baseline and the solvent front travels 10 cm from the baseline. Its Rf value is:
mcqs.why: Working: Rf = distance travelled by component / distance travelled by solvent front = 3 cm / 10 cm = 0.3. The value has no units and lies between 0 and 1.

mcqs.q: A component travels 2 cm from the baseline and the solvent front travels 5 cm from the baseline. Its Rf value is:
mcqs.why: Working: Rf = distance travelled by component / distance travelled by solvent front = 2 cm / 5 cm = 0.4. The value has no units and lies between 0 and 1.

mcqs.q: If the Rf value of an unknown matches the Rf value of a known substance, the notes say this means:
options: The substances are certainly identical in every case
The substances could be the same, though it is not always certain because minor differences can occur
The unknown must be a pure substance
The chromatogram must be repeated with a flame test
mcqs.why: The notes state that the Rf value of an unknown is compared with known values to suggest what the unknown might be, and if the Rf values match the substances could be the same, though it is not always certain because minor differences can occur.
